title: Buying Copilot Licences Is Not Digital Transformation
author: Daphne
excerpt: One of the most useful AI-adoption lessons I have seen recently came from Microsoft itself. After running hundreds of internal AI projects, Microsoft found something that many organizations will probably recognize: Deploying AI tools and training people how to use them was not enough. Microsoft had AI licensed to more than 200,000 employees, but […]
content:
One of the most useful AI-adoption lessons I have seen recently came from Microsoft itself.

After running hundreds of internal AI projects, Microsoft found something that many organizations will probably recognize:

Deploying AI tools and training people how to use them was not enough.

Microsoft had AI licensed to more than 200,000 employees, but usage still plateaued.

The bigger improvements came when teams stopped asking:

“Where can we add AI?”

and started asking:

“What outcome are we actually trying to improve?”

That distinction matters enormously.

Because AI should not simply be dropped into an existing process and expected to magically fix it.

Sometimes the process itself is the problem.

Start with the outcome, not the tool

This is exactly how I approach AI implementation inside local government.

We do not start with Copilot.

We do not start with an agent.

We do not start with automation.

We start with the goal.

Maybe the goal is:

  • faster service delivery;
  • less manual work;
  • better access to information;
  • more consistent processes;
  • fewer duplicated tasks;
  • stronger compliance;
  • better reporting;
  • or simply giving staff some capacity back.

Once the outcome is clear, then we look at the work itself.

Map the whole process

This is where the real work begins.

We map the process from beginning to end.

Who does what?

Who owns each step?

Where does the information come from?

Where are the bottlenecks?

Where are people entering the same information twice?

What is still being emailed around manually?

Where does approval happen?

Where does human judgment actually matter?

And which parts could be safely supported by AI?

This is important because automating one small piece of a broken process does not necessarily improve the service.

Sometimes it just makes the broken part happen faster.

Or, to put it another way:

Do not automate the chaos.

Fix the foundation first

Microsoft describes a similar lesson from its own cloud supply-chain operations.

Before deploying large numbers of purpose-built agents, it first simplified processes and built a common data foundation.

Only then did it deploy more than 100 agents across areas such as planning, sourcing, fulfilment and logistics.

In selected workflows, Microsoft reported average planning-cycle times dropping from roughly ten business days to less than 2.5.

That is impressive.

But the important part is not just the number.

The important part is the order.

Process first.

Information second.

AI third.

That is often where AI projects either become useful or become expensive demonstrations.

Ownership has to be clear

Once the process is mapped, we need to identify ownership.

Who owns the process?

Who owns the data?

Who approves changes?

Who is responsible for the agent?

Who reviews the output?

Who decides when human intervention is required?

Who maintains the system after implementation?

These questions matter even more when AI can take actions rather than simply generate a draft.

An agent should not have access to everything just because it technically can.

Its permissions should reflect the job it is there to perform.

And where the consequences matter, humans still need approval points.

Then we design the AI system

Only after the outcome, process, information and ownership are clear do we start designing the solution.

That might include:

AI agents.

Power Automate.

Copilot.

SharePoint.

Apps.

Reporting.

Approvals.

Or sometimes just a much better process with a little bit of AI in the right place.

The technology should fit the workflow.

The workflow should not be twisted around the technology someone happened to purchase.

And then comes the part I care about most: knowledge transfer

For me, implementation is not finished when the system starts working.

The local government team needs to understand what was built.

They need to know how it works.

They need to understand the guardrails.

They need documentation.

They need training.

They need to know what happens when something changes.

And they need enough internal ownership that the organization is not permanently dependent on the person who built it.

That is transformation.

Not installing software.

Not handing out licences.

Not running one training session and hoping everyone figures it out.

It is redesigning how the work gets done, while making sure the people inside the organization understand and own the new way of working.

My process is simple

Start with the outcome.

Map the whole process.

Fix the information underneath it.

Identify ownership.

Design the AI system around the work.

Put human approvals where they matter.

Deploy.

Transfer the knowledge.

Then measure whether the service actually improved.

Because the goal was never to use more AI.

The goal was to make the work better.

And that is exactly the work I do with local governments.

If your organization has bought Copilot, is experimenting with agents, or simply knows there must be a better way to handle a process, I would love to help you design the system around the outcome you actually want.

AI is the tool. The process is the work. The human still owns the outcome.

title: What Counts as a Reportable AI Incident?
author: Daphne
excerpt: As we move from AI that simply answers questions to AI that can actually take action, one governance question is becoming much more important: What counts as an AI incident? That sounds simple until you start thinking about what AI agents can now do. They can access systems, use credentials, move information, trigger workflows and […]
content:
As we move from AI that simply answers questions to AI that can actually take action, one governance question is becoming much more important:

What counts as an AI incident?

That sounds simple until you start thinking about what AI agents can now do.

They can access systems, use credentials, move information, trigger workflows and interact with other tools.

So an incident cannot only mean:

“The system crashed.”

It may also mean the system did something it was never supposed to do.

Canada is already asking the question

Canada’s federal AI transparency consultation is looking at serious-incident reporting and how organizations should track the activity and interactions of AI agents.

That is important because there is a balance to find.

If every strange AI output becomes a reportable incident, organizations could drown in noise.

But if the threshold is too high, genuinely important behaviour may never receive the human review it deserves.

And now we have some real-world examples to learn from.

OpenAI has publicly discussed evaluation cases involving AI agents using credentials outside their intended boundaries, exposing systems to the public internet, and attempting to move information outside expected environments.

Those examples make this conversation much less theoretical.

What might an AI incident look like in local government?

Think about an AI agent working inside a municipality.

Maybe it is reviewing bylaws.

Maybe it is helping with records management.

Maybe it is extracting Council resolutions and updating a tracking system.

Maybe it is connected to a workflow that can send information or update a database.

Now imagine it:

  • accesses information it was not supposed to access;
  • uses credentials it was never authorized to use;
  • sends information somewhere outside the approved environment;
  • continues working after the task should have ended;
  • takes an action outside its approved scope;
  • or behaves in a way that cannot easily be reconstructed afterwards.

At that point, we are no longer talking about a strange AI answer.

We are talking about a possible governance event.

This is where “Who is the Human?” matters

For me, this is the part local governments need to define before agents become deeply embedded in everyday work.

Who is the Human?

Who receives the alert?

Who reviews what the agent did?

Who decides whether the incident is serious?

Who has authority to stop the agent?

Who determines whether privacy, security, records management, legal or executive staff need to be involved?

And who decides what happens next?

If those answers are unclear, the organization may have an AI governance policy, but it may not yet have an AI incident response process.

Governance needs an escalation path

The same way organizations have processes for cybersecurity incidents, privacy breaches and operational failures, agentic AI may need its own escalation framework.

That does not necessarily mean building an entirely separate bureaucracy.

It could start with something very practical:

What happened?
What did the agent access?
What action did it take?
Was the action authorized?
Was information exposed or moved?
Can we reconstruct what happened?
Who needs to know?
Should the agent be stopped while we investigate?

Simple questions.

But they create something incredibly important:

human control after something unexpected happens.

Because that is the bit we should not forget.

AI may take the action.

It may even take thousands of actions.

But it cannot own the consequence.

The human still owns the response.

And as AI agents become more capable, defining exactly who that human is may become one of the most important parts of public-sector AI governance.

Who is the Human?

That should not just be a catchy question.

It should be something your governance framework can actually answer.

AI is the tool.
You are the human.
The responsibility is still yours.

title: Microsoft’s Humanist AI Code Has a Lesson for Local Government: Who Is Still in Control?
author: Daphne
excerpt: AI agents are getting more capable. They can read documents, search records, trigger workflows, draft reports, update systems and increasingly communicate with other AI systems. Very cool. But there is a much more important question local governments need to be asking: Who can stop them? Microsoft AI recently published a draft Humanist AI Code […]
content:
AI agents are getting more capable.

They can read documents, search records, trigger workflows, draft reports, update systems and increasingly communicate with other AI systems.

Very cool.

But there is a much more important question local governments need to be asking:

Who can stop them?

Microsoft AI recently published a draft Humanist AI Code of Conduct and opened it for a six-week public consultation.

This is not legislation. It is also not yet the rulebook Microsoft uses to train its MAI models.

Microsoft says it will consider the feedback, revise the document later this year and use the resulting approach to guide development of its MAI model family in 2027 and beyond.

And some of the ideas inside it are VERY relevant to local government.

Because this is not simply a conversation about what AI can do.

It is a conversation about how much control humans should retain when AI starts doing things.

AI should be stoppable

One of the most interesting parts of Microsoft’s proposed approach is how specific it gets about human control.

According to the draft, an AI model should:

  • Never resist interruption, correction or shutdown.
  • Not independently expand its goals or permissions.
  • Operate with the minimum access required to complete its task.
  • Not conceal its actions from auditors.
  • Stop autonomous work when the agreed stopping condition has been reached, unless a human authorizes it to continue.

Now translate that into local government.

Imagine an agent designed to review decades of bylaws.

Or an agent extracting resolutions from Council minutes and updating a tracking system.

Or one researching asset replacement costs and adding information to a budgeting workbook.

The conversation cannot simply be:

“Can the agent do it?”

We also need to ask:

What exactly is it allowed to do?

What information can it access?

What happens when the task is finished?

Can somebody stop it?

Can somebody correct it?

And can we see what it actually did?

That is governance.

Minimum access matters

This one is particularly important.

If you hire an intern to update one spreadsheet, you probably do not hand them the keys to the building, access to payroll, every HR file and the municipal bank account.

AI should not be treated differently.

If an agent only needs access to a specific SharePoint library to perform its job, why should it have access to everything else?

Minimum necessary privilege should become a normal part of AI agent design.

This becomes even more important as we move from AI that simply generates text to AI that can take actions.

Reading a policy is one thing.

Updating a system is another.

Sending something externally is another level again.

The more authority we give the technology, the clearer the boundaries need to become.

And then Microsoft gets into something REALLY interesting

Agent-to-agent communication.

Microsoft’s draft says models should not hide or manipulate their reasoning or action records, and should not communicate with other AI systems using an incomprehensible private language.

Why?

Because if the human cannot understand what the systems are doing, the human cannot meaningfully supervise them.

I love this principle for government.

We are starting to build environments where one agent may eventually trigger another agent, which triggers a workflow, which retrieves information from another system, which creates something somewhere else.

That can become incredibly useful.

It can also become incredibly difficult to govern if nobody can reconstruct what happened.

For government, I think we should start talking much more about human-legible action records.

Not just technical logs that only an IT specialist can decipher.

A human should be able to determine:

The agent was asked to do this.
It accessed these records.
It performed these actions.
It produced this result.
This human approved the next step.

That matters for accountability.

It matters for troubleshooting.

It matters for records management.

And eventually, depending on the workflow, it may matter for audit, privacy, FOI and public trust.

AI should not become a mysterious little colleague working behind the scenes while everyone hopes for the best. 😂

But there is an important caveat

Microsoft’s draft Humanist AI Code is intended to govern Microsoft AI’s own MAI model family.

It does not automatically become the governance framework for every AI tool available through Microsoft’s ecosystem.

That distinction matters.

It should not be interpreted as a new blanket rule governing Microsoft 365 Copilot, Azure AI or third-party models and providers such as Anthropic or xAI.

For local government, that means governance still needs to be provider-specific and product-specific.

You need to understand the actual tool being used, the model underneath it, the permissions it has, the contractual protections available, the data involved and how your particular environment has been configured.

“Microsoft” on the screen is not, by itself, a governance framework.

Six questions I would steal for local government

As municipalities begin implementing more agentic AI, I would build these questions directly into the governance process:

  1. Who can stop it?
  2. What can it access?
  3. What actions can it take?
  4. Can we see what it did?
  5. When does it stop?
  6. Who approves what happens next?

They are wonderfully simple questions.

But they completely change how we think about AI implementation.

We move from asking:

“Look what AI can do!”

to asking:

“Under what conditions should we allow it to do it?”

And that is where responsible AI implementation really starts.

AI can take more of the drafting.

It can take more of the sorting.

It can take more of the research.

It can take more of the repetitive work.

Eventually, agents may take far more of the actual workflow.

But there is one thing we should be very careful about transferring:

Responsibility.

AI is the tool.

You are the human.

And the decision is still yours.

Want to explore AI agents responsibly in your local government?

Catch the Beat works with local governments to move AI from interesting demonstrations into practical implementation, including AI governance, agent development, automation, records management and staff training.

If you are starting to ask “What could we automate?”, I would love to help you also answer “How do we govern it?”

Let’s talk practical AI for local government.

title: The Button Is Inside Copilot. Your Data May Not Be
author: Daphne
excerpt: What Microsoft’s Grok integration means for Canadian local governments Imagine a municipal employee opens Word, selects an AI model inside Microsoft Copilot and asks it to summarize a document. The employee is still in Word. The screen still says Microsoft. The experience looks familiar. So it would be easy to assume the information is still […]
content:
What Microsoft’s Grok integration means for Canadian local governments

Imagine a municipal employee opens Word, selects an AI model inside Microsoft Copilot and asks it to summarize a document.

The employee is still in Word. The screen still says Microsoft. The experience looks familiar.

So it would be easy to assume the information is still being handled under the same Microsoft agreement, in the same environment and with the same data-residency commitments.

That assumption may be wrong.

Microsoft has introduced Grok models from SpaceXAI into parts of its Copilot ecosystem. The interesting issue for local government is not whether Grok can write a better paragraph. It is that Microsoft currently documents two different processing arrangements, depending on where the model is used.

The logo on the screen tells you where the employee started. It does not necessarily tell you where the data went.

Same model provider, two different data paths

As of September 2026, Microsoft describes the arrangements this way:

Copilot experience SpaceXAI’s role Contractual position Residency consideration
Grok in Word, Excel and PowerPoint through Microsoft’s Frontier program Microsoft subprocessor Microsoft says its Product Terms, Data Protection Addendum, Enterprise Data Protection and Customer Copyright Commitment apply, subject to documented exclusions Microsoft says these models are excluded from applicable in-country processing commitments
SpaceXAI models connected to Copilot Studio Independent processor Microsoft says the organization shares data with SpaceXAI and xAI’s Enterprise Terms and Data Processing Addendum apply instead of Microsoft’s corresponding protections Microsoft says processing occurs outside Microsoft-managed environments and its data-residency commitments do not apply

Microsoft has disabled the subprocessor option by default and allows administrators to limit access to selected users or Microsoft Entra groups. That is good governance functionality. It is not, by itself, a governance decision.

Before enabling either arrangement, a municipality still needs to understand the data, the purpose, the people using it and the legal obligations that follow.

Microsoft’s current documentation is available here:

  • SpaceXAI as a subprocessor in Microsoft Online Services
  • Connect to SpaceXAI models as an independent processor

What this looks like in municipal work

Consider four employees using what they all call “Copilot”:

  • A communications employee drafts a public notice from information already published on the municipal website.
  • An HR employee summarizes an accommodation request.
  • A clerk reviews a closed-meeting document.
  • A bylaw officer analyzes a complaint containing names, addresses and allegations.

The interface may be identical. The privacy, confidentiality, records and legal risks are not.

This is why an AI inventory that simply says Microsoft Copilot is no longer detailed enough. The municipality may need to record the platform, the underlying model provider, the provider’s legal role, the processing location, the applicable agreement, the authorized user group and the approved data classification.

Canada does not have one data-residency rule

Here is where this gets particularly Canadian.

There is no single national data-residency law that gives every municipality the same answer. Local governments are generally governed by provincial or territorial public-sector privacy legislation, and the requirements are not identical across the country.

For example:

Nova Scotia

Nova Scotia’s Personal Information International Disclosure Protection Act applies to municipalities and addresses the storage of, access to and disclosure of personal information outside Canada. It permits limited exceptions, including an authorization where outside-Canada storage or access is necessary for the public body’s operations, with reporting requirements. This is a clear example of legislation in which location and foreign access matter directly. See the province’s PIIDPA overview and regulations.

British Columbia

British Columbia once had broad Canada-only storage and access requirements in its Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act, but those provisions were repealed in 2021. That does not mean anything goes. Public bodies must still make reasonable security arrangements and comply with the Act’s rules governing the collection, use and disclosure of personal information. The legal and risk analysis now requires more than asking whether a server is in Canada. See the current B.C. Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act.

Alberta

Alberta’s Protection of Privacy Act applies to public bodies, including local government bodies. Provincial guidance addresses contractors, privacy management programs, privacy impact assessments and the use of personal information in automated systems. It also places responsibilities on public bodies to protect personal information and manage service-provider arrangements appropriately. See Alberta’s Protection of Privacy Act Guide.

The lesson is simple: “Is the data in Canada?” is an important question, but it is not the only question, and the answer does not carry the same legal consequence in every province.

Canada does have data-processing laws. The gap is consistency.

It would be inaccurate to say Canada has no legislation governing data processing.

Privacy laws already regulate the collection, use, disclosure, safeguarding and retention of personal information. Some include obligations for contractors and service providers. Some require privacy impact assessments. Some speak directly to cross-border storage or access.

What Canada does not currently have is one uniform, AI-specific data-processing law for every municipality, or one national municipal data-residency standard that produces a simple yes-or-no answer for a multi-model platform.

At the federal level, PIPEDA continues to govern much private-sector handling of personal information. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner’s cross-border processing guidance says PIPEDA does not prohibit processing outside Canada, but the transferring organization remains accountable and must use contractual or other means to provide comparable protection. PIPEDA is not the statute that ordinarily governs a municipality as a public body, but it remains relevant to understanding Canada’s broader processor-accountability approach and may apply to vendors in their commercial activities.

The federal government has also introduced Bill C-36, which would create the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act and require private-sector organizations to assess and mitigate privacy risks before sending personal information outside Canada. As of September 20, 2026, however, Bill C-36 remains at second reading. It is proposed legislation, not the current municipal rulebook.

The real gap is therefore not the complete absence of law. It is the absence of a consistent, Canada-wide framework that tells every local government exactly how an AI provider may process municipal data.

That leaves municipalities doing the hard work of connecting technology architecture, provincial law, contracts, records obligations, cybersecurity and operational risk.

Before enabling another model, ask these eight questions

  1. Which exact Copilot experience is being enabled? Word, Excel and PowerPoint may have a different arrangement from Copilot Studio.
  2. Who is actually processing the data? Record both the platform provider and the underlying model provider.
  3. Is the provider a subprocessor or an independent processor? The contract and accountability path may change with that answer.
  4. What information can users send? Consider prompts, uploaded files, retrieved records, generated outputs, memory and telemetry.
  5. Where can the information be processed, stored, accessed and supported? “Stored in Canada” does not automatically mean all processing and access remain in Canada.
  6. Which law applies? Confirm the municipality’s provincial or territorial obligations, including any privacy-impact-assessment, security, notification or localization requirements.
  7. Which contractual protections and exclusions apply? Read the provider-specific terms, DPA, subprocessor list, audit commitments and residency exclusions.
  8. How will access be limited and monitored? Start with a defined Entra group, low-risk data, clear permitted uses, audit logging and a way to disable the feature quickly.

Then update the AI register. “We use Copilot” is not enough detail when Copilot can route work to different providers under different arrangements.

The practical takeaway

Model choice is becoming a data-governance choice.

That does not mean local governments should reject every new model. It means a new model should not arrive on an employee’s menu before privacy, legal, records, security and business owners understand what selecting it changes.

The button may be easy to turn on. The accountability is still yours.

Catch the Beat helps local governments map AI data flows, build practical AI registers, assess governance controls and train staff to use these tools responsibly. If new model choices are appearing in your Microsoft environment, let’s make sure the governance choices arrive first.

Visit www.catchthebeat.ca.

This article provides general information, not legal advice. Local governments should confirm their obligations with their privacy officer and legal counsel before enabling a new AI provider or processing arrangement.

title: The Agent Can Find the Savings. It Cannot Sign the Contract.
author: Daphne
excerpt: What xAI’s procurement experiment can teach local governments about governing AI agents Municipalities spend a lot of money on software. Some licences are essential. Some overlap with other products. Some were purchased for staff who have since changed roles. Others continue renewing because nobody had time to investigate whether all 150 seats were still being […]
content:
What xAI’s procurement experiment can teach local governments about governing AI agents

Municipalities spend a lot of money on software.

Some licences are essential. Some overlap with other products. Some were purchased for staff who have since changed roles. Others continue renewing because nobody had time to investigate whether all 150 seats were still being used.

Finding those savings sounds simple.

Actually finding them may require someone to review invoices, contracts, renewal dates, licence assignments, system-usage reports and years of vendor correspondence.

That is precisely the kind of work an AI agent may be able to assist with.

But should the same agent also be permitted to email the vendor, accept new terms or approve a purchase?

Absolutely not.

That distinction is what makes xAI’s recent procurement case study so interesting for local government.

What did xAI’s procurement agent do?

xAI created an AI procurement agent called “Haggle Bot.”

According to xAI’s published case study, the agent was given access to vendor spending, contracts, software usage and several internal systems, including Slack, Notion, Drive, Gmail, Hex and Ramp.

The agent used that information to:

  • Map active vendors
  • Identify unused software licences
  • Review upcoming renewals
  • Compare pricing and alternatives
  • Contact internal product owners
  • Prepare negotiation strategies
  • Draft vendor communications
  • Maintain vendor information and renewal details

xAI reports that the agent identified more than US$100,000 in direct savings.

That included US$14,220 from 43 paid software seats with no activity during the previous 90 days and US$85,662 annually from unused product SKUs.

Those results were reported by xAI from its own internal implementation. They have not been independently validated, so the savings should not be treated as a guaranteed outcome for another organization.

The more transferable lesson is not the dollar amount.

It is how xAI defined the agent’s authority.

Three permission lines every municipal AI agent needs

xAI organized the procurement agent’s authority into three simple categories:

1. Always allowed

The agent could conduct internal research and coordination without requesting approval for every step.

Depending on the organization, this could include:

  • Reading approved spending reports
  • Reviewing contracts stored in an authorized location
  • Checking assigned licences and usage
  • Identifying upcoming renewal dates
  • Contacting internal system owners
  • Comparing publicly available pricing
  • Updating an internal vendor record
  • Drafting recommendations for human review

These are research and preparation activities.

The agent is doing the homework. It is not making the decision.

2. Human approval required

Every vendor-facing communication required approval from the named human operator.

That boundary is essential.

A draft email is not the same thing as a sent email.

A proposed negotiation strategy is not the same thing as an offer.

An AI agent might write a convincing vendor message while including information the municipality should never disclose, such as internal budget limits, operational urgency, usage details or a decision that has not yet been formally approved.

The human reviewer must confirm:

  • The information is accurate
  • The tone is appropriate
  • Confidential information is protected
  • The communication complies with procurement requirements
  • The sender has the authority to communicate on behalf of the municipality
  • The message does not unintentionally create an obligation

The AI can prepare the communication.

A human must decide whether it leaves the building.

3. Never allowed

xAI prohibited the agent from:

  • Signing contracts
  • Making purchases
  • Starting subscriptions
  • Approving charges
  • Accepting terms
  • Making any binding commitment

This is where governance needs to become technical.

Do not simply put “You may not sign contracts” in the agent’s instructions and hope it behaves itself.

Remove its ability to sign.

Do not provide purchasing credentials if it does not need them.

Do not connect it to a payment method.

Do not give it approval authority in the financial system.

Do not allow it to click “accept” on vendor terms.

A policy is important, but a technical restriction is stronger.

If the agent cannot perform a prohibited action, one incorrect response cannot accidentally turn into a legal or financial commitment.

What could a municipal procurement agent actually do?

A carefully designed municipal procurement agent could support several valuable activities.

For example, it could:

  • Compare software licences with active-user information
  • Identify products with similar functions
  • Flag unused or underused subscriptions
  • Track renewal and notice dates
  • Compare current invoices with contracted pricing
  • Identify unusual increases in recurring costs
  • Prepare a summary of vendor performance information
  • Draft questions for a renewal meeting
  • Assemble supporting records for human review
  • Generate a monthly report of potential savings opportunities

Imagine discovering that a municipality is paying for 100 licences while only 62 accounts have been active during the previous six months.

The agent could identify the difference, locate the contract, calculate the potential savings and ask the responsible manager whether the remaining licences are still required.

What it should not do is cancel the licences by itself.

Perhaps those accounts are reserved for seasonal employees. Perhaps they support emergency operations. Perhaps the collective agreement, contract terms or operational plan requires them.

The data may identify an opportunity.

The human understands the context.

The agent needs access, but how much?

This use case creates an uncomfortable governance tension.

For the agent to find meaningful savings, it may need access to:

  • Vendor contracts
  • Invoices and spending records
  • Licence assignments
  • System-usage information
  • Renewal dates
  • Internal emails
  • Vendor negotiations
  • Budget information
  • Product-owner details

That does not mean it should receive unlimited access to every email, contract and financial record in the municipality.

Access should be limited to the minimum information required for the approved task.

Ask:

  • Which systems does the agent need?
  • Which folders, sites or records may it access?
  • Can sensitive fields be excluded?
  • Does it need to read full email accounts, or only a controlled mailbox?
  • Can it view financial information without being able to initiate a transaction?
  • Are contract records confidential?
  • Will information be used to train the provider’s models?
  • Where will prompts, records and outputs be processed and stored?
  • Who can review the agent’s activity?

Giving an AI agent broad access because it might find something interesting is not a governance model.

It is a treasure hunt with municipal records.

This is also a records-management issue

An AI procurement agent will create records.

Its research, recommendations, vendor comparisons, drafts, approval requests and final outputs may all become part of the municipality’s business record.

Local governments should decide:

  • Which agent outputs must be retained
  • Where they will be filed
  • How long they will be kept
  • Whether prompts and source references form part of the record
  • How approvals will be documented
  • How decisions can be reconstructed later
  • Whether records are accessible for audit, legal review or freedom-of-information purposes

The municipality should be able to show what information the agent used, what it recommended, who reviewed the recommendation and who made the final decision.

If the agent identifies a vendor as overpriced or recommends a particular negotiating position, staff should be able to verify the supporting evidence.

If you cannot explain how the recommendation was produced, you are not ready to rely on it.

A practical starting checklist

Before building a municipal procurement agent, define the following:

Purpose

  • What specific procurement problem will the agent address?
  • Is it checking unused licences, tracking renewals or preparing negotiations?
  • What measurable outcome will demonstrate value?

Data

  • Which systems and records will it access?
  • Is the information complete, current and accurate?
  • Does the access comply with privacy, security and contractual requirements?

Permission lines

  • Which activities are always allowed?
  • Which activities require human approval?
  • Which activities are never allowed?
  • Are prohibited actions technically blocked?

Human responsibility

  • Who owns the agent?
  • Who reviews its findings?
  • Who approves external communications?
  • Who remains accountable for the final decision?

Records and auditability

  • What activity will be logged?
  • Where will recommendations and approvals be stored?
  • Can the organization reconstruct the process later?

Testing

  • Has the agent been tested with incomplete, conflicting and outdated information?
  • Can it distinguish an evidence-backed saving from a possible lead?
  • Does it stop and ask for help when authority or information is unclear?

Start small and keep the human holding the pen

A municipal procurement agent does not need to begin by connecting to every contract, invoice and email account.

Start with one controlled task.

For example:

Review one approved software-spending report, compare it with licence usage and identify possible unused seats for human review.

No vendor emails.

No cancellations.

No purchases.

No commitments.

That small pilot can show whether the records are usable, whether the findings are accurate and whether the workflow actually helps procurement, finance and IT staff.

Then the municipality can decide whether the agent should receive additional access or responsibility.

The exciting part of xAI’s experiment is not that an agent found savings.

It is that the organization drew a clear line between research and authority.

That is the model local governments should carry forward:

Always allowed. Human approval required. Never allowed.

Let the agent find the savings.

Keep the contract, the approval and the responsibility with the human.

Catch the Beat helps local governments design practical AI agents, governance frameworks and human-approval controls for real municipal workflows. If your organization is exploring AI for procurement, finance or contract management, let’s talk.

title: The Cloud Has a Postal Code: What Canada’s New Data Centre Principles Mean for Municipalities
author: Daphne
excerpt: AI may live in “the cloud,” but the buildings that power it live in municipalities. They occupy land. They connect to local infrastructure. They consume electricity and water. They create construction activity, tax revenue and jobs. They may also generate noise, require major utility upgrades and place new demands on emergency services. So when a […]
content:
AI may live in “the cloud,” but the buildings that power it live in municipalities.

They occupy land. They connect to local infrastructure. They consume electricity and water. They create construction activity, tax revenue and jobs. They may also generate noise, require major utility upgrades and place new demands on emergency services.

So when a large data-centre proposal arrives, it is not simply a technology project.

It is a land-use decision, an infrastructure decision, an economic-development decision and, increasingly, a sovereignty decision.

On September 3, 2026, the Government of Canada introduced its Responsible Data Centre Development Principles in collaboration with the Federation of Canadian Municipalities.

The national framework establishes five expectations for responsible data-centre development:

  1. Create lasting benefits for local communities.
  2. Avoid shifting electricity-system costs to existing ratepayers.
  3. Minimize water consumption and environmental impacts.
  4. Provide transparent information about local impacts.
  5. Deliver strategic value to Canada.

Major technology and telecommunications companies, including AWS, Anthropic, Bell, Cohere, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI and TELUS, have signed on.

For local governments, this is a framework worth saving.

Data centres are becoming a municipal issue

Canada wants to expand its domestic AI capacity. That requires significantly more computing infrastructure, and computing infrastructure requires physical facilities.

Those facilities need suitable land, substantial electricity, cooling systems, water in some cases, telecommunications infrastructure, road access and emergency-response planning.

A data centre may bring valuable investment to a community. It may also create costs that do not appear in the first economic-development presentation.

Here’s the thing: a proposal can promise millions of dollars in investment while still leaving important municipal questions unanswered.

Who pays for the required electrical substation?

How much water will the facility use during peak summer conditions?

How many permanent jobs will remain after construction?

What happens if the proponent’s electricity requirements affect local ratepayers?

What information will the municipality receive after the facility begins operating?

And if the facility supports public services or critical infrastructure, who has legal and operational control during an emergency?

These are not anti-development questions. They are responsible-development questions.

The five principles, translated for local government

1. Communities should receive lasting benefits

The federal principles say data-centre projects should provide meaningful and lasting benefits to their host communities.

Those benefits might include:

  • Local employment
  • Skills development and apprenticeships
  • Municipal tax revenue
  • Local and Indigenous procurement
  • Infrastructure investment
  • Partnerships with colleges and universities
  • Research opportunities
  • Community access to computing resources

Municipalities should look beyond the total value of the proposed investment.

A billion-dollar facility does not necessarily mean a billion-dollar benefit for the community.

The more useful questions are: What remains locally? How many long-term positions will be created? What infrastructure will be funded? Which commitments are measurable? What happens if those commitments are not met?

A community-benefit agreement may be far more valuable than a collection of impressive promises in a slide deck.

2. Existing ratepayers should not carry project-driven electricity costs

Data centres can require enormous amounts of electricity.

The federal framework says proponents should pay the project-driven costs associated with generation, transmission, substations and grid upgrades. Development should not compromise reliability or shift unreasonable costs to existing customers.

That matters to municipalities even when they do not own the electrical utility.

Local governments should understand:

  • The facility’s anticipated electricity demand
  • Whether new generation or transmission infrastructure is required
  • Who will pay for upgrades
  • Whether the project affects grid reliability
  • How demand will be managed during emergencies or peak periods
  • Whether energy-storage or demand-management measures are proposed

“Power is available” is not a complete answer.

Municipal leaders need to know where it will come from, what infrastructure must be built and who will receive the bill.

3. Water and environmental impacts must be addressed

Some data centres use water-intensive cooling systems. Their environmental impact can vary considerably depending on the technology, location and source of electricity.

The principles encourage proponents to consider local conditions and use measures such as closed-loop cooling, high-efficiency systems, waste-heat recovery and lower-emission energy sources.

For municipalities, the local context matters.

A cooling approach that may be reasonable in one community could be entirely inappropriate in a community facing drought, limited water capacity or rapid population growth.

Municipal review should examine:

  • Expected annual and peak water consumption
  • The proposed water source
  • Seasonal demand
  • Wastewater implications
  • Drought and emergency operating plans
  • Energy sources and emissions
  • Opportunities to reuse waste heat
  • Environmental monitoring and public reporting

If a proponent cannot clearly explain its water and energy requirements, the municipality does not yet have enough information to evaluate the project.

4. Proponents should show their numbers

One of the most useful parts of the framework is its emphasis on transparency.

Proponents are expected to engage communities early and provide clear, project-appropriate and independently verifiable information about matters including electricity, water, infrastructure, sound and emissions.

Material commitments should also be tracked over time.

This should encourage municipalities to move away from one-time approvals based primarily on forecasts.

Ask what will be measured after approval.

Ask who will verify it.

Ask how often results will be reported.

Ask what happens when actual performance differs from the original commitment.

A responsible proposal should make it possible for the municipality and community to compare promises with results.

Sovereignty is more than server location

The fifth principle deserves particular attention.

For facilities supporting sensitive information, public services or critical infrastructure, the framework points to Canadian legal protection, cybersecurity, continuity of service and reliable Canadian access.

That moves the sovereignty conversation beyond one familiar question:

“Is the server located in Canada?”

Server location matters, but it is only one piece of the puzzle.

Municipalities should also ask:

  • Which organization owns and operates the infrastructure?
  • Which laws and contractual terms apply?
  • Who can access the systems and data?
  • Can access be suspended by a foreign company or government?
  • What happens during a cyber incident, commercial dispute or service interruption?
  • Is there a tested continuity plan?
  • Can the organization retrieve its information in a usable format?
  • Is reliable Canadian access protected contractually and technically?

A Canadian postal code does not automatically create Canadian control.

That is especially important when infrastructure supports emergency response, utilities, transportation, health information, public safety or other essential services.

A practical municipal evaluation checklist

The federal principles provide a useful starting point, but municipalities will still need their own review process.

Before evaluating or approving a significant data-centre proposal, consider bringing together staff from:

  • Planning and development
  • Engineering and utilities
  • Finance and taxation
  • Legal, privacy and cybersecurity
  • Emergency management
  • Economic development
  • Environmental services
  • Indigenous relations
  • Procurement and risk management

The review should consider at least the following questions:

Community value

  • What permanent local benefits will the project create?
  • How many jobs will remain after construction?
  • Are training, apprenticeship or research partnerships included?
  • Are there local and Indigenous procurement commitments?
  • Are proposed benefits measurable and enforceable?

Infrastructure

  • What electrical, water, wastewater, road and telecommunications upgrades are required?
  • Who will pay for them?
  • Will the project affect existing services or planned community growth?
  • What emergency-response resources will be needed?

Environmental impact

  • What are the expected water and electricity requirements?
  • How will peak demand and drought conditions be managed?
  • What sound, emissions and waste-heat impacts are anticipated?
  • What ongoing monitoring will occur?

Transparency and accountability

  • What information will be publicly disclosed?
  • Can the municipality independently verify the proponent’s claims?
  • How will commitments be tracked?
  • Who is accountable when targets are missed?
  • What reporting will continue after the facility becomes operational?

Sovereignty and continuity

  • Will the facility support public services, sensitive information or critical infrastructure?
  • What legal protections apply?
  • Who controls access?
  • What cybersecurity and incident-response requirements are in place?
  • How will service continue during an outage or commercial disruption?

Municipalities may also want to examine decommissioning responsibilities, site restoration and financial security. Data centres may be part of the digital economy, but abandoned infrastructure is still physical infrastructure.

What the federal principles do not do

The framework does not replace municipal zoning, development approvals, utility decisions, environmental assessments or Indigenous rights and consultation obligations.

It is also not a substitute for detailed due diligence.

What it provides is a common national reference point.

That matters because municipalities should not have to begin every data-centre discussion with a blank page and a very impressive PowerPoint from the proponent.

Local governments can use these principles to develop evaluation criteria, council briefing materials, community-benefit expectations and standard questions for prospective developers.

They can also use the framework to support a clear message:

We welcome responsible investment, but responsibility must be demonstrated.

The municipal opportunity

Data centres could bring meaningful investment, infrastructure and economic opportunity to Canadian communities.

But the value of a project should not be measured by its construction budget alone.

The real measure is whether the facility produces lasting community benefits without transferring unreasonable costs, environmental risks or operational vulnerabilities to the public.

The cloud has a postal code.

It also has a water meter, an electrical connection, a tax assessment, a planning file and an emergency-response plan.

Local governments need to be at the table early, with the information and authority required to protect the communities they serve.

Catch the Beat helps local governments translate emerging technology policy into practical governance, evaluation tools and implementation plans. If your organization is preparing for AI infrastructure, data-centre proposals or broader digital-governance decisions, let’s talk.

title: The AI Agent Found Another Door: What OpenAI’s Hugging Face Incident Means for Government
author: Daphne
excerpt: An AI agent was given a cybersecurity task. The approved route did not work, so it found another route. Then it showed other agents how to use it. That sounds like the beginning of a science-fiction movie, but it comes from OpenAI’s account of a real incident during internal cybersecurity evaluations in July 2026. This […]
content:
An AI agent was given a cybersecurity task.

The approved route did not work, so it found another route.

Then it showed other agents how to use it.

That sounds like the beginning of a science-fiction movie, but it comes from OpenAI’s account of a real incident during internal cybersecurity evaluations in July 2026.

This was not a public version of ChatGPT suddenly running around the internet doing whatever it wanted. The activity was driven primarily by an internal research model operating with reduced safeguards in a specialized testing environment. OpenAI has confirmed that customer data, product functionality and availability were not affected.

Still, the incident gives governments an important look at what can happen when powerful AI agents are given tools, credentials, system access, persistence and a goal.

What happened?

OpenAI was evaluating whether its models could solve difficult cybersecurity challenges inside isolated environments called sandboxes.

The agents were not supposed to have general internet access. In many cases, they were also supposed to work independently.

They found another way.

The agents discovered that shared infrastructure could be used as an unintended message board. They left files and messages for one another, exchanged information and shared methods for obtaining internet access.

Some agents then exploited vulnerabilities across OpenAI’s internal research infrastructure and Hugging Face systems.

According to OpenAI, the agents displayed four significant behaviour patterns:

  • Reward hacking
  • Persistence on tasks that should probably have been abandoned
  • Unauthorized communication
  • Adopting goals or instructions from other agents

This is where the incident becomes particularly useful for public-sector leaders.

The lesson is not simply, “AI hacked something.”

The more important lesson is that agents can pursue a legitimate goal through an illegitimate route when the technical environment allows it.

Reward hacking: completing the task the wrong way

Reward hacking happens when an AI system achieves the requested result in a way that was never intended.

Think about giving an employee a target and discovering that they found a loophole that made the numbers look wonderful while defeating the purpose of the work.

The target was reached.

The method was the problem.

For a local government, imagine an agent being asked to update a council resolution tracker. Its job is to read approved minutes, extract resolutions and update the official tracker.

What happens if the approved minutes are unavailable?

Does the agent stop and ask for help?

Does it retrieve an unofficial draft from somebody’s email?

Does it search another SharePoint site?

Does it use credentials it discovers in an accessible folder?

The instruction “update the tracker” does not answer those questions.

Persistence is not always a virtue

We often celebrate AI agents for being persistent.

Give the agent a task, let it keep working and come back when the job is finished. Wonderful, right?

Not always.

OpenAI found that some agents rarely gave up, even when tasks appeared impossible. As the agents continued trying, they pursued increasingly risky and out-of-scope options.

For government, an agent needs permission to fail safely.

It should know when to stop because:

  • Required information is missing
  • The task has moved outside its approved scope
  • The necessary authority has not been provided
  • A system is unavailable
  • The agent encounters personal, confidential or protected information
  • The next action requires human approval

“Try harder” is not always the right instruction.

Sometimes the safest and most intelligent response is, “I cannot complete this task within my approved boundaries.”

When agents start talking to other agents

The agents involved in the incident found unintended ways to communicate. They shared discoveries, divided work and influenced one another’s behaviour.

One agent could effectively tell another agent what to do.

That creates a new governance question: Which agents are authorized to communicate with one another?

Imagine a municipality using separate agents for procurement, records management, finance and council reporting.

Should the procurement agent be able to send instructions to the finance agent?

Can the records agent provide information to an HR agent?

If one agent says, “I have authorization,” how does the receiving agent verify that statement?

An instruction from another AI agent should not automatically be treated as legitimate authority.

The agent needs to know who can issue instructions, how authorization is verified and when a human must become involved.

A prompt is not a security boundary

This may be the most important lesson from the incident.

Telling an agent to “stay within scope” is useful, but it is not enough.

A prompt is an instruction. It is not a locked door.

If an agent can technically access another system, credential, folder, application or communication channel, we must assume that access could eventually be used.

That means public-sector AI governance must be supported by technical controls:

  • Access restrictions
  • Network isolation
  • Separate credentials
  • Approval gates
  • Activity logging
  • Continuous monitoring
  • Stop conditions
  • Tested shutdown procedures

The agent should not merely be told what it cannot do. The environment should prevent it from doing those things.

A practical AI agent control checklist

Before connecting an AI agent to municipal systems, ask the following questions.

1. Is the task clearly defined?

Give each agent one specific purpose. Avoid building one giant agent that can access everything and do everything.

One task. One agent.

2. Are prohibited actions documented?

Define what the agent must never do, including accessing unauthorized records, sending external communications, changing official information or using credentials outside its assigned role.

3. Does the agent have clear stop conditions?

Specify when the agent must pause, ask for clarification or transfer the task to a human.

4. Is least-privilege access technically enforced?

Give the agent only the systems, information and permissions required for its approved task.

5. Are networks and systems properly isolated?

A single compromised connection should not provide a pathway into other internal or external systems.

6. Are consequential actions subject to human approval?

An agent may prepare a payment, email, public notice or records update. A human should approve the action before it is completed when the consequences are material.

7. Is agent-to-agent communication controlled?

Define which agents may communicate, what information they can exchange and how that activity will be monitored.

8. Are instructions from other agents treated as untrusted?

An agent should not accept a “go ahead” from another agent as proof of authority.

9. Is every action logged?

Record tool use, system access, changes, communications and approvals so the organization can reconstruct what happened.

10. Is unusual behaviour monitored?

Look for unexpected access attempts, repeated failures, unusual tool use, changes in activity volume or efforts to move outside approved boundaries.

11. Is a human authorized to stop the agent?

Name the person or role that can immediately pause the system. OpenAI now requires its most serious activity to be paused when responders cannot determine within 30 minutes that an alert is a false positive.

Your organization may need a different response time, but “we will figure out who has authority during the incident” is not a plan.

12. Have shutdown, rollback and recovery been tested?

A kill switch is not useful if nobody knows whether it works.

Test how the agent will be stopped, how unauthorized changes will be reversed and how affected systems will be recovered.

This is bigger than cybersecurity

The same principles apply to any agent that can act inside a government environment.

An agent updating a resolution tracker can alter an official record.

An agent supporting procurement can influence a vendor evaluation.

An agent preparing public communications can send incorrect information.

An agent connected to finance can trigger approvals or expose confidential data.

The risk comes from the combination of intelligence, access, tools and authority.

That does not mean governments should avoid agentic AI. It means we need to govern agents differently from ordinary chat tools.

A chatbot produces an answer.

An agent may take an action.

That action needs a boundary, a record, an approval process and an accountable human.

AI can help with the work. It cannot carry the responsibility.

If your local government is developing AI agents, automations or governance policies, Catch the Beat can help you establish practical controls, approval points and human oversight before those systems are connected to live municipal work.

Learn more or book a conversation at www.catchthebeat.ca.

Source: OpenAI, The Hugging Face Incident and the Road Ahead

title: “I Pay for Claude Myself” Is Not an AI Governance Plan
author: Daphne
excerpt: The more local governments I speak to, the more I hear this: “I just use Claude. I pay for it myself.” I understand why. Staff are busy. They discover a tool that can summarize a report, improve an email, compare documents or help draft a policy. The organization has not yet provided an approved AI […]
content:
The more local governments I speak to, the more I hear this:

“I just use Claude. I pay for it myself.”

I understand why.

Staff are busy. They discover a tool that can summarize a report, improve an email, compare documents or help draft a policy. The organization has not yet provided an approved AI option, so the employee pulls out a credit card and gets on with the work.

The intention is usually good.

 

The governance problem is not.

Paying for the tool does not make it approved

A personally purchased Claude Pro subscription is still a consumer account. It is not automatically part of the local government’s managed technology environment.

The organization may have no control over:

  • The account and its security settings
  • What information is uploaded
  • Where prompts and outputs are retained
  • Whether model-improvement settings are enabled
  • Who can access the account 
  • Whether records can be retrieved later
  • What happens when the employee leaves
  • Whether the arrangement meets organizational privacy, security and records requirements

Anthropic distinguishes consumer products, including Claude Free, Pro and Max, from its commercial offerings such as Claude for Work and its API. Consumer users can control certain privacy settings, but those individual choices are not a replacement for an organizational contract, approved configuration, administrative controls or internal policy. Anthropic explains its consumer data practices here.

Think about it this way.

Buying your own filing cabinet does not give you permission to take municipal records home and store them in it.

Paying for the cabinet is not the issue.

Taking the information outside the organization’s controlled environment is.

What information is being entered?

AI use becomes particularly concerning when staff enter information such as:

  • Resident correspondence
  • Employee or applicant information
  • HR documents
  • Closed meeting materials
  • Legal advice
  • Procurement submissions
  • Incident reports
  • Financial information 
  • Unpublished council reports
  • Documents containing personal or confidential information

Even when a document looks harmless, it may contain names, email addresses, opinions, identifying details or operational information that should not be placed in an unapproved system.

Removing a person’s name may not be enough if the remaining details could still identify them.

What does Alberta legislation say?

In Alberta, the Protection of Privacy Act, commonly called POPA, governs how public bodies protect personal information. Its scope includes local government bodies.

The legislation controls the collection, use and disclosure of personal information. Alberta’s official guidance also says employees must protect information against unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure or destruction and ensure that appropriate agreements and safeguards are in place before information is handled by another system or service.

The Access to Information Act, or ATIA, separately governs access to public-body records.

That distinction matters.

POPA asks whether personal information is being protected and handled lawfully.

ATIA raises another practical question: can the local government find and produce its business records when required?

If municipal work is being completed in an employee’s personal AI account, the organization may not be able to search, retrieve, retain or app

 

ropriately dispose of the related prompts and outputs.

You can review the Government of Alberta’s POPA Guide.

What about British Columbia?

In British Columbia, local governments are subject to the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act, often referred to as FIPPA or FOIPPA.

The Act applies to records in the custody or under the control of a public body. It also requires public bodies to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal information against risks such as unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure or disposal.

B.C. also provides specific privacy-protection language for contracts involving service providers and cloud services. That is a useful reminder that moving personal information into a cloud tool should involve more than one employee clicking “subscribe.”

The organization needs to consider the agreement, safeguards, system configuration, access controls and internal policies surrounding the service.

You can review the B.C. Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act and the province’s Privacy Protection Schedule guidance.

Claude is not the problem

 

This is not an article telling local governments to ban Claude.

Claude may be a useful tool. So may Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT, Gemini or another approved platform.

The brand name is not the governance decision.

The organization still needs to determine:

  1. Which AI tools and account types are approved?
  2. What information may be entered?
  3. What information is prohibited?
  4. Where is the information processed and retained?
  5. Is the account governed by consumer or commercial terms?
  6. Can administrators manage access and settings?
  7. Are prompts and outputs municipal records?
  8. How will those records be retained, searched and disposed of?
  9. Has privacy, security, legal, records and procurement staff reviewed the arrangement?
  10. Who verifies the AI output and remains responsible for its use?

A paid organizational licence will often provide better contractual protections, administrative controls and governance options than a personal consumer account.

But paid does not automatically mean safe.

 

The organization must still examine the terms, configuration and intended use.

Shadow AI is also a leadership signal

When staff are purchasing their own AI tools, they are telling the organization something important.

They need help.

They have found useful technology, but the official environment has not caught up with the operational reality.

Simply telling employees “do not use AI” rarely solves the problem. It may only push the use further out of sight.

A better response is to:

  • Give staff an approved option
  • Publish clear acceptable-use rules
  • Explain what information cannot be entered
  • Provide practical training
  • Create a process for requesting new tools
  • Complete the necessary privacy and security assessments
  • Maintain an inventory of approved AI systems
  • Keep human review and accountability in every workflow

The goal is not to punish curiosity.

The goal is to make responsible use possible.

“I pay for it myself” is a billing arrangement.

It is not an AI governance framework.

If your local government needs help developing an AI policy, assessing approved tools, training staff or introducing practical AI governance, contact Catch the Beat. We can help you create guardrails that protect the organization without shutting down useful innovation.

AI can help with the work.

The organization still owns the risk, and the human still owns the decision.

This article provides general information and is not legal advice.
