title: Memphis, Canada… Space? AI Infrastructure Is Getting Very Real
author: Daphne
excerpt: AI may live on your laptop. But AI at scale lives in buildings. Very large buil dings. Buildings full of specialized computer chips, connected to enormous amounts of electricity, cooling systems, fibre networks, backup power and physical infrastructure. And that is exactly why local government should be paying attention. Because the next big AI conversation […]
content:
AI may live on your laptop.

But AI at scale lives in buildings.

Very large buil

dings.

Buildings full of specialized computer chips, connected to enormous amounts of electricity, cooling systems, fibre networks, backup power and physical infrastructure.

And that is exactly why local government should be paying attention.

Because the next big AI conversation may not arrive in the form of a new software licence.

It may arrive as a development application.

First stop: Memphis

Project Colossus in Memphis is a good example of what happens when AI computing gets very, very large.

Colossus is the giant supercomputing facility behind Grok, SpaceXAI’s AI system. SpaceXAI says Colossus 1 now has more than 220,000 NVIDIA GPUs, and the company reported ending 2025 with more than one million H100-equivalent GPUs across Colossus I and II. 

Now, if you are a fisherman and “GPU” means absolutely nothing to you, fair enough.

A GPU, or graphics processing unit, is basically a specialized computer chip that does the heavy lifting for AI.

Think of it this way.

One ordinary computer can do some work.

Put hundreds of thousands of extremely powerful AI chips together and suddenly you have something closer to a giant industrial-scale AI brain.

That is Colossus.

And giant AI brains are hungry.

They need electricity.

They need cooling.

They need land.

They need fibre connections.

They need emergency power.

They need roads, substations, construction crews and local services.

At that point, AI stops being only an IT conversation.

It becomes an infrastructure conversation.

Then look north

Canada has noticed the same thing.

Canada’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, AI for All, includes a major focus on building more Canadian-controlled AI computing infrastructure.

The federal government says it will continue more than $2 billion in existing AI compute investments and wants to attract significant private capital into large-scale Canadian data centres. The strategy describes projects capable of scaling beyond 100 megawatts, with proposed partnerships representing 850 MW of capacity by 2030 and the potential to scale to 2.3 gigawatts. 

And yes, that sounds like electricity alphabet soup.

So here is the fisherman version.

A megawatt, or MW, is a measurement of power.

A gigawatt, or GW, is 1,000 megawatts.

When governments start talking about hundreds or thousands of megawatts for AI infrastructure, we are no longer talking about plugging a few extra computers into the wall.

We are talking about electricity demand at a scale that can require new transmission lines, substations, power generation and major infrastructure planning.

That is a very different conversation.

Canada has one rather handy advantage

We are cold.

Data centres are hot.

There is an opportunity there.

Data centres produce enormous amounts of heat because thousands of computers are operating continuously.

Normally, you need cooling equipment to remove that heat.

But Shared Services Canada says two of its federal enterprise data centres use large cooling wheels that exchange cold outside air with hot inside air. For eight to ten months of the year, those facilities do not need additional heating or air conditioning. 

In plain English?

Open the cold-air door.

Let Canada do some of the cooling.

That does not make a data centre environmentally harmless, but our climate can reduce some of the energy required for cooling.

Canada’s government is explicitly pointing to climate, sustainable energy and geography as advantages for attracting AI infrastructure investment. 

And the money involved is getting serious.

Bell’s proposed Saskatchewan expansion could reach 1.2 GW of capacity and as much as $52.5 billion in capital investment. The federal government says it is exploring opportunities that could support up to six gigawatts of new data-centre capacity and more than $100 billion in potential investment across Canada. 

That is not a server-room upgrade.

That is nation-building-scale infrastructure.

So who is actually paying for all of this?

On the Colossus side, xAI has raised enormous private investment.

Its 2024 Series C round included Andreessen Horowitz, BlackRock, Fidelity, Kingdom Holdings, Lightspeed, MGX, Morgan Stanley, Oman Investment Authority, Qatar Investment Authority, Sequoia Capital, Valor Equity Partners and Vy Capital, with NVIDIA and AMD also participating strategically. 

In January 2026, xAI announced another $20 billion Series E round involving Valor Equity Partners, StepStone Group, Fidelity, Qatar Investment Authority, MGX, Baron Capital Group, NVIDIA and Cisco Investments, among others. 

Canada works differently.

There is no single investor list because AI for All is a national strategy rather than one private project.

The federal government is funding infrastructure programs while trying to bring private capital alongside them. Canada has already advanced work with TELUS on proposed sovereign AI infrastructure in British Columbia, while Bell is planning its massive Saskatchewan expansion. 

Canada’s Responsible Data Centre Development Principles have also been signed by companies including Amazon Web Services, Anthropic, Bell, Cohere, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, TELUS, Equinix and others. 

That tells us something important.

This is not one tech company experimenting in a corner.

AI infrastructure is becoming an industry.

And then somebody looked at Earth and said: “What about space?”

This is where my rabbit hole got considerably more entertaining.

Companies are now seriously exploring orbital data centres.

That simply means putting computing equipment on satellites or spacecraft instead of inside a building on Earth.

The attraction is pretty obvious.

Solar power.

No competition for municipal land.

Potentially less terrestrial cooling-water demand.

Less direct pressure on local electrical grids.

SpaceXAI has already said Anthropic expressed interest in partnering on multiple gigawatts of orbital AI compute capacity. 

Other companies are also working on orbital computing concepts and early demonstrations. 

At first glance, this sounds genius.

Space is nearly absolute zero.

Put the hot computers up there.

Problem solved.

Except physics apparently enjoys ruining perfectly good ideas.

Space is cold. But that does not mean cooling is easy.

On Earth, we remove heat using air and water.

Fans blow air.

Liquid cooling moves heat.

Cold outside air can help.

In space?

There is no air.

No wind.

No giant cosmic HVAC vent.

Because space is a vacuum, heat cannot be carried away through normal convection.

The heat has to leave primarily through radiation.

Here, “radiation” does not mean something scary or nuclear.

It simply means heat leaving an object as energy.

That is why spacecraft need radiators, which are large surfaces designed to release heat into space.

The more computing power you add, the more heat you have to get rid of.

And that can mean very large radiator systems. Research on orbital computing describes thermal management as one of the defining engineering challenges of running large-scale computing in space. 

So yes, space-based computing may reduce some problems on Earth.

But it creates new ones.

Launches.

Materials.

Replacement cycles.

Communications.

Radiator size.

Radiation damage.

Orbital debris.

Maintenance.

Suddenly, we have not eliminated infrastructure.

We have moved it.

And THAT is the point local government should be paying attention to

Here is what fascinates me most about all of this.

Memphis.

Canada.

Space.

Three very different approaches.

Same basic reality.

AI needs infrastructure.

Memphis needs electricity, land and cooling.

Canada needs electricity, transmission, land, water planning and community infrastructure.

Space may reduce some terrestrial pressures, but introduces an entirely different set of technical and environmental risks.

The infrastructure never disappeared.

It changed address.

This is already becoming a municipal issue

In September 2026, Canada released its Responsible Data Centre Development Principles.

And one line should get the attention of every CAO, planner, CFO, utility manager and Council:

Data centre development decisions are fundamentally local. 

The federal principles say data centres should:

  • create lasting local benefits
  • avoid shifting electricity costs onto existing ratepayers
  • minimize water use and environmental impacts
  • be transparent about their local impacts
  • provide strategic value to Canada 

The framework also says proponents should provide information about power use, water use, infrastructure needs, sound and emissions, and should engage local governments early. 

Now we are very firmly out of the IT department.

This affects:

  • Planning.
  • Utilities.
  • Finance.
  • Economic development.
  • Emergency services.
  • Engineering.
  • Environmental management.
  • Indigenous relations.
  • Communications.
  • Council.

And potentially every resident who wants to know why their community is being asked to host a very large industrial facility that happens to be full of computers.

So what should local government be asking?

If an AI data-centre proposal landed on your desk tomorrow, I would not start with:

“How advanced is the AI?”

I would start with questions like:

  • Who pays for the electrical upgrades?
  • How much electricity will this facility require?
  • Does new transmission infrastructure need to be built?
  • How much water will be used?
  • What happens during drought conditions?
  • What backup power is proposed?
  • What happens during an outage or emergency?
  • What are the noise and emissions impacts?
  • How much land does it require?
  • What happens if the facility doubles in size?
  • Who pays for roads and other municipal infrastructure?
  • What jobs and economic benefits actually stay in the community?
  • What happens if the company leaves?
  • How transparent will the operator be about power, water and environmental impacts?

And perhaps the biggest question:

What does the community receive in return for hosting infrastructure of this scale?

Those are not anti-AI questions.

They are governance questions.

The cloud was never really a cloud

We have spent years talking about “the cloud” as though our information floats gently around somewhere above us.

It does not.

The cloud is buildings.

Servers.

Chips.

Electricity.

Cooling systems.

Fibre.

Water.

Concrete.

People.

And increasingly, enormous infrastructure decisions.

Now apparently some of the cloud may actually end up in space, which is a sentence I did not expect to write this year.

But the principle stays exactly the same.

Technology can move the work.

It can move the data.

It can even move the data centre.

It does not remove the responsibility.

For local government, the question is no longer simply:

“Should we use AI?”

We also need to ask:

“What physical infrastructure is required to support the AI economy, what does it mean for our communities, and who remains responsible for the consequences?”

That is where the human comes in.

AI is the tool.

You are the human.

And the decision is still yours.

Want help making sense of what AI means for your local government?

Catch the Beat works with local governments on practical AI implementation, governance, privacy, policy and digital transformation.

 

If your municipality is trying to understand what AI means for staff, Council, infrastructure or governance, get in touch and let’s work through it in plain English.

title: Responsible AI Governance Starts With Clear Boundaries
author: Daphne
excerpt: One of the biggest mistakes I see in AI conversations is starting with: “Can the AI do this?” That is not really the governance question. The better question is: Should it do this, under what conditions, with what controls, and who remains accountable? That is where responsible AI governance actually starts. For local government, this […]
content:
One of the biggest mistakes I see in AI conversations is starting with:

“Can the AI do this?”

That is not really the governance question.

The better question is:

Should it do this, under what conditions, with what controls, and who remains accountable?

That is where responsible AI governance actually starts.

For local government, this matters a LOT.

AI can help draft reports, analyze information, review bylaws, support records management, automate workflows, assist with cyber security and help staff work through enormous amounts of information much faster.

Awesome.

But before we hand an AI system a job, we need to define the boundaries around that job.

1. Define the Approved Use Case

Start with the job.

What exactly is the AI being asked to do?

Not:

“Help with records.”

Instead:

“Review these records against this classification guide and recommend a filing code for human verification.”

The clearer the purpose, the easier it becomes to govern.

The AI should know what it is supposed to do.

And just as importantly, what it is not supposed to do.

2. Limit What the AI Can Access

AI does not need access to everything just because it technically can access everything.

Use least-privilege principles.

If an agent only needs access to one SharePoint library, why are we giving it access to the entire environment?

If it only needs a specific dataset, why give it ten?

The more access an AI system has, the greater the potential consequence if something goes wrong.

Good governance means giving the AI the minimum access required to complete the approved task.

3. Tell It Which Rules It Must Follow

This part is incredibly important for local government.

An AI system may need to operate within:

  • legislation
  • municipal policies
  • records requirements
  • privacy requirements
  • procurement rules
  • internal procedures
  • collective agreements
  • security standards
  • approved templates and processes

Those requirements should not live somewhere completely separate from the AI implementation.

They should form part of the system design.

If the AI is helping with a Council report, what standards apply?

If it is helping with records management, which classification system should it use?

If it is supporting procurement, which policy governs the process?

AI needs boundaries.

Policies help create them.

4. Test Before You Trust

Please do not build an AI workflow on Tuesday and let it loose on Wednesday because the first three outputs looked fantastic.

AI systems need testing.

Test normal situations.

Test strange situations.

Test incomplete information.

Test incorrect information.

Test what happens when the source material contradicts itself.

Test whether the system follows the rules you gave it.

And then test it again when the model, workflow, data or environment changes.

Because AI can produce something that looks incredibly convincing while still being wrong.

That is where the human comes in.

5. Keep Meaningful Human Approval Points

Human oversight cannot simply mean:

“A human is somewhere in this process.”

The approval point needs to matter.

For higher-risk or consequential actions, the human should be able to review the information, understand what the AI did, challenge it, and stop the action if necessary.

Think about things like:

Public communications.

Financial decisions.

Access permissions.

Procurement recommendations.

Council information.

HR matters.

Records decisions.

The more significant the consequence, the stronger the human decision point should be.

AI can make the recommendation.

The human owns the decision.

6. Make the Process Auditable

If somebody asks six months from now:

“Why did we make this decision?”

Can you answer?

Can you see:

What information the AI used?

What instructions it received?

What output it produced?

Who reviewed it?

What changed?

Who approved the final action?

Auditability becomes especially important when AI moves beyond simple drafting and begins influencing operational decisions.

If you cannot explain what happened, you are going to have a very difficult time defending it later.

7. Plan for AI to Fail

This one is not nearly as exciting as building an AI agent.

But it may be one of the most important.

What happens when the AI is unavailable?

What happens when the vendor goes down?

What happens when the model changes?

What happens when the output becomes unreliable?

What happens when your licence expires?

What happens when the integration breaks?

Critical municipal services should not suddenly grind to a halt because an AI system decided today was the day for a little nap.

There needs to be a fallback.

There needs to be a manual process.

There needs to be somebody who understands how the work happens without the AI.

That is resilience.

Governance Is Not About Stopping AI

This is the part I really want local governments to hear.

Governance is not there to stop people from using AI.

It is there to help us use AI safely, consistently and responsibly.

Good governance gives staff confidence.

It tells them:

This is what you can use.

This is what you cannot use.

This is the information you can provide.

This is where the human must approve.

This is how we check the output.

This is what happens when something goes wrong.

Those boundaries actually make it easier to adopt AI because staff do not have to guess.

The Question Is Not Just “Can It?”

AI capabilities are moving incredibly quickly.

Increasingly, the answer to:

“Can AI do this?”

will probably be yes.

That makes the governance questions even more important.

Should it?

Under what circumstances?

What information should it access?

Which rules must it follow?

How will we test it?

Where does the human approve?

Can we explain what happened later?

And what happens if it stops working?

That is responsible AI governance.

AI can do the task.

Local government still owns the responsibility.

Need Help Building Practical AI Governance?

If your local government is beginning to use AI, build agents, automate workflows or develop internal AI policies, I can help turn governance principles into practical rules staff can actually use.

That might include AI policies, governance frameworks, approved-use guidance, staff training, human-oversight models, testing requirements, agent design or implementation controls.

Because responsible AI governance should not live in a document nobody reads.

It should live inside the way the work is actually done.

Use the tool. Set the boundaries. Stay the human.

title: AI May Not Be Taking Canadian Jobs the Way We Think. But It May Already Be Changing Who Gets Hired.
author: Daphne
excerpt: The conversation about AI and jobs usually goes straight to one question: “Is AI going to replace people?” But the Bank of Canada recently published a labour-market analysis that suggests the picture may be more complicated than that. Their researchers found no evidence yet of a broad AI-driven restructuring of Canada’s labour market. That is […]
content:
The conversation about AI and jobs usually goes straight to one question:

“Is AI going to replace people?”

But the Bank of Canada recently published a labour-market analysis that suggests the picture may be more complicated than that.

Their researchers found no evidence yet of a broad AI-driven restructuring of Canada’s labour market.

That is important.

But they also found an early signal that deserves attention:

People looking for work in occupations that are highly exposed to AI appear to be having more difficulty finding jobs.

In other words, the first labour-market effect may not be mass layoffs.

It may be slower hiring.

Slower Hiring, Not Widespread Layoffs

The Bank of Canada compared labour-market outcomes across occupations with different levels of exposure to AI.

Between the 2015 to 2019 average and 2025, the estimated job-finding gap between fully AI-exposed and non-exposed occupations widened by 11.7 percentage points.

By comparison, the difference in job-separation rates changed by only 0.1 percentage point.

That is a very different story from:

“AI is eliminating jobs everywhere.”

The pattern so far looks more like:

Certain occupations may be becoming harder to enter.

And that has huge implications for workforce planning.

The Bank Is Very Careful About Causation

This part matters too.

The Bank of Canada is clear that the data does not prove AI caused these changes.

Canada’s labour market has been affected by many other forces, including:

  • COVID-19
  • immigration
  • trade changes
  • broader economic conditions
  • changing labour demand

So this is not proof that AI is responsible.

It is an early signal.

And early signals are exactly what workforce leaders should be watching.

One-Third of Canadian Jobs Could See Significant Task Changes

The Bank estimates that roughly one-third of Canadian jobs may experience substantial task changes based on current AI capabilities.

Notice the wording.

Task changes.

Not necessarily job elimination.

That distinction is incredibly important.

A role can still exist while the work inside that role changes dramatically.

And that is where this becomes very relevant for local government.

These Are Municipal Roles

Some of the more AI-exposed occupations identified by the Bank include:

  • records management technicians
  • payroll and accounting clerks
  • customer service representatives
  • receptionists
  • office-support workers

Those are not abstract technology-sector jobs.

Those are roles found across municipalities every day.

Think about records staff using AI to classify, search and summarize documents.

Payroll teams using automation to reduce repetitive processing.

Customer service staff using AI to help answer routine resident questions.

Reception and administrative staff using AI to draft correspondence, organize information and complete repetitive tasks.

The job may still exist.

But the job description may start changing.

Younger Workers May Feel This First

The Bank also notes that younger workers may have greater exposure because they are more heavily represented in some of these occupations.

That creates another workforce question for local government.

What happens to traditional entry-level roles?

For years, many people entered organizations through administrative, customer service or clerical positions and learned the organization from there.

If AI starts taking over more of the repetitive work in those roles, we need to think carefully about how junior employees gain experience.

Because eliminating repetitive tasks can absolutely be positive.

But those tasks have also historically been where people learned.

How does a future records professional learn records management if AI performs much of the first-pass classification?

How does a junior finance employee build judgment if automation handles most routine transactions?

How does someone learn municipal operations if the entry-level work changes completely?

Those are not reasons to avoid AI.

They are reasons to redesign development pathways.

Do Not Wait for the Job Description to Become Obsolete

This is probably my biggest takeaway for local governments.

We should not wait until an employee says:

“Half of my job is now being done by AI. What am I supposed to do?”

We can start earlier.

Look at roles now.

Break them into tasks.

Ask:

Which tasks are repetitive?

Which require judgment?

Which require relationships?

Which involve accountability?

Which could AI assist with?

Which should remain human?

Then redesign the role around the work that actually matters.

The Future Role May Be Better, Not Smaller

This is where I think the conversation becomes much more optimistic.

Take a customer service role.

Instead of spending most of the day searching for information and repeating the same answers, AI could help with the search.

That gives the human more time for:

Complex resident issues.

Empathy.

Problem solving.

Escalations.

Relationship building.

Judgment.

Take records management.

AI can assist with classification, extraction and search.

But humans still need to understand:

Legislation.

Retention.

Context.

Privacy.

Risk.

Corporate history.

The role becomes less about manually moving information around and more about governing it properly.

That could be a much stronger role.

Workforce Planning Is Now Part of AI Strategy

When municipalities talk about AI strategy, we often focus on:

Tools.

Policies.

Privacy.

Security.

Automation.

But workforce planning needs to sit beside all of that.

Ask:

What roles will change first?

What skills will employees need?

Which entry-level pathways need to be redesigned?

What training should happen now?

How will supervisors manage teams where AI handles more routine work?

What higher-value work should employees move toward?

That is how we move from fear to preparation.

The Human Work Is Not Disappearing

AI is incredibly good at certain types of work.

Finding information.

Drafting.

Summarizing.

Pattern recognition.

Repetitive processing.

But local government also depends on things AI cannot simply take responsibility for:

Judgment.

Relationships.

Trust.

Community context.

Accountability.

Leadership.

Ethics.

Human consequences.

Those become more important as the technology becomes more capable.

So the question is not simply:

“Which jobs will AI replace?”

A better question is:

“How should these jobs evolve now that AI can do some of the tasks?”

Need Help Preparing Your Workforce for AI?

If your municipality is starting to think about how AI will affect administrative, finance, records, customer service or other municipal roles, I would love to help.

I work with local governments to identify where AI can assist, redesign workflows, build practical staff capability and make sure the human work becomes more valuable, not less.

Because AI may not remove the job.

It may change what the job is for.

And the municipalities that start thinking about that now will be much better prepared for what comes next.

title: Before You Give an AI Agent Access, Clean Up the Permissions
author: Daphne
excerpt: The smarter our AI agents get, the more important our underlying Microsoft 365 permissions become. That is one of my biggest takeaways from Microsoft’s recent look at how it is using Copilot Cowork internally. Cowork can do some pretty powerful things. It can complete multi-step work across Microsoft 365. It can keep working in a […]
content:
The smarter our AI agents get, the more important our underlying Microsoft 365 permissions become.

That is one of my biggest takeaways from Microsoft’s recent look at how it is using Copilot Cowork internally.

Cowork can do some pretty powerful things.

It can complete multi-step work across Microsoft 365.

It can keep working in a sandboxed cloud environment even when the employee’s device is unavailable.

It can run scheduled tasks.

It can use custom skills.

And with Work IQ, it can reason across relevant files, meetings, chats, collaborators and other organizational signals.

Very cool.

But for local government, this creates a very practical governance question:

What can the human account already see?

Because the agent is only as well-governed as the access sitting underneath it.

The Permission Problem

Think about a municipality that has been using Microsoft 365 for years.

SharePoint sites have grown.

Teams have multiplied.

People have changed roles.

Staff have left.

Permissions were added for temporary projects.

Folders were shared “just for now.”

And sometimes “just for now” turns into seven years.

Then along comes an AI agent that can reason across organizational context.

Now the issue is no longer only:

“What can the AI do?”

It is also:

“What can the AI reach because the user can already reach it?”

That is a very different question.

AI Governance Is Becoming Access Governance

This is why AI governance can no longer sit off on its own.

It is becoming deeply connected to:

  • identity and access management
  • SharePoint permissions
  • Teams memberships
  • file sharing
  • records management
  • information classification
  • stale accounts
  • oversharing
  • role changes

If a staff member has access to far more information than they actually need, an AI agent working on their behalf may inherit that same broad context.

And then congratulations.

You may have just given your clever digital coworker access to the organizational junk drawer. 😂

Approval Checkpoints Are Good, But They Are Not Enough

Microsoft includes approval checkpoints for sensitive actions.

Users can also pause, resume or cancel work.

That is useful.

But those controls do not replace the need to get the foundation right first.

A checkpoint can help with a sensitive action.

It does not magically fix:

A badly configured SharePoint site.

An old Team membership.

A folder shared too broadly.

An account with years of accumulated permissions.

That work still matters.

What Local Governments Should Be Reviewing

Before giving an AI agent broad organizational context, I would be asking:

  • Does this person still need access to everything they can currently see?
  • Are old SharePoint permissions still appropriate?
  • Have Teams memberships been reviewed recently?
  • Are sensitive files broadly shared?
  • Are former staff accounts fully disabled?
  • Are role changes reflected in permissions?
  • Are records properly classified?
  • Do we know which systems and folders the agent can reach?
  • Are there areas that should be deliberately excluded?

Those are not glamorous questions.

But they are exactly the questions that determine whether an AI agent becomes useful or risky.

The Bigger Lesson

As AI becomes more capable, we are going to hear more about:

Agents.

Automation.

Context.

Memory.

Skills.

Scheduled work.

Cross-system reasoning.

But underneath all of that sits something much less exciting:

Permissions.

And permissions matter enormously.

Because a well-designed AI system sitting on top of messy access controls is still sitting on messy access controls.

The technology can be excellent.

The governance underneath it still needs to be excellent too.

Clean the Foundation First

For local government, I think the sequence is simple:

Clean the permissions.

Review the memberships.

Fix the oversharing.

Remove stale access.

Understand where sensitive information lives.

Then give the agent broader context.

Because the goal is not to make the AI blind.

The goal is to make sure it can see exactly what it needs to see.

No more.

No less.

Need Help Getting Microsoft 365 Ready for AI?

If your municipality is moving toward Copilot, agents or broader AI use inside Microsoft 365 and you are not sure whether your SharePoint permissions, Teams access or information governance are ready, I would love to help.

I work with local governments to connect AI governance with the practical Microsoft 365 controls underneath it.

Because sometimes the smartest AI project starts with the least exciting task:

Cleaning up who can see what.

Fix the access. Then bring in the clever coworker.

title: Speaking English and French Does Not Automatically Mean AI Understands Canada
author: Daphne
excerpt: One of the easiest assumptions to make with AI is this: If it works in English and French, it must be ready for Canada. Not quite. Recent research from Cohere Labs looked at more than 5.6 million training samples and found something really interesting. They describe what they call a “cultural data funnel.” In simple […]
content:
One of the easiest assumptions to make with AI is this:

If it works in English and French, it must be ready for Canada.

Not quite.

Recent research from Cohere Labs looked at more than 5.6 million training samples and found something really interesting.

They describe what they call a “cultural data funnel.”

In simple terms, cultural information can become less visible as AI systems move from broad pre-training into the later stages of post-training and alignment.

At the same time, those later training stages can become increasingly focused on technical tasks like mathematics, coding and other benchmark-style work.

That matters.

Because an AI system can become very capable technically while still losing important cultural context along the way.

Language Is Not the Same as Culture

This is the part I think Canadian public bodies should pay very close attention to.

Testing an AI in English is useful.

Testing it in French is useful.

But that does not automatically tell us whether the AI understands:

  • Indigenous communities
  • regional differences
  • Northern communities
  • immigrant communities
  • local history
  • community language and terminology
  • cultural expectations
  • different ways people describe land, identity, services and relationships

Canada is not culturally uniform.

And local government definitely is not.

A municipality in northern British Columbia does not operate in exactly the same context as a municipality in southern Ontario.

A First Nations government will have a different cultural, legal and historical context again.

A community with a large newcomer population may have different communication needs.

So when we test AI, language alone cannot be the finish line.

Cultural Suitability Needs Its Own Test

Cohere’s experiments suggest that deliberately marking cultural attributes in training data can improve performance on cultural benchmarks without sacrificing general multilingual performance.

That is an important finding.

And from an implementation perspective, I think the lesson for local government is pretty simple:

Cultural testing should be treated as its own evaluation.

Not buried inside language testing.

Not assumed because the AI sounds fluent.

Not checked once and forgotten.

Actually tested.

What Could This Look Like in Local Government?

Imagine a municipality using AI to help with:

  • public notices
  • resident FAQs
  • emergency communications
  • tourism content
  • Indigenous relations
  • community engagement
  • website content
  • service information
  • translation support

The AI might produce something grammatically perfect.

But is it culturally appropriate?

Does it use the right community terminology?

Does it understand that certain words carry different meaning locally?

Does it reflect the history of the community?

Does it accidentally flatten a very specific local identity into something generic?

Does it understand when a topic needs more care?

Those are not small questions.

They affect trust.

Technically Correct Can Still Be Wrong

This is something I keep coming back to with AI.

AI can produce an answer that is technically correct and still not be the right answer for the community.

That is why the human matters so much.

Especially in public-facing work.

You need someone who understands the people being served.

Someone who knows the history.

Someone who recognizes when the wording is off.

Someone who can say:

“That might be accurate, but that is not how we would say it here.”

AI cannot always know that on its own.

This Is Also a Governance Issue

When local governments build AI governance frameworks, we talk a lot about:

Privacy.

Security.

Bias.

Human oversight.

Data ownership.

Accuracy.

But cultural suitability belongs in that conversation too.

Especially where AI is being used in public communications or community-facing services.

A practical AI evaluation might include questions like:

  • Was the content reviewed by someone with local context?
  • Were Indigenous or cultural considerations tested?
  • Does the language reflect how the community actually describes itself?
  • Are there regional terms the system consistently gets wrong?
  • Are there topics where human review should always be required?
  • Are we testing for cultural appropriateness, not just grammar and factual accuracy?

That is good governance.

The Bigger Lesson

AI does not only need to understand words.

It needs to understand context.

And context is often where culture lives.

For Canadian public bodies, that means multilingual capability is important.

But multilingual does not automatically mean multicultural.

Those are different things.

And if AI is going to help governments communicate with residents, support public services or participate in community engagement, then that difference matters a lot.

Because technically correct does not always mean culturally right.

And in local government?

Context matters.

Need Help Evaluating AI for Public-Facing Use?

If your municipality is using AI for communications, resident services, engagement or community-facing content and you want help building practical testing around accuracy, privacy, governance and cultural suitability, I would love to help.

I work with local governments to build AI systems and guardrails that fit the actual communities they serve.

Because the goal is not just to make AI speak our language.

It is to make sure it understands enough of our context to be useful responsibly.

Use the tool. Test the context. Stay the human.

title: Zero Data Retention: A Big Privacy Shift for Government AI
author: Daphne
excerpt: One of the biggest questions I hear from local governments looking at AI is: “What happens to our data after we send it?” That question matters enormously. Especially in Canada, where municipalities are working within provincial public-sector privacy laws, security requirements, records obligations, and expectations around public trust. OpenAI has introduced an important enterprise privacy […]
content:
One of the biggest questions I hear from local governments looking at AI is:

“What happens to our data after we send it?”

That question matters enormously.

Especially in Canada, where municipalities are working within provincial public-sector privacy laws, security requirements, records obligations, and expectations around public trust.

OpenAI has introduced an important enterprise privacy option for eligible API customers called Zero Data Retention.

In plain language, it means:

  • prompts and model responses are not retained after processing
  • customer content is not available to OpenAI personnel for review
  • enterprise data is not used for model training unless the customer explicitly opts in

That is a meaningful change.

But it is also important to understand what it does not mean.

Zero Data Retention Does Not Mean “Anything Goes”

This is where the human still needs to do the thinking.

A municipality cannot look at “Zero Data Retention” and translate that into:

“Excellent. Upload whatever you want.”

Nope.

You still need to ask:

  • Is this information appropriate to process through the tool?
  • Does it contain personal information?
  • What privacy law applies in our province?
  • Where is the processing happening?
  • What contractual terms apply?
  • Are we required to complete a privacy impact assessment?
  • What access controls are in place?
  • Who can use the system?
  • What records need to be retained internally?
  • Who verifies the output?
  • Who remains accountable?

Zero retention can reduce one category of risk.

It does not remove all the others.

Why This Matters for Canadian Local Government

Canadian municipalities do not operate under one single privacy framework.

The rules differ by province.

That means local governments need to evaluate AI tools in the context of their own legislative environment.

For example, public bodies in British Columbia operate under FIPPA.

Alberta public bodies now operate under POPA.

Other provinces have their own public-sector privacy frameworks.

So when a municipality is evaluating an AI implementation, the question should not simply be:

“Does the vendor say it is secure?”

The better question is:

“Does this configuration meet our legal, privacy, security, and records-management obligations?”

That is a much stronger governance question.

Why Zero Retention Is Still Important

Despite those caveats, this is a significant improvement.

Why?

Because retention is one of the core issues organizations need to understand before they send sensitive information to an AI system.

If content is retained, that creates questions around:

  • access
  • storage
  • secondary use
  • breach exposure
  • deletion
  • auditability
  • contractual control

Reducing retention can reduce some of that exposure.

And for municipalities exploring more advanced AI use cases, especially those involving internal workflows, automation, or agents, that matters.

Privacy Is Not Just About Training Data

Another important point:

A lot of AI conversations focus almost entirely on:

“Is my data being used to train the model?”

That is only one piece.

We also need to care about:

Where is the data processed?

How long is it retained?

Who can access it?

What systems can the AI connect to?

What permissions does it have?

What logs are created?

Can those logs themselves contain sensitive information?

What happens if the AI is integrated into another vendor’s system?

This is why AI governance needs to look at the whole workflow.

Not just the chatbot.

Good Privacy Controls Make Better AI Adoption Possible

I actually think developments like this are encouraging.

Better enterprise privacy controls give organizations more options.

More options mean municipalities can design AI implementations that are better matched to their legal and operational environment.

That does not mean we stop asking hard questions.

It means we have better answers available.

And that is exactly what responsible AI adoption should look like.

Not:

“AI is risky, so do not use it.”

And not:

“The vendor says it is safe, so carry on.”

Instead:

Understand the setting.

Understand the law.

Understand the data.

Understand the controls.

Then decide whether the use case makes sense.

The Bottom Line

Zero Data Retention is a very positive step.

But it is not a privacy program.

It is one control inside a much bigger governance picture.

For Canadian local governments, the opportunity is to use these stronger enterprise controls together with proper privacy assessments, approved data-handling rules, access controls, records practices, and human oversight.

Because the technology is getting better.

Now our governance has to keep up.

Need Help Assessing AI Privacy and Security?

If your municipality is evaluating ChatGPT, API-based AI tools, Copilot, agents, or other generative AI systems and you are trying to work out whether the privacy and security controls actually fit your legislative requirements, I would love to help.

I work with local governments to turn AI privacy, governance, and security requirements into practical implementation rules that staff can actually follow.

title: AI Governance Might Not Be the Brake. It Might Be the Guardrail.
author: Daphne
excerpt: One of the biggest concerns I hear when we talk about AI governance in government is: “Won’t all these controls slow us down?” And I get it. Nobody wants to create a giant approval maze where every AI idea needs six committees, three forms, two lawyers and a small miracle before anyone is allowed to […]
content:
One of the biggest concerns I hear when we talk about AI governance in government is:

“Won’t all these controls slow us down?”

And I get it.

Nobody wants to create a giant approval maze where every AI idea needs six committees, three forms, two lawyers and a small miracle before anyone is allowed to test it.

But a recent McKinsey & Company article on AI adoption in government makes a really important point:

Strong controls can actually help public-sector organizations move faster.

Not because governance disappears.

Because governance is built in from the start.

And that changes everything.

The Problem With Bolting Governance On at the End

McKinsey describes a pattern that will feel very familiar to many public-sector organizations.

A team starts building something.

The technology looks promising.

The pilot works.

Everyone gets excited.

Then, right near the end, somebody asks:

What data is this using?

Who approved that?

What happens if the AI gets it wrong?

Can this decision be challenged?

Where are the logs?

Who owns the risk?

And suddenly the whole thing stops.

That is not really governance.

That is cleanup.

McKinsey’s argument is that controls should be designed into the AI use case from the beginning, carried through development, launch and ongoing monitoring.

That makes a lot of sense for local government.

Decide the Rules Before the Robot Arrives

Before building an AI workflow, municipalities should already be asking:

  • Should AI even be used for this task?
  • What information can it access?
  • Which sources are approved?
  • What is it allowed to do?
  • When must it stop and escalate to a human?
  • How will we test it?
  • Who owns the outcome?
  • What happens if something goes wrong?

Those questions are not there to kill the project.

They are there to make sure the team can keep moving.

Because once those rules are clear, developers, staff, privacy teams, IT and leadership are not constantly renegotiating the same questions.

Human Oversight Should Match the Consequence

This was probably one of my favourite parts of the article.

McKinsey argues that human oversight should be based on the consequence of the action, not simply on the fact that AI was involved.

Think about that in local government.

AI checking grammar in a draft email?

Probably not something that needs executive approval.

AI helping summarize a document?

A human should verify it, but we do not need to create a massive governance process around every comma.

Now compare that with:

A licence being revoked.

A benefit being denied.

A public safety decision.

A decision that materially affects a resident.

Very different situation.

The higher the consequence, the stronger the human control should be.

That is practical governance.

The Human Still Owns the Decision

The article also reinforces something I talk about constantly.

As the decisions become more complex and the consequences of getting them wrong become more serious, AI autonomy should decrease.

AI might handle simple, repetitive, low-risk work.

AI might recommend something in a medium-risk process while a human approves it.

And for complex, high-stakes decisions?

The human stays in charge.

There it is again.

Who is the human?

Because the AI can assist.

It can analyze.

It can recommend.

It can automate parts of the workflow.

But accountability does not magically move into the software.

Data Still Matters

McKinsey also brings the conversation straight back to data.

AI-enabled workflows are only as trustworthy as the information they use.

That means local governments still need to know:

Is the information current?

Is it legally permitted to be used?

Is personal information being handled appropriately?

Are the sources approved?

Is the AI pulling from a clean knowledge base or from the organizational equivalent of a junk drawer?

Because feeding AI a messy shared drive and hoping for excellent decisions is… optimistic. 😂

The article specifically emphasizes using clean, approved information and building privacy protections into AI systems from the beginning.

Stop Measuring Success by the Number of Pilots

This is another point I LOVE.

McKinsey argues that public-sector AI should not be measured by how many pilots were launched.

It should be measured by outcomes.

Did residents experience shorter wait times?

Were there fewer errors?

Did response times improve?

Were answers clearer?

Did staff gain capacity?

Did service quality improve?

That is the measure.

Not:

“We launched 14 AI pilots this year.”

Very cool.

But did anything get better?

That is the question.

AI Adoption Is Also a Change Management Project

The article also points out that technology is only one piece of the investment.

Organizations need training.

Adoption.

Capability building.

New ways of working.

Clear ownership.

And people who understand both the service and the risks.

That matters enormously in local government.

Because giving staff access to an AI tool does not mean they will suddenly redesign how they work.

They need time to learn it.

They need practical examples.

They need guidance.

They need to understand what they are allowed to do.

And most importantly, they need to understand why the new way is actually better than the old one.

Governance Should Help Us Move

The lesson I take from McKinsey’s article is not:

“Government needs more AI committees.”

It is almost the opposite.

We need better-designed governance.

Governance that is built into the workflow.

Governance that matches the level of risk.

Governance that gives staff clear boundaries.

Governance that allows low-risk experimentation.

Governance that keeps humans firmly in control of consequential decisions.

Governance that measures what actually improved.

Because the goal is not to move recklessly fast.

And it is not to move painfully slow.

The goal is to move safely, deliberately and continuously.

That is where the guardrail analogy works so well for me.

A guardrail is not there to stop the car from moving.

It is there so the car can move with less chance of ending up somewhere it really should not be.

Need Help Building Practical AI Governance?

If your municipality is trying to introduce AI without creating either a free-for-all or a giant approval bottleneck, I would love to help.

I work with local governments to build practical AI governance frameworks, policies, staff guidance and implementation processes that keep humans accountable while still allowing teams to actually use the technology.

Because governance should not be the brake.

Done properly, it is the guardrail that lets us move.

Credit to McKinsey & Company, and authors Hrishika Vuppala, Roger Roberts, Tim Fountaine and Tim Ward, for the public-sector research and framing that informed this piece.

title: AI Success Is Not a Great Demo. It Is Better Work
author: Daphne
excerpt: One of the easiest things to do with AI is create an impressive demonstration. Look! It wrote the report. It analyzed the spreadsheet. It found the information. It created an agent. Very cool. But here is the slightly less exciting question: Did anything actually improve? That is the part I think local governments need to […]
content:
One of the easiest things to do with AI is create an impressive demonstration.

Look!

It wrote the report.

It analyzed the spreadsheet.

It found the information.

It created an agent.

Very cool.

But here is the slightly less exciting question:

Did anything actually improve?

That is the part I think local governments need to get much better at measuring.

Scale AI recently published guidance drawing on more than 200 Canadian AI projects, and one of the points that really stood out to me was this:

Technical model performance alone is not enough.

In other words, we should not call an AI pilot successful simply because the AI gave us a good answer.

We need to look at the whole system around it.

What Does Success Actually Look Like?

For a municipality, success might mean:

  • a Council report takes less time to prepare
  • fewer errors need to be corrected
  • staff can process more work without adding capacity
  • repetitive manual steps disappear
  • information is easier to find
  • service quality improves
  • staff actually use the system after the pilot ends

That last one matters enormously.

Because you can build the cleverest AI agent in Canada…

and if nobody uses it six months later, I am going to struggle to call that a successful implementation. 😂

Generative AI Is More Than the Model

This becomes even more important as municipalities start introducing generative AI and agents.

An agent should not only be evaluated based on whether it produces a clever answer.

We need to evaluate the complete operational system.

That includes:

Workflow Integration

Does it actually fit into the way staff work?

Or does using the AI require six extra steps that eventually make everyone go back to the old process?

Reliability

Does it work consistently in real operating conditions?

A controlled demonstration is very different from using the system every Tuesday morning when five other things are happening and the information is not perfectly organized.

Adoption

Are the people who were supposed to use it actually using it?

Do they trust it?

Do they understand it?

Have they been trained?

Cost

What does the AI actually cost to operate?

That could include licences, tokens, integrations, staff time, support and ongoing maintenance.

Risks and Controls

What new risks did the implementation introduce?

Who verifies the output?

What information can the system access?

What requires human approval?

Can the organization audit what happened later?

Organizational Outcomes

And finally:

What actually got better?

That is the question I care about most.

Set the Measures Before You Start

This is my biggest takeaway for local government.

Define success before the pilot begins.

If you are testing an AI agent to help produce Council reports, establish the baseline first.

How long does the process take now?

How many steps are involved?

How often are corrections required?

Where are the delays?

How much staff time is being used?

Then decide what success would look like.

Maybe the target is a 30% reduction in preparation time.

Maybe it is fewer formatting errors.

Maybe it is reducing a ten-step process to five.

Maybe it is freeing staff to spend more time reviewing content rather than assembling it.

Whatever the measure is, decide that before the shiny robot arrives.

Otherwise, it becomes very easy to finish a pilot and go searching for something impressive to put in the final report.

Adoption Is a Success Measure Too

I think this one gets missed constantly.

If the technology works but the humans do not use it, the implementation did not work.

That is not necessarily a technology failure.

It could be:

Poor training.

A bad workflow.

Lack of trust.

Too many extra steps.

No clear ownership.

No champion.

Or simply that the tool did not solve a problem staff actually cared about.

That is why change management belongs inside AI measurement.

The human is part of the system.

Measure the Municipality, Not Just the Robot

This is the shift I would love to see.

Instead of asking:

“How accurate was the model?”

Also ask:

“What improved for the municipality?”

Did staff save time?

Did quality improve?

Did capacity increase?

Did residents receive better service?

Did risk decrease?

Was the solution worth what it cost?

Could we sustain it?

Because that is the actual purpose of implementing AI.

Not to prove that AI is clever.

We already know it can be clever.

The goal is to make the work better.

Start With the Outcome

Before your next AI pilot, write down five things:

  1. What problem are we solving?
  2. What does the current process look like?
  3. How will we know it improved?
  4. What risks and controls need to be measured?
  5. Will staff actually use it?

Then pilot.

Then measure.

Then decide whether it deserves to grow.

That is a much stronger AI strategy than:

“Look what the robot can do!”

Because a great demo gets attention.

A measurable improvement creates value.

Want Help Measuring Whether Your AI Pilot Is Actually Working?

If your municipality is piloting generative AI, building agents or trying to figure out whether an existing AI implementation is actually delivering value, I would love to help.

I work with local governments to identify the right use cases, establish practical baselines, build success measures and implement AI with the humans, workflows and governance around it.

Because the goal is not simply to adopt AI.

The goal is to make municipal work better.

Measure the impact. Keep the human. Build what works.

title: Microsoft Azure Copilot Just Added More Agent Controls. Government Administrators Should Care.
author: Daphne
excerpt: Microsoft has expanded Azure Copilot with four specialized agents focused on: troubleshooting deployment optimization resiliency That is interesting on its own. But from a government perspective, the part I care about most is not actually the clever agents. It is the control around them. Organizations can now manage the availability of individual Azure Copilot agents […]
content:
Microsoft has expanded Azure Copilot with four specialized agents focused on:

  • troubleshooting
  • deployment
  • optimization
  • resiliency

That is interesting on its own.

But from a government perspective, the part I care about most is not actually the clever agents.

It is the control around them.

Organizations can now manage the availability of individual Azure Copilot agents through the Azure Copilot Admin Center.

And if Azure Copilot is disabled for the tenant, those agents stay disabled too.

That is exactly the kind of practical governance control I like to see.

Why This Matters

As AI becomes more agentic, organizations need to move beyond one very basic question:

“Do we allow AI?”

That question is no longer enough.

We now need to ask:

Which agents do we allow?

Who can use them?

What can they access?

What can they recommend?

What can they act on?

Which environments are appropriate?

Who is responsible for reviewing what they do?

That is a much more useful governance conversation.

The Four Specialized Agents

Microsoft is making four specialized Azure Copilot agents directly available:

Troubleshooting

This agent is designed to help find issues faster and support problem solving across Azure environments.

Deployment

This one focuses on helping with deployments and implementation tasks.

Optimization

This agent can help identify ways to improve performance and potentially reduce unnecessary costs.

Resiliency

This agent focuses on strengthening systems and supporting better reliability.

All very useful.

But useful does not automatically mean enabled.

And that distinction matters.

Off Should Sometimes Be the Default

One of the things I like about the current setup is that organizations can control the availability of individual agents.

That gives administrators an actual decision point.

Instead of:

“Here are four shiny new agents. Everyone go play.”

The better approach is:

“Which of these agents make sense for our environment?”

“What permissions should they have?”

“Who should be allowed to use them?”

“What oversight do we need?”

That is governance.

Not fear.

Not blocking innovation.

Just making deliberate decisions.

Why This Is Especially Important for Local Government

Local governments increasingly rely on cloud environments for applications, systems, infrastructure and service delivery.

That means AI agents may eventually sit very close to operational systems.

And once an AI system can recommend or take actions in those environments, the risk profile changes.

You are no longer only asking AI to write a paragraph.

You may be asking it to help troubleshoot infrastructure.

Assist with deployment.

Recommend optimization.

Support resiliency decisions.

That means permissions, oversight, logging and accountability become incredibly important.

Give the Robot a Job Description

This is probably the simplest way I explain it.

If you hired four new employees tomorrow, you would not give all four of them access to everything in the organization.

You would decide:

What is your job?

What can you access?

What can you change?

Who supervises you?

What needs approval?

What happens if something goes wrong?

AI agents should not be treated differently.

Give the clever robot a job description before you give it the keys.

Practical Questions Government Administrators Should Be Asking

Before enabling an AI agent in Azure, I would be asking:

  • What exactly does this agent do?
  • What information can it access?
  • What systems can it influence?
  • Can it take actions or only recommend them?
  • Who can enable or disable it?
  • What permissions does it inherit?
  • Are its actions logged?
  • Can we review what it did later?
  • Which actions require human approval?
  • What happens if the recommendation is wrong?

Those are implementation questions.

And they matter just as much as the technology itself.

Better Controls Make Responsible Adoption Easier

The good news is that enterprise AI tools are increasingly giving administrators more practical controls.

That is exactly what organizations need.

Because good AI governance is not simply writing a policy that says:

“Use AI responsibly.”

That is far too vague.

Good governance looks more like:

This agent is approved.

This one is not.

These staff can use it.

These permissions are allowed.

These actions require human approval.

These activities are logged.

That is much more useful.

The Human Still Owns the Outcome

No matter how capable these agents become, the core principle does not change.

AI can troubleshoot.

AI can recommend.

AI can assist with deployments.

AI can help identify improvements.

But accountability still sits with the organization and the authorized human.

The tool can help with the work.

It cannot carry the responsibility.

Need Help Turning AI Controls Into Practical Governance?

If your municipality or public-sector organization is starting to use Azure Copilot, Microsoft Copilot or other agentic AI tools, I would love to help.

I work with local governments to turn AI governance into practical settings, permissions, staff guidance and workflows that people can actually understand and follow.

Because responsible AI does not mean saying no to the clever robot.

It means deciding exactly what job the clever robot is allowed to do.

Use the tool. Set the limits. Stay the human.

title: Alberta’s AI Data Centre Conversation Is One Local Governments Should Be Watching
author: Daphne
excerpt: Alberta is continuing its public engagement on AI data centres, and this is one conversation local governments should absolutely be paying attention to. Because when we talk about AI, we often talk about what happens on the screen. The tools. The models. The automation. The productivity. But AI also needs physical infrastructure. content:
Alberta is continuing its public engagement on AI data centres, and this is one conversation local governments should absolutely be paying attention to.

Because when we talk about AI, we often talk about what happens on the screen.

The tools.

The models.

The automation.

The productivity.

But AI also needs physical infrastructure.

And that infrastructure lands somewhere.

In communities.

On land.

Connected to power.

Using water.

Affecting local services.

That is why Alberta’s public engagement on AI data centres is so important.

What Is the Province Asking About?

The province is inviting discussion around some very practical issues:

  • electricity costs
  • water use
  • land
  • environmental impacts
  • community effects
  • taxpayer protections

Those are not abstract technology questions.

Those are municipal questions.

They affect planning.

They affect infrastructure.

They affect economic development.

They affect residents.

And they affect how communities grow.

AI Data Centres Could Bring Opportunity

There is absolutely potential here.

AI data centres could bring investment.

Jobs.

New infrastructure.

Economic activity.

Technology growth.

And opportunities for communities that are looking to attract new industries.

That part is exciting.

But local government also needs to understand what comes with that opportunity.

How much power is required?

How much water is required?

What infrastructure needs to be upgraded?

Who pays for those upgrades?

What happens to nearby land uses?

What are the environmental impacts?

What protections are in place for taxpayers?

Those are the questions that need to be asked before the ribbon cutting.

This Is Why Local Government Needs a Seat at the Table

Municipalities are often where big policy decisions become very practical.

A provincial decision can sound great on paper.

But local government is the one looking at zoning.

Servicing.

Roads.

Water.

Emergency response.

Community concerns.

Economic development.

And long-term infrastructure.

That is why these conversations matter.

Local governments should not just be reacting after a major AI infrastructure project lands in their community.

They should be part of the conversation early.

Because the question is no longer only:

“How will we use AI?”

It is also:

“What will AI require from our communities?”

And that is a much bigger planning conversation.

Need Help Thinking Through AI at the Community Level?

If your municipality is starting to think about AI infrastructure, AI governance, community impacts or what AI could mean for local planning and economic development, I would love to help.

I work with local governments to turn AI from a big abstract idea into something practical, responsible and grounded in how municipalities actually operate.

Because AI might live in the cloud.

But the infrastructure still lives somewhere.

title: How Will AI Change the Communities We Govern?
author: Daphne
excerpt: Canada is now part of a new international conversation about what AI could actually do to our economy. And I think local government should be paying very close attention. OpenAI has funded 14 independent research projects looking at the economic and societal effects of AI. One of those projects, led by the Windfall Trust, will […]
content:
Canada is now part of a new international conversation about what AI could actually do to our economy.

And I think local government should be paying very close attention.

OpenAI has funded 14 independent research projects looking at the economic and societal effects of AI. One of those projects, led by the Windfall Trust, will establish or expand AI economic policy working groups in several regions, including Canada.

The groups will be looking at areas such as:

  • fiscal policy
  • labour markets
  • welfare systems
  • competitiveness

At first glance, those may sound like federal or provincial issues.

But eventually, the impacts land somewhere.

They land in communities.

What Could This Mean for Local Government?

If AI changes the labour market, municipalities may feel it through:

  • workforce shortages
  • retraining needs
  • changes in local employment
  • economic development priorities
  • changes in the types of businesses operating locally
  • shifts in demand for municipal services
  • pressure on community support systems

If AI changes productivity or competitiveness, that may eventually affect local business growth, investment, tax bases and community planning.

If AI changes how governments think about transfers, welfare or fiscal policy, municipalities may also feel the downstream effects of those decisions.

That is why I think the local government conversation about AI needs to become bigger than:

“Which AI tool should we buy?”

That question still matters.

But there is another one coming:

“How is AI going to change the community we are governing?”

And that is a very different conversation.

Some of the Other Research Is Worth Watching Too

Several of the other funded projects are particularly interesting from a government perspective.

One project will look at an incident classification framework for uncontrolled self-improving AI systems.

Another will examine a privacy-preserving agent framework for simulating how households might respond to government transfers and industrial policy.

Another will explore human-validated AI for legislative accountability.

Those are fascinating areas.

But there is an important distinction here:

These are newly funded research projects. They are not proven government systems.

That matters.

There is a big difference between interesting research and something a municipality should put into production tomorrow morning.

Results from the broader program are expected in 2027, and I will definitely be watching what comes out of it.

Why Municipal Leaders Should Watch This Now

Local governments do not need to predict exactly what AI will do to the economy.

Nobody can.

But we can start asking better questions.

What occupations in our community could change?

What new skills might local employers need?

Could AI help address chronic capacity shortages?

Which sectors in our region could benefit most?

What happens if certain jobs decline while entirely new ones appear?

How could this affect workforce planning inside the municipality itself?

How might local economic development strategies need to change?

Those are strategic planning questions.

They are workforce questions.

They are economic development questions.

And increasingly, they are AI questions too.

AI Strategy Is Becoming Community Strategy

For the last few years, much of the government AI conversation has focused on internal use.

Can AI help write reports?

Can it review records?

Can it automate processes?

Can it help staff find information faster?

Absolutely.

But the next stage of the conversation is much bigger.

AI does not only change how government employees work.

It may change the economy, workforce and communities those employees are serving.

That means AI should start appearing in conversations about:

  • strategic planning
  • economic development
  • workforce planning
  • service delivery
  • community resilience
  • budgeting
  • long-term organizational capacity

Not because municipalities need to become AI research labs.

But because local government is where many of these societal changes eventually become very real.

Need Help Bringing AI Into Your Strategic Planning?

If your municipality is trying to understand what AI means beyond simply buying a tool, I would love to help.

I work with local governments on practical AI implementation, governance, workforce readiness and strategic planning so that AI becomes something the organization can understand, manage and actually use.

The conversation does not have to start with technology.

It can start with a much better question:

How could AI change our organization, our workforce and the community we serve?

That is the conversation I think local governments should be having now.

title: Want to Use AI for Cyber Security? First, Is Your Data Actually Ready?
author: Daphne
excerpt: Want to use AI for cyber security? Here is the slightly uncomfortable question first: Is your data actually ready? One of my favourite parts of the new international AI cyber defence guidance is that it does not pretend the AI tool is the hero. It points straight back to the boring stuff. Asset inventories. Logs. […]
content:
Want to use AI for cyber security?

Here is the slightly uncomfortable question first:

Is your data actually ready?

One of my favourite parts of the new international AI cyber defence guidance is that it does not pretend the AI tool is the hero.

It points straight back to the boring stuff.

Asset inventories.
Logs.
Identity information.
Permissions.
Vulnerability records.
Configurations.
Data quality.

Because AI can only analyze what you give it.

And if what you give it is messy, incomplete, outdated or inconsistent, the result is going to reflect that.

AI Does Not Magically Fix Bad Data

This is where organizations can get a little too excited about the shiny tool.

If your organization does not know what systems it owns…

If half your logs are missing…

If old accounts are still floating around…

If permissions have grown for ten years because nobody wanted to remove anything…

Then congratulations.

You have just given your very clever AI assistant a beautifully organized pile of confusion. 😂

And that matters.

A lot.

Especially in local government, where teams are often working across old systems, shared drives, legacy accounts, multiple vendors and years of changing permissions.

Before You Buy the AI Tool, Ask These Questions

Before spending money on a new AI cyber security platform, I would be asking:

  • Do we actually know what systems and assets we have?
  • Is our data current?
  • Are our permissions clean?
  • Are old accounts disabled?
  • Are our logs complete?
  • Do we know what “normal” activity looks like in our environment?
  • Are our vulnerability records current?
  • Do we have confidence in our configurations?
  • Can we trust the information the AI will be analyzing?

Because if the answer to those questions is “sort of”…

Then the AI project might not actually be an AI project yet.

It might be a data readiness project.

This Is the Part People Skip

AI cyber defence can absolutely help.

It can help identify patterns.

It can support faster detection.

It can help prioritize vulnerabilities.

It can assist with incident response.

It can reduce repetitive manual work.

But none of that removes the need for strong fundamentals.

The international guidance makes this point very clearly.

Good cyber security still depends on things like:

  • identity and access management
  • secure configurations
  • patch management
  • logging and monitoring
  • network segmentation
  • incident response
  • reliable data

AI can strengthen those things.

It cannot replace them.

Local Government Should Pay Particular Attention to This

This is especially important for smaller municipalities.

When resources are tight, it can be tempting to look at AI as a way to leapfrog some of the foundational work.

But if your asset list is incomplete or your permissions are a mess, the AI is not going to magically fix the underlying problem.

It may actually make it harder to see what is going wrong.

And this is where the human comes in.

We still need people to:

Review the data.

Clean the permissions.

Validate the logs.

Understand the systems.

Question the output.

Make the decision.

AI can help with the work.

It cannot carry the responsibility.

Sometimes the Best AI Strategy Is Pretty Boring

And I actually love that.

Because sometimes the smartest AI strategy starts with the least glamorous work in the building.

Clean the data.

Fix the permissions.

Know your environment.

Get the basics right.

Then bring in the clever robot.

Because strong AI starts with strong data.

And strong cyber defence starts with knowing what you actually have.

Need Help Getting AI-Ready?

If your local government is thinking about using AI for cyber security, automation or broader digital transformation, but you are not sure whether the underlying data, permissions, records or governance are ready yet, I would love to help.

I work with municipalities to assess the practical foundation first, then build AI use cases on top of something that can actually support them.

Because the best AI implementation is not always the fanciest one.

Sometimes it starts with cleaning up the mess.

Good data. Good governance. Better AI.

title: You Have a Copilot Licence. But Which AI Model Is Actually Doing the Work?
