content:
GitHub Copilot is becoming a very interesting example of why AI governance needs to go deeper than simply asking:

“Which AI tool do we use?”

GitHub has added xAI’s Grok 4.6 to GitHub Copilot.

It is rolling out across:

  • Visual Studio Code
  • Visual Studio
  • Copilot CLI
  • GitHub Copilot cloud agent
  • the GitHub Copilot app
  • JetBrains
  • Xcode
  • Eclipse

Depending on the plan and environment, users may now be able to choose Grok 4.6 as the model behind their Copilot experience.

And that is where this gets interesting for government.

Copilot Is Becoming a Multi-Model Environment

We have become used to thinking about AI products by their brand name.

ChatGPT.

Copilot.

Claude.

Gemini.

But increasingly, the application we see on the screen is only one layer of the technology.

Behind that interface may be a choice of different models from different providers.

So someone might say:

“We are using GitHub Copilot.”

Great.

But the next question may now need to be:

“Which model are you using inside Copilot?”

That distinction matters.

Different models can have different providers, capabilities, pricing arrangements, technical behaviours and organizational considerations.

A licence for one AI product no longer necessarily tells you everything about the model processing the work.

The Part I Really Like: It Is Off by Default

For GitHub Copilot Business and Enterprise, administrators must explicitly enable access to Grok 4.6.

The policy starts off by default.

From a governance perspective?

I really like this.

Because the organization gets a deliberate decision point.

Rather than a new model simply appearing and staff immediately using it, an administrator has to decide whether it should be available.

That creates an opportunity to ask some questions first.

And there is our human again.

What Should Organizations Be Asking?

As AI products become multi-model environments, I think organizations need a model-level governance process.

Not necessarily something enormously complicated.

But somebody should know the answers to questions like:

Which models are approved?

Your organization might approve certain models for particular types of work and not others.

The decision might depend on privacy, security, contractual terms, technical requirements, cost or the type of information being processed.

Who can enable a new model?

If a new provider appears inside an existing AI application, who decides whether staff can use it?

IT?

Privacy?

Information security?

A governance committee?

The answer will differ between organizations.

What matters is that somebody owns the decision.

What information crosses provider boundaries?

This is especially important when we are talking about development environments.

Developers may be working with:

  • source code
  • internal systems
  • configuration information
  • technical documentation
  • organizational context
  • sensitive operational information

Organizations should understand what information is sent to the selected model and what terms apply to that processing.

How do we record model changes?

This is another little governance question that could become much more important.

Imagine reviewing an AI-assisted workflow six months later.

You know it used GitHub Copilot.

But which model?

Was it Grok?

Another provider?

Did the organization change the approved model halfway through the project?

If model choice can materially affect the way work is processed, that choice may eventually need to form part of your implementation and audit documentation.

“We Use Copilot” Is No Longer Enough

This is probably my biggest takeaway from the change.

Organizations are going to need to think about AI in layers.

You may have:

The platform
GitHub Copilot.

The model
Grok 4.6 or another available model.

The provider
xAI or another model provider.

The organizational settings
Which models and features administrators have allowed.

The human
Who selected the model, reviewed the work and remains responsible for the result.

That is a much more useful governance picture than simply maintaining a list that says:

“GitHub Copilot: Approved.”

This Is Exactly Why AI Governance Needs to Keep Moving

AI governance cannot be a policy we write once and then put on SharePoint for the next five years.

The products themselves are changing too quickly.

Features change.

Models change.

Providers change.

Pricing changes.

New controls appear.

And sometimes a product that looked like one AI system becomes an environment containing several of them.

The good news is that enterprise controls like off by default give organizations a practical way to manage that change.

But the setting only helps if somebody actually has a process around it.

Who reviews the new model?

Who approves it?

Who turns it on?

Who records the change?

And who makes sure staff understand what has changed?

That is practical AI governance.

Not just controlling access.

Understanding what is actually sitting behind the button.

Need Help Turning AI Governance Into Something Practical?

If your municipality or public-sector organization is using Copilot, ChatGPT or other AI tools and trying to work out which models should be approved, how staff access should be controlled, or what needs to be documented as these platforms change, I would love to help.

I work with local governments to turn AI governance into practical policies, settings and staff guidance that people can actually use.

Because having an approved AI tool is only the start.

You also need to know what is doing the work inside it.

Use the tool. Know the model. Stay the human.

title: ChatGPT Project Memory Just Got More Useful for Organizations
author: Daphne
excerpt: ChatGPT Projects just got an update that I think organizations should pay attention to. Eligible unshared Projects can now switch between: Default memory and Project-only memory even after the Project has already been created. That might sound like a small settings update. For local government, I think it is much more useful than that. So […]
content:
ChatGPT Projects just got an update that I think organizations should pay attention to.

Eligible unshared Projects can now switch between:

Default memory

and

Project-only memory

even after the Project has already been created.

That might sound like a small settings update.

For local government, I think it is much more useful than that.

So What Is the Difference?

With default memory, ChatGPT may use relevant context from outside that specific Project, depending on your settings and account.

With project-only memory, the context stays within that Project.

That means ChatGPT can use the conversations and information inside the Project to help with the work, but it does not bring in outside conversations as context.

And information from that Project is not used as memory elsewhere.

Think about it practically.

A municipality might have separate Projects for:

  • Council work
  • HR
  • Privacy
  • Records management
  • Finance
  • Policy development
  • A specific implementation project

There are times when broader context can be useful.

And there are definitely times when you want:

What happens in this Project, stays in this Project.

That is where project-only memory becomes really interesting.

But Project-Only Does Not Mean “Anything Goes”

This is the part I really want organizations to pay attention to.

A memory setting is not the same thing as a privacy program.

It does not replace:

  • organizational permissions
  • approved AI platforms
  • privacy requirements
  • records-management rules
  • information security controls
  • retention requirements
  • staff procedures
  • human oversight

If a staff member sees the words “project-only,” I do not want them automatically thinking:

“Excellent. Now I can put anything in here.”

Nope.

The organization still needs to decide what information is appropriate to use with AI in the first place.

This Is What Practical AI Governance Looks Like

When people hear “AI governance,” they sometimes imagine a giant policy document filled with legal language.

And yes, policies matter.

But governance also happens at the settings level.

Sometimes good governance is simply saying:

For this type of work, use project-only memory.

For this type of information, do not upload it at all.

For this Project, these people should have access.

For this output, a human must review it before it goes anywhere.

That is practical governance.

It is not only about telling staff what they cannot do.

It is about showing them exactly how to use the tool properly.

Shared Projects Are Different Too

Shared Projects remain project-only.

That makes sense because the Project becomes a contained collaborative workspace rather than something drawing from each individual user’s broader memory.

But again, the fact that something is contained inside a Project does not automatically make the content appropriate.

The same questions still apply:

Who should have access?

What data are we putting in?

Is this an approved use?

How long should the information be retained?

What becomes an organizational record?

Who is responsible for checking the output?

There is our human again.

The Bigger Lesson

AI tools are becoming more configurable.

That is good.

Organizations are getting more ways to control context, memory, permissions and workflows.

But more settings also mean staff need clearer guidance.

We cannot hand someone an AI account and assume they will automatically understand what “memory,” “project-only,” “shared,” or “private” actually means from a governance perspective.

That needs to be taught.

Because good AI implementation is not just:

Here is the tool. Go use it.

It is:

Here is the tool. Here is when to use it. Here is how to configure it. Here is what information belongs in it. And here is where the human stays responsible.

That is the difference between simply adopting AI and implementing it properly.

Need Help Building Practical AI Guidance for Your Team?

If your local government is starting to use ChatGPT, Copilot or other AI tools and you are trying to figure out what staff guidance, settings, governance rules or training should sit around them, this is exactly the work I love doing.

I help municipalities turn AI governance into practical instructions staff can actually follow.

Because sometimes responsible AI really does come down to knowing which button to click.

Use the tool. Stay the human.

title: AI Watermarks Are Coming. What Does That Mean for Local Government?
author: Daphne
excerpt: This one made my records-management brain very happy. Anthropic has announced that future Claude models will watermark AI-generated text. And before you imagine a giant “MADE BY AI” stamped across the bottom of your Council report, that is not what is happening. The watermark is essentially invisible. Claude generates text by making thousands of tiny […]
content:
This one made my records-management brain very happy.

Anthropic has announced that future Claude models will watermark AI-generated text.

And before you imagine a giant “MADE BY AI” stamped across the bottom of your Council report, that is not what is happening.

The watermark is essentially invisible.

Claude generates text by making thousands of tiny choices between possible words. When there are several equally reasonable options, Anthropic’s watermarking approach changes the source of randomness used to make those choices.

Those choices collectively create a pattern that can later help determine whether Claude was likely involved in producing the text.

No hidden characters are inserted.

No additional tokens are required.

The watermark does not identify the person, organization or conversation that created the content.

Anthropic says the approach is based on Google DeepMind’s SynthID-Text technology.

And from a government perspective, I think this gets REALLY interesting.

Imagine This in Local Government

Think about how much content moves through a municipality:

Council reports.

Public notices.

Media releases.

Correspondence.

Policies.

Reports.

Website content.

Emergency communications.

Staff documents.

Records requests.

And increasingly, AI may assist with creating some of it.

Being able to identify that an AI system was likely involved in producing a piece of content could become another useful piece of information for communications, records, privacy and governance teams.

But we need to be incredibly careful about what that information actually tells us.

A Watermark Does Not Prove Authorship

This is probably the most important part.

Anthropic is very clear about the limitation.

Its watermark can help answer something closer to:

“How likely is it that Claude was involved with this text?”

That is NOT the same question as:

“Did Claude write this?”

And it definitely is not the same as:

“Is this document authentic?”

Claude could have drafted the whole thing.

Claude could have substantially edited something written by a human.

Or a person could have used Claude as one small part of a much larger process.

The watermark cannot tell us who ultimately authored, approved or took responsibility for the content.

And there are other limitations.

Short pieces of text are harder to detect because there simply are not enough word choices to build a strong signal.

Highly factual writing can contain less watermarking because there are fewer reasonable alternatives.

Code can also contain less watermarking because sometimes there is simply one correct answer.

And significant rewriting can weaken or remove the signal.

So please, please do not turn this into another magic AI detector.

AI Provenance and Record Authenticity Are Two Different Things

This is where I think local government policy needs to become more sophisticated.

We need to separate two questions.

Question 1: Was AI involved?

A watermark may eventually help us answer that.

Question 2: Is this an authentic organizational record?

That requires something different.

Where did the document come from?

Was it published through an official municipal channel?

Who approved it?

Do we have the original record?

Was it digitally signed?

Is there an audit trail?

Does the organization have another way to verify its provenance?

Those are records-management and governance questions.

And an AI watermark does not replace them.

Files Are Getting Provenance Information Too

Anthropic is taking a different approach with certain supported files such as PNG, JPG and SVG files.

Instead of the text watermark, those files can include C2PA Content Credentials.

Think of these more like a cryptographically signed note attached to the file’s metadata.

It can indicate that Claude was involved in creating or processing the file.

Again, though, that does not automatically mean:

“This is an official City document.”

It means:

“Claude was involved with this file.”

Those are VERY different things.

Why I Think Municipalities Need to Start Talking About This Now

We are moving beyond the question:

“Did someone use AI?”

AI is becoming part of normal workplace processes.

The bigger governance question is becoming:

“Can we explain how this information was created, reviewed, approved and published?”

That is where human oversight comes straight back into the conversation.

AI may create the first draft.

It may edit the language.

It may generate an image.

It may summarize the research.

It may even leave behind a machine-readable signal saying it was involved.

But AI does not approve the public notice.

AI does not become the Corporate Officer.

AI does not take responsibility for the Council report.

AI does not suddenly become the official record.

The human and the organization still own that responsibility.

What I Would Start Adding to AI Governance

Local governments do not necessarily need an entirely new policy tomorrow because Claude has a watermark.

But this development is a very good reason to review existing AI, communications and records-management policies.

I would start asking:

  • How do we identify AI-assisted content?
  • Do staff need to disclose AI use, and under what circumstances?
  • How do we verify the authenticity of official municipal communications?
  • What systems establish the official record?
  • Who approves AI-assisted material before publication?
  • How should staff interpret AI-detection or watermark results?
  • How do we prevent a watermark from being treated as proof of authorship?
  • What provenance information should we retain with organizational records?

Because the technology is changing.

Our governance needs to change with it.

And I actually think developments like this are encouraging.

More provenance tools can give organizations better information about how digital content was created.

We just need to understand what those tools can tell us and, equally importantly, what they cannot.

AI can leave clues about its involvement.

The human still needs to establish authenticity, approve the work and own the outcome.

Need Help Turning This Into Practical AI Governance?

If your local government is trying to update its AI policy, records practices, staff procedures or governance framework to deal with AI-generated content, I would love to help.

I work with municipalities to take developments exactly like this and turn them into practical rules staff can actually use, without creating another 47-page policy nobody wants to read.

AI is changing fast.

Our governance can keep up.

title: Paid AI vs. Free AI: Who Is Actually the Product?
author: Daphne
excerpt: When we talk about using AI at work, especially in local government, one of the first questions I ask is: Are you using the paid version or the free version? Because there can be a pretty significant difference. Here’s the simplest way I explain it. With a paid AI service, there is usually a transactional […]
content:
When we talk about using AI at work, especially in local government, one of the first questions I ask is:

Are you using the paid version or the free version?

Because there can be a pretty significant difference.

Here’s the simplest way I explain it.

With a paid AI service, there is usually a transactional agreement.

You pay for the product or service, and depending on the platform and licence, you may receive additional contractual protections, administrative controls, privacy settings, security features, and governance options.

With a free consumer version, the transaction can look very different.

You are not necessarily paying with money.

Sometimes, you are the product.

What Does “You Are the Product” Actually Mean?

Some free AI services may use your prompts, interactions, feedback, or other information to improve their models or services, depending on the platform, account type, settings, and terms of use.

And this is where I start getting a little twitchy when we talk about local government.

Think about what municipal employees work with every day:

  • Council information
  • HR questions
  • Draft reports
  • Resident information
  • Internal policies
  • Procurement documents
  • Financial information
  • Records
  • Operational information

Now imagine someone copying that information into a free AI tool without first understanding what happens to it.

That is where convenience can very quickly become a governance problem.

Before You Paste, Ask the Questions

Before putting organizational information into an AI system, ask:

Who owns this data?

Where is the information stored?

Can my prompts or files be used to train or improve the system?

Can an administrator control how the tool is used?

Is there an audit trail?

What did we actually agree to when we clicked “accept”?

Those questions matter a whole lot more than whether the AI can write a beautiful Council report in 30 seconds.

Because the output might be impressive.

The data handling behind it matters too.

Paid Does Not Automatically Mean Safe

This is an important distinction.

I am not saying:

Paid = safe. Free = unsafe.

That would be far too simple.

A paid organizational licence will often provide stronger protections and controls than a free consumer account, but your organization still needs to understand the terms, configuration, privacy requirements, data residency, security settings, and internal policies.

The human still needs to do the homework.

There it is again.

The human.

AI does not suddenly remove our responsibility because we bought a licence.

My Simple Rule

When someone tells me an AI tool is completely free, one of my first questions is:

What is the transaction?

Because there is usually one.

Maybe you are paying with money.

Maybe you are paying with data.

Maybe the company is funding the free version as part of another business model.

Whatever the answer is, organizations should understand it before employees start putting work information into the system.

Especially in local government, where privacy, public trust, records management, security, and accountability matter enormously.

So before celebrating that shiny new free AI tool, ask one more question:

If I am not paying for the product, what exactly am I exchanging for it?

Sometimes you are using the product.

And sometimes, you may be the product.

AI can be incredibly useful. Use it.

Just know what you are agreeing to before you hand it your information.

If your municipality is trying to figure out which AI tools are appropriate, what guardrails should be in place, or how to introduce AI without creating a privacy and governance headache, that is exactly the kind of practical implementation work I love helping with.

Use the tool. Stay the human.

title: Is It AI? Canada Is Asking Some Very Important Questions About Transparency
author: Daphne
excerpt: If a resident is chatting with an artificial intelligence system, should they be told? If an AI agent is taking actions inside an organization, should someone be tracking what it does? If an AI system causes a serious incident, who records it, investigates it, and explains what happened? These are no longer hypothetical questions. Innovation, […]
content:
If a resident is chatting with an artificial intelligence system, should they be told?

If an AI agent is taking actions inside an organization, should someone be tracking what it does?

If an AI system causes a serious incident, who records it, investigates it, and explains what happened?

These are no longer hypothetical questions.

Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada has released a detailed discussion paper as part of its ongoing consultation on AI transparency.

The paper, Enhancing Trust in Artificial Intelligence Through Increased Transparency, asks Canadians to consider whether government action may be needed in five important areas.

For local governments, this consultation is worth watching closely.

This is not only about adding a label to an AI generated image. It could eventually affect how municipalities procure AI systems, disclose their use to residents, document their agents, and respond when something goes wrong.

The Five Areas Canada Is Examining

The federal discussion paper focuses on five areas where greater transparency may be needed.

1. Identifying AI Generated Content

As AI generated images, videos, audio, and written content become more convincing, people may have difficulty determining what is authentic.

The consultation asks whether tools such as watermarking, metadata, labels, or other forms of identification should be used to help people recognize AI generated content.

For local government, this could matter when creating public notices, emergency messages, consultation materials, social media posts, presentations, and other public communications.

If AI helped create or substantially alter the content, should the municipality disclose that?

The answer may depend on the purpose, the risk, and the expectations of the public. A decorative image in a newsletter is not the same as an altered video of an elected official speaking.

Context matters.

2. Telling People When They Are Interacting With AI

Imagine a resident visits a municipal website and begins chatting with what appears to be a staff member.

The system answers questions about property taxes, recreation programs, permits, bylaws, or garbage collection.

Should the resident be clearly told that the response is being provided by AI?

I believe that answer should usually be yes.

Residents should know whether they are speaking with a person or a system. They should also know what the system can and cannot do, how to reach a human, and whether the information provided needs to be confirmed.

A friendly robot avatar is not a replacement for meaningful disclosure.

Municipalities should also consider what happens when the system gets something wrong.

Who corrects the information?

Who contacts the affected resident?

Who owns the final outcome?

AI can assist with public service. It cannot carry public responsibility.

3. Providing Understandable Information About AI Systems

Transparency does not mean giving residents a fifty page technical manual filled with terminology that requires three engineers and a pot of coffee to understand.

It means providing useful information in plain language.

People may need to know:

  • What the AI system is being used for
  • What information it can access
  • What decisions it can influence
  • What its known limitations are
  • Whether a human reviews its output
  • How someone can question or challenge an outcome

Local governments should be able to explain their AI systems to Council, staff, residents, auditors, and other interested parties.

If the organization cannot explain what a system does, it probably should not be relying on it for important municipal work.

4. Tracking Serious AI Incidents

The consultation also asks whether serious incidents involving AI systems should be tracked.

This could include situations where an AI system causes harm, exposes sensitive information, produces discriminatory outcomes, provides dangerously incorrect information, or takes an unauthorized action.

Local governments already plan for emergencies, cybersecurity events, privacy breaches, workplace incidents, and service disruptions.

AI incidents should not sit outside those established processes.

Organizations may need clear procedures that identify:

  • What qualifies as an AI incident
  • Who must be notified
  • How the system will be contained
  • What records must be preserved
  • Who investigates the incident
  • How affected people will be informed
  • When Council or senior leadership must be advised

Waiting until something goes wrong to decide who owns the response is not an incident plan. It is a group panic with a meeting invitation.

5. Tracking AI Agents and Their Activities

This may be the most important part of the consultation for organizations beginning to use AI agents.

An AI agent can do more than draft text. Depending on its permissions, it may retrieve information, update records, monitor an inbox, create reports, send notifications, or trigger another action.

That means organizations need to know which agents exist and what each one is allowed to do.

A municipal AI agent inventory could record:

  • The name and purpose of the agent
  • The department responsible for it
  • The system where it operates
  • The information it can access
  • The actions it can perform
  • The human accountable for reviewing its work
  • The risks and controls associated with it
  • The date it was approved and last reviewed

One task. One agent. One accountable human.

Please do not create a giant know it all municipal robot, give it access to everything, and then act surprised when nobody knows what it is doing.

What Could This Mean for Municipal Procurement?

The consultation may also influence what public sector organizations eventually need to ask vendors.

Future procurement requirements could include questions about disclosure, incident reporting, system documentation, audit logs, data sovereignty, watermarking, agent tracking, and human oversight.

Municipalities do not need to wait for formal requirements before improving their procurement questions.

Before purchasing or approving an AI system, ask:

  • Where will municipal information be stored?
  • Who owns the information entered into the system?
  • Can the provider use that information for model training?
  • What audit and activity records are available?
  • How are serious incidents reported?
  • Can the municipality identify every action performed by an agent?
  • Can access be limited or removed?
  • What happens to the information when the contract ends?

Paid organizational licences often provide stronger administrative and governance options, but the municipality still needs to review the terms, configuration, and internal policy fit.

Paid does not automatically mean appropriate.

The Outcome Is Not Predetermined

Importantly, ISED says the results of the consultation are not predetermined.

The federal government is asking which interventions would be proportionate and where existing laws, standards, or market practices may already be sufficient.

That is an important approach.

Good AI governance should address real risks without creating unnecessary administration. Local governments already have policies and processes covering privacy, records, procurement, cybersecurity, communications, workplace conduct, and incident response.

In many cases, the best approach may be to add AI responsibilities to those existing systems instead of creating an entirely separate universe of forms, committees, and binders.

The consultation remains open until September 23, 2026.

Start With Visibility

Local governments do not need to predict every future federal requirement.

They can begin with one practical question:

Do we know which AI systems and agents our organization is already using?

If the answer is no, start there.

Create an inventory. Identify the owners. Review the permissions. Document the risks. Decide how residents will be informed. Establish an incident response process.

AI transparency is not about explaining every line of code.

It is about ensuring that people understand when AI is involved, what it is doing, where its limits sit, and which human remains responsible.

Use the tool. Stay the human.

Ready to Build Practical AI Governance?

If your local government is using AI or preparing to introduce agents, now is the time to put practical governance in place.

Book time with me to discuss AI inventories, agent governance, procurement questions, staff training, public disclosure, and incident response planning.

Let’s make AI useful, understandable, and accountable before someone has to explain to Council why the robot did not introduce itself.

title: Who Gets Plugged In? Ontario’s Data Centre Playbook Raises Big Questions for Local Government
author: Daphne
excerpt: Ontario has released a draft Data Centre Playbook, and this is one Canadian public sector development that local governments should be watching closely. The playbook will help the province determine which large data centre projects should receive approval to connect to Ontario’s electricity grid. But this is not only about power supply. The proposed framework […]
content:
Ontario has released a draft Data Centre Playbook, and this is one Canadian public sector development that local governments should be watching closely.

The playbook will help the province determine which large data centre projects should receive approval to connect to Ontario’s electricity grid.

But this is not only about power supply.

The proposed framework will also evaluate projects based on economic development, data security, digital sovereignty, and the benefits provided to host communities.

That last part is particularly important.

A data centre may be presented as a major investment, but a large building filled with servers does not automatically create meaningful or lasting community benefit.

AI Infrastructure Is Becoming Municipal Infrastructure

Data centres support artificial intelligence, cloud computing, digital services, and the growing amount of information organizations create and store.

They also exist in real communities.

They require land. They consume electricity. Depending on their design, they may affect local water systems. They can place new demands on roads, emergency services, utilities, planning departments, and other municipal infrastructure.

This means local governments need to be part of the conversation before a data centre is approved and connected, not after construction begins.

Municipal leaders should be asking:

  • How much electricity will the facility require?
  • Will local infrastructure need to be expanded?
  • Who will pay for those improvements?
  • How will water be used and managed?
  • What emergency planning will be required?
  • How many permanent local jobs will actually be created?
  • What tax revenue or community benefits will remain locally?
  • How will residents be consulted?

The promise of economic development needs to be supported by a clear understanding of the long term municipal impact.

Digital Sovereignty Is Not Just a Federal Issue

Ontario’s inclusion of data security and digital sovereignty is particularly significant.

Digital sovereignty is about more than knowing where a server is physically located. It also includes who owns the data, which laws apply to it, who can access it, and how much control Canadian organizations retain over their information.

For local governments, these questions are already very real.

Municipalities hold sensitive information about residents, employees, properties, infrastructure, emergency response, finances, and Council decisions. As more public sector work moves into cloud and artificial intelligence systems, understanding where that information travels becomes essential.

Before adopting an artificial intelligence platform or digital service, local governments should be able to answer:

  • Where is the information stored?
  • Who owns the information uploaded into the system?
  • Can the provider use that information to train its models?
  • Who can access the information?
  •  
  • Which country’s laws govern the data?
  • Can the municipality retrieve or delete its information?
  • Is there a clear record of how the information was processed?

If those questions cannot be answered, the organization is not ready to rely on the system.

Community Benefit Must Be More Than a Promise

Ontario’s playbook recognizes that host communities should receive meaningful benefits from large data centre projects.

That is a good start, but local governments will need to define what meaningful benefit actually looks like.

It could include local employment, infrastructure investment, emergency preparedness funding, community amenities, environmental protections, education partnerships, or direct support for local digital capacity.

The benefit should be specific, measurable, and documented.

“Jobs and investment” may sound wonderful in a presentation to Council, but elected officials and staff need enough information to determine what those words mean in practice.

How many jobs?

For how long?

At what cost to municipal infrastructure?

What happens if the facility changes ownership or operations?

Who remains accountable if the promised benefits do not materialize?

That is where the human comes in.

Local Governments Need a Seat at the Table

The 30 day public consultation on Ontario’s draft playbook began on August 13, 2026. The final framework is expected to support the province’s upcoming AI Industrial Strategy.

Although this is an Ontario initiative, the questions it raises matter across Canada.

Every province, territory, and municipality will eventually need to consider how data centres fit into economic development, energy planning, land use, environmental responsibility, public safety, and digital sovereignty.

Artificial intelligence may operate in the cloud, but the infrastructure supporting it sits somewhere very real.

It sits on land.

It draws electricity.

It may use water.

It affects a community.

Local governments cannot treat data centres as purely technical projects. These are governance, infrastructure, economic development, and public trust decisions.

The question is not simply whether a data centre can be connected.

The better question is whether the project creates responsible, measurable, and lasting value for the community hosting it.

Ready to Prepare Your Local Government?

If your local government is exploring artificial intelligence, digital governance, data security, or the municipal impacts of emerging technology, let’s talk.

Book time with me to discuss practical AI implementation, staff training, governance, and how your organization can prepare before the technology arrives at your door asking to be plugged in.

title: AI Is Getting Cheaper
author: Daphne
excerpt: That Does Not Mean Local Government Should Chase the Cheapest Tool. AI pricing is coming down. That sounds like great news, and it is. But for local government, price should never be the only question. The better question is: What are we actually buying, and how well does it fit inside the environment we already […]
content:
That Does Not Mean Local Government Should Chase the Cheapest Tool.

AI pricing is coming down.

That sounds like great news, and it is.

But for local government, price should never be the only question.

The better question is:

What are we actually buying, and how well does it fit inside the environment we already govern?

ChatGPT Business pricing has dropped. Anthropic has also introduced lower pricing and additional savings through things like prompt caching and batch processing.

And Microsoft has lowered the cost of Microsoft 365 Copilot Business as well.

On the surface, this looks like a pricing battle.

For municipalities, I think there is a much more interesting conversation happening underneath it.

The Cheapest AI Tool May Not Be the Cheapest AI Strategy

Imagine your organization already uses:

Microsoft 365

Outlook

Teams

SharePoint

Word

Excel

PowerPoint

Entra identity and permissions

Records and documents are already moving through that environment every single day.

Then someone introduces another AI platform.

The subscription might be cheaper.

But now ask the next questions.

Where does staff access it?

What information can they upload?

Who manages permissions?

How is organizational data handled?

Can IT manage access centrally?

How do staff know which AI tool they should use for which task?

How do you train everyone?

How do you govern another platform?

Suddenly, the monthly licence price is only one tiny part of the actual cost.

This is where Microsoft Copilot becomes particularly interesting for local government.

Sometimes the Restrictions Are Actually the Selling Point

People often talk about AI restrictions like they are a negative.

For municipal organizations, I do not necessarily see them that way.

Microsoft 365 Copilot works within the Microsoft environment and the permissions already attached to it.

That matters.

If an employee cannot access a SharePoint document normally, AI should not suddenly become the magical back door to it.

That is exactly the kind of boring governance feature I get excited about.

And yes, I just called permissions exciting.

Welcome to local government AI.

Microsoft also offers Copilot Chat with many qualifying Microsoft 365 licences, which gives organizations another opportunity to introduce AI without immediately handing every employee the most powerful licence available.

You can start smaller.

Train people.

Establish your rules.

Understand the workflows.

Then expand where there is a legitimate business case.

That is a much healthier AI strategy than buying every shiny tool because somebody saw a fantastic demo on LinkedIn.

This Is Not an Argument That Copilot Is Automatically Safe

No AI platform gets a magical governance halo because you paid for it.

Your municipality still needs to understand its licensing, configuration, privacy requirements, security controls, data handling, permissions and acceptable use.

You still need human verification.

You still need staff training.

You still need governance.

And the human still owns the outcome.

That principle does not change because Microsoft, OpenAI or Anthropic built the tool. It is central to responsible municipal AI adoption. 

DT Content DNA.docx

Think About the Whole Environment

When I work with local governments on AI implementation, I encourage them to look beyond the monthly licence cost.

Look at the whole operating environment.

Where are your records?

Where are your policies?

Where do staff work?

What software is already governed?

What permissions already exist?

What systems does IT already administer?

Where can AI genuinely reduce workload without creating five new governance problems?

If most of your municipal work already lives inside Microsoft 365, there is a very strong argument for investigating what can be accomplished within that environment before building an entirely separate AI ecosystem.

Not because Microsoft automatically wins every AI comparison.

It does not.

But because the best AI tool is not necessarily the model with the lowest monthly price or the flashiest benchmark.

For local government, the better tool may be the one your organization can actually govern, train, manage and use responsibly.

Want Help Figuring Out What That Looks Like?

I help local governments move from “We have Copilot” to “We actually know what to do with Copilot.”

That can include licensing and readiness reviews, AI governance, staff and Council training, practical Microsoft 365 use cases, Copilot agents, workflow design and implementation planning.

If your organization already lives in Microsoft and you are wondering whether you should stay there, expand Copilot, introduce other AI tools, or build a mixed environment, contact me.

We can figure out what makes sense for the work your municipality actually does.

AI is the tool. You are the human. The decision is still yours.

title: AI Transparency: Does Everything Need a Label?
author: Daphne
excerpt: AI Transparency: Does Everything Need a Label? Europe has decided that people should know when they are interacting with certain AI systems or viewing certain AI generated or manipulated content. On August 2, 2026, transparency obligations under Article 50 of the European Union’s AI Act became applicable. Among other requirements, interactive AI systems such as […]
content:
AI Transparency: Does Everything Need a Label?

Europe has decided that people should know when they are interacting with certain AI systems or viewing certain AI generated or manipulated content.

On August 2, 2026, transparency obligations under Article 50 of the European Union’s AI Act became applicable. Among other requirements, interactive AI systems such as chatbots may need to tell users they are dealing with AI. Deepfakes and certain AI generated or manipulated content must also be labelled, while providers face requirements involving machine readable markings. 

At first glance, the principle sounds obvious.

People should know when they are dealing with AI.

But should they know every single time AI touches something?

That is where the question becomes much more interesting.

AI Is Already Everywhere

Most people use AI throughout the day without announcing it.

Netflix recommends a show based on viewing history.

Google Maps recommends a route.

Email systems filter spam.

Phones enhance photographs.

Online stores suggest products.

Grammar tools improve writing.

Few people finish watching a movie and say, “For transparency, an algorithm recommended this.”

They simply watch it.

The same is true when Google Maps redirects a driver around traffic. The person does not usually explain that an AI supported system helped select the route.

These tools are becoming ordinary.

Eventually, using AI may be as unremarkable as using a calculator, spreadsheet or search engine.

So, should every use require a disclosure?

I am not convinced it should.

When Transparency Becomes Noise

Transparency is valuable when it helps someone understand something meaningful.

But disclosure can lose its value when it appears everywhere.

Think about the warning messages people already click through without reading.

Cookie notices.

Terms and conditions.

Software permissions.

Privacy notices.

If every municipal document, image, email and social post carries a broad statement that AI was involved somewhere in the process, the disclosure may become background noise.

The public may stop noticing it.

That creates an uncomfortable possibility.

Could maximum transparency actually weaken meaningful transparency?

When everything carries a label, the labels attached to genuinely significant uses may no longer stand out.

A disclosure that matters should tell the reader something important. It should not simply confirm that a common workplace tool helped with spelling, formatting or organization.

The Better Question

Instead of asking only:

Was AI used?

Perhaps public bodies should ask:

Did AI materially shape the decision, communication or interaction in a way the affected person should understand?

That question moves us away from automatic disclosure and toward proportional disclosure.

Consider a few municipal examples.

If AI corrects grammar in a community newsletter, does the public need a warning?

Probably not.

If AI helps an employee organize background information for a council report, but the employee verifies the material and owns the recommendation, is a public label necessary?

Perhaps not.

If a resident is speaking directly with a municipal chatbot and could reasonably believe it is a human employee, disclosure makes sense.

If a synthetic image depicts an emergency, public official or community event that never occurred, clear labelling is essential.

If an AI system influences eligibility for housing, recreation assistance, employment, enforcement or access to a municipal service, transparency becomes much more important.

The difference is not merely whether AI was present.

The difference is what role it played.

Assistance Is Not the Same as Influence

Not all AI use carries the same consequences.

There is a meaningful difference between AI assisting with a task and AI materially influencing an outcome.

AI might assist by:

  • correcting spelling
  • adjusting formatting
  • organizing notes
  • suggesting headings
  • improving image quality
  • summarizing information for human review

AI might exert greater influence by:

  • recommending who receives a service
  • assessing a permit or application
  • prioritizing enforcement activity
  • scoring procurement submissions
  • generating public safety information
  • producing synthetic media about a public issue
  • communicating directly with residents without an obvious human presence

Those uses should not necessarily be governed by the same disclosure rule.

A blanket label may be easy to write into policy, but easy is not always thoughtful.

The Public Sector Has a Higher Trust Obligation

Municipalities are not Netflix.

A streaming recommendation might affect how someone spends an evening.

A municipal system can affect rights, access, public money, safety and trust.

That does not mean every municipal use of AI must be publicly announced.

It does mean the threshold for meaningful disclosure should reflect the power of the interaction.

Residents should understand when they are communicating with a machine rather than a person.

They should understand when synthetic media could reasonably be mistaken for reality.

They should understand when automation materially affects a decision concerning them.

They should also know how to question an outcome, request human review or correct inaccurate information.

That is transparency with purpose.

What About Human Accountability?

Disclosure should never become a substitute for accountability.

A municipality should not be able to place a small “AI generated” label on a communication and treat the matter as resolved.

The harder questions remain:

Who approved the content?

Who verified the facts?

Who assessed the risks?

Who owns the final decision?

Who responds when the system is wrong?

Can a resident reach a human?

A label may tell the public that AI was involved.

It does not tell them whether the organization used it responsibly.

That is why transparency must sit alongside governance, training, records practices, privacy controls and human oversight.

AI can help create the work.

It cannot carry the responsibility.

A Proportionate Disclosure Test

Canadian public bodies could use the EU requirements as a benchmark while developing a more contextual test for their own policies.

Before requiring disclosure, an organization could ask:

Could a reasonable person mistake the AI for a human?

A chatbot presenting itself as a municipal representative should probably disclose that it is automated.

Could the content reasonably be mistaken for an authentic event, person or statement?

Synthetic audio, video and imagery create obvious risks, particularly during emergencies, elections and contentious public debates.

Did AI materially influence a decision affecting someone?

The greater the impact on rights, services, finances or opportunities, the stronger the case for transparency.

Would knowing about the AI involvement change how someone interprets the information?

If the answer is yes, disclosure may be valuable.

Would the disclosure provide meaningful information, or merely add another ignored disclaimer?

Transparency should improve understanding, not simply increase the volume of legal language.

Canada Should Learn Without Copying Blindly

Canadian public bodies may face direct EU obligations in some circumstances, including through services operating in Europe, interactions involving people in the EU or vendors applying European requirements across global products. The exact legal application will depend on the facts and should be assessed carefully.

But even where the EU AI Act does not directly apply, it provides a useful opportunity to examine Canadian public sector practices.

The lesson should not necessarily be:

Label everything.

The better lesson may be:

Define when disclosure protects trust, and make those disclosures clear enough to matter.

There is a danger in saying too little.

There may also be a danger in saying so much that nobody pays attention.

Meaningful Transparency, Not Maximum Transparency

AI will likely become an ordinary part of work.

People will use it to write, search, plan, navigate, design, calculate and communicate.

Pretending that every use is exceptional will eventually become unrealistic.

But treating every use as invisible would also be irresponsible.

The balance lies in understanding when AI meaningfully changes the relationship between a public body and the person it serves.

Transparency matters most when AI can mislead, impersonate, influence or decide.

For routine assistance, disclosure may add little.

For consequential uses, it may be non negotiable.

The goal should not be to tell people that AI exists.

They already know.

The goal should be to help them recognize when its role actually matters.

Where should public bodies draw the line between ordinary tool use and AI involvement that deserves clear disclosure?

title: An 87% AI Score Means Almost Nothing Without Context
author: Daphne
excerpt: An AI evaluation score without context is just a very confident number. A vendor tells you their AI system achieved an 87% accuracy score. Wonderful. But what was tested? Which model version was used? What counted as a correct answer? Was the system tested using real municipal situations, or a tidy dataset that bears very […]
content:
An AI evaluation score without context is just a very confident number.

A vendor tells you their AI system achieved an 87% accuracy score.

Wonderful.

But what was tested? Which model version was used? What counted as a correct answer? Was the system tested using real municipal situations, or a tidy dataset that bears very little resemblance to the beautiful chaos of local government?

That 87% may be impressive.

It may also be very fancy nonsense.

The Canadian Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute recently outlined what AI evaluators should share so that evaluation results can be properly understood, compared and used.

This is technical guidance, but its message matters enormously for local government leaders, procurement teams and anyone being asked to approve an AI tool.

A Score Is Not the Same as Evidence

Think about it this way.

If someone told Council that a bridge was “87% safe,” the next question would not be, “Where do we sign?”

Council would want to know:

  • Who conducted the assessment?
  • What standards were used?
  • What conditions were tested?
  • What was not tested?
  • How confident are we in the result?
  • Who paid for the assessment?
  • What happens in the other 13%?

We need to bring that same level of curiosity to AI.

A benchmark score cannot tell us whether a system is appropriate for drafting council reports, summarizing bylaws, reviewing procurement documents, answering resident questions or supporting service delivery.

The evaluation must reflect the way the system will actually be used.

What Should an AI Evaluation Tell Us?

The federal guidance identifies several areas evaluators should clearly report.

1. The Purpose of the Evaluation

What question was the evaluation designed to answer?

A test of an AI system’s general writing ability is not the same as testing whether it can accurately summarize a 200-page municipal agenda package.

An evaluation may measure capability, safety controls, alignment or performance in a specific environment. Unless the purpose is clear, we cannot know whether the result applies to our intended use.

2. The Context in Which the AI Was Tested

Who was expected to use the system?

Was it tested with ordinary users, technical experts, malicious users or people repeatedly trying to bypass its safeguards?

The context matters because AI performance can change depending on the task, the user, the instructions and the information provided.

A model that performs well in a controlled demonstration may behave very differently when ten departments use it for ten different purposes.

3. The Methodology

Evaluators should explain:

  • What was measured
  • Which metrics were used
  • Which datasets were included
  • How answers were scored
  • Whether another AI system judged the results
  • Whether humans reviewed the outputs
  • Why the chosen method was appropriate

This is where it gets interesting.

An evaluation may use automated scoring, human reviewers or even another large language model to judge whether the first model provided a good answer.

If AI is grading AI, we should probably ask whether a human checked the homework.

4. The Exact System and Settings Tested

AI tools change quickly.

Evaluators should identify the model version, configuration, prompts and relevant settings used during testing. A result from one model version may not apply after the provider updates the system.

This creates a very practical procurement question:

Are we buying access to the same system that was evaluated, under the same conditions?

If the answer is unclear, the benchmark may not tell us very much about what municipal staff will actually receive.

5. Uncertainty and Limitations

A score is rarely as precise as it appears.

The federal guidance recommends reporting confidence intervals and other information that helps readers understand uncertainty. For example, one model may score 83% and another 87%, but overlapping confidence intervals could mean there is no statistically meaningful difference between them.

Four percentage points can look very impressive in a sales presentation.

It may not mean the second system is actually better.

Evaluators should also explain where the results may not apply, whether the benchmark is becoming outdated and what errors may have been introduced by the testing method.

6. Potential Conflicts of Interest

Who conducted the evaluation, and what is their relationship with the company that developed or sells the system?

A vendor’s internal evaluation can still provide useful information, but it is not the same as independent testing.

Local governments should know whether the evaluator is completely independent, funded by the developer or otherwise connected to the system being assessed.

That information helps decision-makers determine whether additional testing or verification is required.

Transparency Does Not Mean Publishing Everything

There is an important balance here.

The federal guidance recognizes that some information should not be publicly released.

Cybersecurity testing methods, jailbreak instructions and datasets containing dangerous information could become a step-by-step guide for misuse. Publishing an entire test dataset can also contaminate future evaluations if AI models are later trained on those same questions and answers.

The recommended approach is layered disclosure.

Different information may be shared with:

  • The public
  • Governments and trusted oversight bodies
  • Independent evaluators
  • System developers and owners

The goal is to provide enough information for meaningful accountability without creating new safety risks or weakening future evaluations.

That is not secrecy.

It is responsible transparency.

What This Means for Local Government Procurement

Before accepting an AI benchmark, assurance statement or vendor performance claim, municipalities should ask:

  1. What exactly was tested?
  2. Does the test reflect our intended municipal use?
  3. Which model version and settings were evaluated?
  4. What data, prompts and languages were included?
  5. How were the answers scored?
  6. Did humans audit the results?
  7. What uncertainty or limitations were identified?
  8. Who conducted and funded the evaluation?
  9. Can the test be independently replicated?
  10. What important information has been withheld, and why?

These questions should form part of AI procurement, pilot planning, privacy reviews and ongoing vendor management.

AI evaluation is not simply a technical exercise for IT.

It affects procurement, governance, privacy, service delivery and public trust.

The Human Still Owns the Decision

AI can produce the benchmark.

A vendor can present the score.

An evaluator can explain the methodology.

But the organization still has to decide whether that evidence is relevant, reliable and sufficient for the proposed use.

AI is the tool.

You are the human.

The decision is still yours.

Before approving the next AI pilot, ask one critical question:

Are we evaluating the system, or are we simply trusting the marketing?

Need Help Asking the Right AI Questions?

If your municipality is exploring, purchasing or already using AI, I can help your staff and Council understand the technology, evaluate the risks and build practical guardrails around its use.

Learn more about my practical AI Workshop for local government and book me to help your team use AI with confidence, curiosity and human accountability.

title: I Took Alberta’s AI Academy for a Spin. Here’s My Local Government Review.
author: Daphne
excerpt: I have spent enough time inside the Alberta AI Academy to confirm three things. First, Alberta is taking AI adoption seriously. Second, Deputy Ministers apparently teach masterclasses now. And third, somewhere between NotebookLM, Nano Banana, Copilot and agentic workflows, I began to feel as though I had wandered into an AI buffet with a very […]
content:
I have spent enough time inside the Alberta AI Academy to confirm three things.

First, Alberta is taking AI adoption seriously.

Second, Deputy Ministers apparently teach masterclasses now.

And third, somewhere between NotebookLM, Nano Banana, Copilot and agentic workflows, I began to feel as though I had wandered into an AI buffet with a very small plate.

Let’s start with the part I found genuinely impressive.

The Academy begins with a masterclass led by Janak Alford, Alberta’s Deputy Minister of Technology and Innovation.

Not a consultant hired to narrate the slides.

Not a mysterious voice floating over stock footage of people pointing at holograms.

The Deputy Minister himself.

I really like that.

Leadership matters during organizational change. When a senior public servant is prepared to learn the technology, use it and personally teach it, that sends a much stronger message than an email telling everyone else to “embrace innovation.”

It says: I am learning this too.

That may be one of the strongest features of the entire Academy.

What the Academy Gets Right

The Alberta AI Academy is open access, does not require a login and was created primarily for Alberta public servants, although much of the content is available to everyone.

That is fantastic.

AI literacy should not be locked behind a $4,999 course, three promotional webinars and a countdown clock telling you the price will disappear at midnight.

The Academy gives people a structured place to begin.

There are frequent quizzes, clear learning paths and a combination of articles, videos, examples and practical exercises. The quizzes are a particularly good touch because they force you to stop and ask:

Did I actually understand that?

Or did I simply nod confidently while the video played?

We have all done both.

Level 1: The Great AI Tasting Menu

Level 1 is a 10-day foundational program, and it covers a lot.

It introduces:

  • What AI is and how it works
  • Why AI hallucinates
  • Prompting and context
  • The RICECO prompting framework
  • The T.R.U.S.T. verification framework
  • NotebookLM
  • Microsoft 365 Copilot
  • AI assistants and agents
  • Public-sector research
  • JSON
  • Nano Banana image generation
  • Sora video generation
  • ElevenLabs voice tools
  • Agentic workflows
  • Albert, Alberta’s own AI assistant

As an introduction to the AI landscape, it is very good.

It gives beginners a strong vocabulary and helps people understand that AI is much more than asking ChatGPT to rewrite an email while desperately hoping it removes the phrase “I hope this email finds you well.”

The prompting content is useful. The explanation of hallucinations is important. The RICECO and T.R.U.S.T. frameworks give learners a practical structure for generating and checking outputs.

NotebookLM is also one of my favourite tools, so I was delighted to see it included.

Level 1’s greatest strength is its breadth.

Its greatest weakness is also its breadth.

There is so much included that it sometimes becomes an overview of what exists rather than a demonstration of how public servants would use it inside a real workflow.

The Google flavour is noticeable. There is dedicated content on NotebookLM, Gemini GEMs and Nano Banana, while Microsoft 365 Copilot receives one dedicated introductory day followed by some agent material.

For a general public-service audience, that mix may work.

For local government, I would shift the balance.

Most municipalities I work with live inside Microsoft 365. Their work moves through Outlook, Word, Excel, Teams, SharePoint, Power Automate, Power BI and Power Apps.

That is their habitat.

Google tools can absolutely be useful, but if the learner returns to an organization built almost entirely around Microsoft, they still need help crossing the gap between:

“This tool is very cool.”

And:

“This is how I use it on Monday morning without creating a privacy incident before lunch.”

One reference in the masterclass also described what “most Americans” want. In a Canadian public-service course, that landed a little strangely for me. It was not catastrophic. Nobody needed to activate the emergency operations centre. But it did make me wonder who the course imagined as its primary audience.

The presentation style can also lean into broad, theatrical humour. That will help some learners stay engaged. For me, a few moments were close to slapstick territory.

I enjoy humour. I have been known to explain hallucinations in ways that would make a risk manager gently close their laptop.

But humour works best when it helps the practical lesson land. Occasionally, I wanted less performance and more:

“Here is the municipal task. Here is the tool. Here is the workflow. Here is the risk. Here is where the human verifies it.”

Level 2: Now We Are Getting Somewhere

Level 2 is currently structured over five days, not 10.

This is where the Academy starts moving from using AI to building with it.

It covers:

  • Prompting and context engineering
  • The difference between an assistant and an agent
  • Agentic workflows
  • Computer languages
  • Alberta’s Agent Builder Console
  • Probabilistic versus deterministic work
  • Copilot Cowork
  • Reusable AI skills
  • Microsoft 365 Copilot agents

There is much more Microsoft content here, which is excellent.

The Academy starts showing how prompts can become repeatable skills and how AI can participate in longer workflows rather than producing one isolated answer.

But I still wanted the technology connected more directly to recognizable local government work.

For example, imagine a municipal learning exercise where:

  1. Adopted council minutes land in SharePoint.
  2. AI extracts the resolutions, motion numbers and responsible departments.
  3. Power Automate populates a tracking list.
  4. Staff verify the information and update its status.
  5. Power BI produces the dashboard.
  6. A Power App gives management a simple view of outstanding actions.
  7. Copilot prepares a summary before the next meeting.

That is not a hypothetical “AI may someday improve efficiency” example.

It is an actual municipal workflow.

It can remove roughly 90 minutes to two hours of repetitive entry and reporting work from each meeting cycle, while keeping the human responsible for verification.

That is the moment when staff understand why the technology matters.

Not because the Academy told them an agent could do something interesting.

Because they just watched it solve work they do every month.

Level 3: Bring Your Hard Hat

Level 3 is presented as a 10-day advanced pathway focused on building, deploying and scaling AI systems.

It goes much further into:

  • Agent architecture
  • Claude Code
  • Memory and instructions
  • Reusable execution templates
  • Database integration
  • Application development
  • Quality assurance
  • Security
  • Deployment
  • Multi-agent orchestration
  • Prototyping and real-client delivery

This is impressive material.

It is also a substantial jump.

We have moved from “how do I write a better prompt?” to “let us build and deploy a full-stack application.”

Please bring water and appropriate footwear.

For technical teams and advanced practitioners, this could be extremely valuable. For the average municipal employee, CAO, clerk, communications officer or finance professional, it may be more technical than necessary.

Most local governments do not initially need staff to become AI developers.

They need staff to become confident, responsible AI users who can recognize an opportunity, improve a workflow, protect municipal information and keep human accountability firmly in place.

What Is Missing for Local Government?

This is the biggest opportunity I see.

The Academy provides a strong general foundation, but it does not yet consistently translate that knowledge into the everyday operating environment of a municipality.

A dedicated local government pathway could include:

  • Drafting and verifying council reports
  • Extracting resolutions from adopted minutes
  • Reviewing bylaws and policies
  • Building records-management agents
  • Researching legislation with source verification
  • Creating public notices and emergency communications
  • Comparing procurement submissions
  • Processing routine finance information
  • Managing SharePoint-based approval workflows
  • Supporting FOI and privacy reviews
  • Using Copilot inside Word, Excel, Outlook and Teams
  • Connecting SharePoint, Power Automate, Power BI and Power Apps
  • Establishing the human verification point in every workflow

Each lesson could begin with a real municipal problem.

Not “Today we will learn about agentic orchestration.”

More like:

“Corporate Services is tracking 147 resolutions in a spreadsheet held together by conditional formatting, institutional memory and prayer. Let’s fix that.”

Now we have everyone’s attention.

My Overall Take

As a general AI literacy program, the Alberta AI Academy is a strong and generous public resource.

It is accessible.

It is broad.

It introduces important concepts.

It gives people a structured learning journey.

It includes verification, prompting, agents, public-sector research and advanced development.

And having Janak Alford lead the masterclass demonstrates something I wish we saw more often: senior leaders visibly participating in the change they are asking others to make.

As a local government learning pathway, however, it is not quite there yet.

It teaches what the platforms are and what they can potentially do.

The next step is showing municipalities exactly how those tools connect to their work, systems, governance obligations and public accountability.

That is where AI adoption becomes real.

I have reached out to Janak about the possibility of working together and followed up using the email he provided. I would still love the opportunity to have a recorded conversation with him about what Alberta is building, what the Academy is learning and how this work could be translated more directly into practical local government use.

Because the foundation is strong.

The opportunity is enormous.

Now we need to take AI out of the demonstration environment and place it inside the council report, the SharePoint library, the approval process, the records system and the work municipal staff are actually doing.

That is where the aha moment happens.

AI is the tool.

The municipality still owns the work.

And the human still owns the decision.

title: Municipal AI Adoption: Start With People, Not the Tool
author: Daphne
excerpt: Municipal AI Adoption Won’t Fail Because of AI. It Will Fail Because We Forgot About People. Every now and then, I read something that makes me stop and think, “Yes… this is exactly the conversation local government should be having.” That was my reaction after reading Janak Alford’s Velocity White Papers, developed through Alberta Technology […]
content:
Municipal AI Adoption Won’t Fail Because of AI. It Will Fail Because We Forgot About People.

Every now and then, I read something that makes me stop and think, “Yes… this is exactly the conversation local government should be having.”

That was my reaction after reading Janak Alford’s Velocity White Papers, developed through Alberta Technology and Innovation and Alberta Innovates.

There’s plenty of AI content online telling us about the latest model, the newest feature, or the next productivity breakthrough.

This wasn’t that.

Instead, the papers ask a much more important question:

How do we build organizations that are actually ready for AI?

For municipalities, I think that’s exactly the right question.

AI Is Not the Transformation. People Are.

One message comes through loud and clear.

Don’t start with the technology.

Start with your people.

Start with capability.

Start with the work.

That might sound simple, but it’s a significant shift in thinking.

Too often, organizations buy an AI licence, run a one-hour demonstration, and expect staff to suddenly transform the way they work.

When that doesn’t happen, the technology gets blamed.

In reality, nothing changed except the software.

The workflow stayed the same.

The approvals stayed the same.

The habits stayed the same.

The training lasted an afternoon.

That’s not transformation.

That’s software deployment.

What Does This Mean for Local Government?

Municipalities don’t need AI because it’s exciting.

They need it because capacity is becoming one of the biggest challenges facing local government.

Across Canada we’re seeing:

  • Staff shortages
  • Increasing legislative complexity
  • Growing resident expectations
  • More reporting requirements
  • Higher demands for transparency
  • Limited budgets

Every department is being asked to do more with the same people.

That is where AI becomes valuable.

Not because it replaces staff.

Because it gives staff more capacity to focus on work that actually requires human judgment.

Think about the tasks we repeat every week:

  • Drafting council reports
  • Reviewing procurement submissions
  • Preparing public notices
  • Researching bylaws and policies
  • Organizing records
  • Summarizing legislation
  • Creating emergency communications
  • Responding to common resident questions

These are all excellent candidates for AI assistance.

Notice I said assistance.

That distinction matters.

One Idea I Loved: The Rule of Three

One of the concepts Janak introduces is the Rule of Three.

If you perform the same task more than three times a week, it’s worth asking whether that work should become an AI-supported workflow or a dedicated AI agent.

I love the simplicity of that idea.

Imagine applying it across a municipality.

How many times do we:

  • Write similar emails?
  • Answer the same resident questions?
  • Review similar policies?
  • Search multiple folders for the same information?
  • Recreate reports from scratch?

Those aren’t just AI opportunities.

They’re capacity opportunities.

Municipal AI Isn’t an IT Project

One of the strongest themes throughout the Velocity White Papers is that AI adoption is fundamentally a people strategy.

I couldn’t agree more.

Successful municipalities won’t necessarily be the ones with the most AI tools.

They’ll be the ones that invest in:

  • Staff capability
  • Clear governance
  • Responsible experimentation
  • Repeatable workflows
  • Change management
  • Leadership

Technology is the easy part.

Changing how an organization works is the real challenge.

The Human Still Owns the Decision

If you’ve attended one of my workshops, you’ve probably heard me say this before:

AI is the tool. You are the human. The decision is still yours.

That message aligns beautifully with what I took away from Alberta’s work.

AI can draft.

AI can summarize.

AI can compare.

AI can organize.

AI can even recommend.

But it cannot carry responsibility.

The municipality still owns the data.

The staff member still verifies the output.

Council still owns the decision.

Residents will never ask, “Which AI model wrote this?”

They’ll ask why their municipality made the decision it did.

That’s why governance matters.

Start Small

One thing I appreciate about Alberta’s approach is that it doesn’t encourage organizations to automate everything overnight.

Instead, it encourages capability building.

Learn prompting.

Build confidence.

Create focused AI agents.

Improve one workflow at a time.

Measure success.

Then build from there.

That’s exactly how municipalities should approach AI.

Not as one giant transformation project.

But as hundreds of small improvements that, over time, make work calmer, faster, and more consistent.

Final Thoughts

Janak Alford and the teams at Alberta Technology and Innovation and Alberta Innovates have produced a body of work that I think every municipal leader should spend time with.

Not because it has all the answers.

But because it asks the right questions.

For local government, AI isn’t about replacing people.

It’s about giving good people better tools.

And if we keep the human firmly in the loop, invest in capability before technology, and build governance alongside innovation, I think municipalities have an incredible opportunity over the next few years.

Because AI can absolutely help with the work.

It just can’t carry the responsibility.

  • Deepfakes

That is HR.

That is resident trust.

The federal government is also saying AI can improve public service delivery, but humans still need to stay involved in meaningful decisions.

AI can draft.
AI can summarize.
AI can compare.
AI can help staff move faster.

You are.

AI adoption is becoming a governance issue, not just an IT issue.

Before local governments rush into tools, they need to ask:

Who owns the data?
Where is it stored?
Who verifies the output?
What happens if it is wrong?
Is there a human in the loop?
Do staff and Council understand the risks?

Use the tool.
Train your people.
Build the policy.

The question is whether local governments are ready to govern it properly.
