title: BC’s New FOIPPA Changes Signal a Bigger Question: Is Your Organization Ready for AI?
author: Daphne
excerpt: On May 28, 2026, the Government of British Columbia introduced significant amendments to the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act (FOIPPA). While much of the public discussion has focused on access to information requests, these changes reveal something much larger happening across the public sector. Governments are preparing for a future where information […]
content:
On May 28, 2026, the Government of British Columbia introduced significant amendments to the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act (FOIPPA). While much of the public discussion has focused on access to information requests, these changes reveal something much larger happening across the public sector.

Governments are preparing for a future where information moves faster, systems are more connected, and digital services are becoming the norm.

The question is no longer whether artificial intelligence will impact local government.

The question is whether your organization is prepared when it does.

The Real Story Behind the FOIPPA Amendments

Several of the proposed changes are intended to reduce administrative burden, clarify records access requirements, and support modern digital service delivery.

Among the changes are:

  • Stronger requirements for applicants to clearly define records being requested
  • New provisions related to records involved in legal proceedings
  • Greater flexibility around response timelines
  • Expanded authorities related to information sharing and digital government services
  • Increased focus on privacy, security, and governance standards

These amendments reflect a growing reality. Public bodies are managing larger volumes of information than ever before. Staff capacity remains limited. Residents expect faster service. Technology continues to evolve at a pace that legislation struggles to match.

This creates both opportunities and risks.

Why AI Governance Matters More Than Ever

Many local governments are already using AI, whether they realize it or not.

Staff are experimenting with ChatGPT to draft reports.

Teams are using AI tools to summarize documents.

Consultants are introducing AI-powered software into municipal workflows.

Employees are uploading information into third-party platforms.

The challenge is that most organizations have not yet established clear governance frameworks around these activities.

Without proper oversight, organizations may face:

  • Privacy breaches
  • Inaccurate or misleading information
  • Reputational damage
  • Poor records management practices
  • Regulatory non-compliance
  • Unclear accountability for decisions

FOIPPA compliance is no longer just about managing records.

It is increasingly about understanding how information is collected, processed, shared, and used within emerging technologies.

The Hidden Organizational Risk

When I work with municipalities and public sector organizations, one of the most common observations is that technology adoption often happens faster than policy development.

Staff are innovative.

They want to improve service delivery.

They want to save time.

They want to eliminate repetitive tasks.

But without governance, organizations can unintentionally create significant risks.

A simple AI-generated council report, procurement summary, policy draft, or public communication can raise questions about:

  • Accuracy
  • Transparency
  • Data ownership
  • Retention requirements
  • Human accountability
  • Public trust

The organizations that will succeed are not the ones that ban AI.

They are the ones that learn how to govern it effectively.

What an AI Readiness Assessment Reveals

An AI readiness and organizational risk assessment helps leaders understand:

  • Where AI is already being used
  • What privacy and security risks exist
  • Whether current policies are sufficient
  • How records management practices may be affected
  • Which business processes are suitable for automation
  • Where staff training is needed
  • How governance structures should evolve

The results are often surprising.

Many organizations discover they are already using AI across multiple departments without a consistent framework.

Building a Responsible Path Forward

The goal is not to replace people.

The goal is to increase organizational capacity while maintaining accountability.

Responsible AI implementation can help organizations:

  • Reduce administrative workload
  • Improve consistency
  • Enhance customer service
  • Support decision making
  • Strengthen records management
  • Improve operational efficiency

Most importantly, it can be done in a way that aligns with public sector values, legislative requirements, and community expectations.

The Future Belongs to Prepared Organizations

The recent FOIPPA amendments are a reminder that digital transformation is not a future conversation.

It is happening now.

Organizations that proactively assess their risks, establish governance frameworks, and invest in staff education will be far better positioned than those that wait until problems arise.

AI is not simply a technology project.

It is an organizational change initiative that touches governance, privacy, records management, communications, human resources, procurement, and leadership.

The sooner organizations begin preparing, the greater the opportunity to realize the benefits while minimizing the risks.

Ready to Assess Your Organization’s AI Risk?

I work with local governments, public sector organizations, and leadership teams across Canada to deliver:

  • AI awareness and governance training
  • Organizational AI readiness assessments
  • AI policy and framework development
  • Risk identification and mitigation strategies
  • Responsible AI implementation planning
  • Executive and leadership workshops

If your organization is wondering where to start, let’s have a conversation. Together, we can identify opportunities, reduce risk, and build a practical roadmap for responsible AI adoption that aligns with your operational realities and legislative obligations. Get in Touch Here

title: The Biggest Election Risk May Not Be AI. It May Be Knowing What to Trust.
author: Daphne
excerpt: When people talk about artificial intelligence and elections, the conversation usually starts with misinformation. Fake images. Fake videos. Fake audio recordings. Fake social media posts. Those risks are real. But I believe the bigger challenge is something local governments have been wrestling with for decades. Trust. Because trust is what determines whether people believe […]
content:
When people talk about artificial intelligence and elections, the conversation usually starts with misinformation. Fake images. Fake videos. Fake audio recordings. Fake social media posts.

Those risks are real. But I believe the bigger challenge is something local governments have been wrestling with for decades.

Trust. Because trust is what determines whether people believe information in the first place. And AI is about to test that trust like never before.

A New Reality for Elections

OpenAI recently announced expanded election security initiatives, partnerships, and support aimed at combating AI-generated misinformation and protecting election integrity. The timing is not surprising. Around the world, governments, election administrators, and technology companies are recognizing that generative AI is changing the information landscape.

For the first time in history, it is becoming possible to generate convincing:

  • Images
  • Videos
  • Audio recordings
  • Statements
  • Documents
  • Social media content

At a scale and speed that would have been impossible only a few years ago. That creates entirely new challenges for democratic institutions. Including local government.

AI Did Not Create the Trust Problem. 

One of the most interesting things about this discussion is that AI did not create the underlying issue. Communities have always relied on trust. Trust in institutions. Trust in elected officials. Trust in administration. Trust in information. Trust in processes. AI simply increases the pressure.

Because when anyone can generate convincing content, people naturally begin asking: “How do I know this is real?” That question is becoming increasingly important. And increasingly difficult to answer.

Why This Matters for Local Government

Many municipalities are already preparing for the 2026 local government elections. Traditionally, election planning focused on areas such as:

  • Voting locations
  • Ballot security
  • Staff training
  • Candidate nominations
  • Voter communications
  • Legislative compliance

Those responsibilities remain critical. But election readiness now includes a new consideration. Information integrity.

Municipalities may need to prepare for scenarios such as:

  • Fake candidate statements
  • AI-generated robocalls
  • Synthetic audio recordings
  • Manipulated videos
  • False election notices
  • Misleading social media content
  • Fabricated municipal documents

The challenge is not simply identifying misinformation. The challenge is maintaining public confidence when misinformation appears.

Trust Is Infrastructure

When we think about infrastructure, we usually think about roads, bridges, water systems, and facilities. But trust is infrastructure too.

Without trust:

  • Communication becomes harder.
  • Engagement becomes harder.
  • Decision-making becomes harder.
  • Elections become harder.

The organizations most resilient to misinformation are often those that have already invested in trust.

  • They communicate clearly.
  • They communicate consistently.
  • They communicate transparently.
  • They build strong relationships with residents long before problems emerge.

Because when trust exists, communities are more likely to seek information from reliable sources.

The Importance of Verified Information

As AI-generated content becomes more common, municipalities may need to place greater emphasis on:

  • Official websites
  • Verified communication channels
  • Transparent election processes
  • Clear information sharing
  • Consistent messaging
  • Rapid response protocols

Residents need confidence that they know where to find accurate information. And organizations need confidence that they can respond quickly when misinformation appears. The question is no longer whether misinformation will occur. The question is whether organizations are prepared when it does.

AI Governance and Election Readiness

This is one of the reasons AI governance is becoming increasingly important. Governance is not simply about technology. It is about preparation.

Questions local government leaders should consider include:

  • How would we identify AI-generated misinformation?
  • Who would be responsible for responding?
  • How quickly could we communicate accurate information?
  • Do we have communication protocols in place?
  • Are staff trained to recognize AI-generated content?
  • How would we protect public trust during an incident?
  • Have we incorporated AI risks into election planning?

These questions are becoming part of modern election administration.

Why Business Risk Identification Matters

Many organizations still view AI as a future issue. The reality is that AI-related risks are already emerging.

That is why I have expanded my services to include Business Risk Identification focused on:

  • AI governance
  • Election readiness
  • Communications risk
  • Organizational preparedness
  • Operational vulnerabilities
  • Information integrity
  • Records management
  • Workforce readiness

The objective is simple. Help organizations identify potential risks before they become incidents. Because preparation is almost always less expensive than response. The Question Every Municipality Should Be Asking

Imagine a convincing AI-generated video appears online tomorrow. It shows a candidate saying something they never said. Or a municipal official making a statement they never made. Or false information about voting locations spreading rapidly through social media. Would your organization know exactly what to do?

Would staff know how to respond?

Would residents know where to find verified information?

Would your community trust the response?

Those are no longer hypothetical questions.

They are becoming part of modern election planning.

Building Resilience Before It Is Needed

The good news is that local governments already possess many of the tools needed to address these challenges.

  • Strong governance.
  • Strong records.
  • Transparent processes.
  • Clear communication.
  • Trusted relationships.

The challenge is ensuring those strengths evolve alongside the technology. Because AI may change how misinformation is created. But trust remains the foundation of how communities respond.

title: The Future of Work Isn’t Reading 500 Pages. It’s Knowing Which 5 Pages Matter.
author: Daphne
excerpt: I have a theory. One of the biggest hidden costs in local government isn’t software. It isn’t staffing. It isn’t even meetings. It’s reading. Think about how much time organizations spend reviewing information. Council reports. Engineering studies. Asset management plans. Consultant reports. Grant applications. Strategic plans. Master plans. Audit reports. Bylaws. Policies. Contracts. Every […]
content:
I have a theory.

One of the biggest hidden costs in local government isn’t software.

It isn’t staffing.

It isn’t even meetings.

It’s reading.

Think about how much time organizations spend reviewing information.

Council reports.

Engineering studies.

Asset management plans.

Consultant reports.

Grant applications.

Strategic plans.

Master plans.

Audit reports.

Bylaws.

Policies.

Contracts.

Every important decision seems to come attached to another 100, 200, or 500 pages of documentation.

And somebody has to read it.

The Information Explosion Problem

Local governments have never had access to more information.

Unfortunately, having more information doesn’t automatically lead to better decisions.

In fact, the opposite can sometimes happen.

Decision-makers become overwhelmed.

Staff spend hours searching for key details.

Important insights get buried on page 347.

Critical risks are hidden in appendices.

Recommendations become difficult to compare.

And everyone is trying to find enough time to review everything properly.

The challenge is no longer access to information.

The challenge is extracting meaning from information.

Why Microsoft’s Latest AI Move Matters

Microsoft recently expanded Microsoft 365 Copilot’s ability to work directly with PDF documents.

At first glance, this sounds like a technical feature.

I think it’s something much bigger.

For decades, knowledge work has followed a simple process:

Read.

Analyze.

Summarize.

Recommend.

Decide.

Artificial intelligence is beginning to change the first three steps.

Imagine uploading a lengthy consultant report and asking:

  • What are the key risks?
  • What recommendations require Council action?
  • What are the financial implications?
  • What changed from the previous version?
  • What decisions need to be made?

Instead of spending hours reviewing hundreds of pages, staff receive a structured summary in seconds.

That doesn’t replace decision-making.

It enhances it.

The Real Value Isn’t Speed

Many people immediately focus on time savings.

That’s understandable.

But I don’t think speed is the biggest opportunity.

Capacity is.

Every hour spent searching through documents is an hour not spent:

  • Engaging with residents
  • Developing strategy
  • Evaluating risks
  • Solving problems
  • Supporting Council
  • Improving services

The true value of AI may not be that it helps us read faster.

It may be that it gives us more time to think.

And thinking is where human expertise still matters most.

Local Government Is Built on Documents

This is why document analysis matters so much for municipalities.

Local governments operate in highly regulated environments.

Every decision needs documentation.

Every recommendation needs evidence.

Every project generates reports.

Every program produces records.

Every process creates information.

The result is an enormous volume of documentation that staff must continually review and understand.

AI has the potential to significantly reduce the administrative burden associated with that work.

But that opportunity comes with responsibility.

The Governance Questions Are More Important Than the Technology

Whenever a new AI capability appears, people naturally ask:

“How much time will this save?”

I think a more important question is:

“What governance needs to exist before we use it?”

Questions local government leaders should be asking include:

  • Which documents should AI have access to?
  • Which documents should remain restricted?
  • How are summaries verified?
  • How are records managed?
  • How do privacy requirements apply?
  • What policies need updating?
  • How are outputs validated?
  • What training do staff require?

These are not technical questions.

They are governance questions.

And governance is where successful AI adoption will ultimately succeed or fail.

The Organizations That Benefit Most Will Be Intentional

The municipalities that gain the greatest value from AI won’t necessarily be the ones using the most AI.

They’ll be the ones using it thoughtfully.

The ones that understand:

  • Where AI creates value
  • Where risk exists
  • Where human oversight is required
  • Where governance needs strengthening
  • Where processes need redesigning

Technology alone rarely solves organizational challenges.

Good governance does.

Why Business Risk Identification Matters

One of the most common questions I receive is:

“Where should we start?”

The answer is different for every organization.

That is why I now offer Business Risk Identification Assessments focused specifically on AI readiness, governance, operational risk, workflow impacts, records management, privacy considerations, and organizational preparedness.

Because before implementing AI, organizations need to understand:

  • What opportunities exist
  • What risks exist
  • What processes may change
  • What governance gaps need attention

The goal is not simply adopting AI.

The goal is adopting AI responsibly.

The Bigger Question

Imagine a future where every report, policy, consultant study, engineering assessment, audit finding, and strategic plan could be summarized in seconds.

That future is arriving quickly.

The technology is exciting.

But the most important question isn’t whether AI can read 500 pages.

The question is whether your organization is prepared for what happens when it can.

Through AI Governance Workshops, Business Risk Identification Assessments, Council Orientations, Executive Training, and Organizational Readiness Reviews, I help local governments navigate both the opportunities and the responsibilities that come with AI adoption.

It’s knowing which 5 pages matter.

title: The Future of Work Isn’t Searching. It’s Asking.
author: Daphne
excerpt: The Future of Work Isn’t Searching. It’s Asking. Think about how much time your organization spends looking for information. Not creating it. Not analyzing it. Not acting on it. Simply looking for it. A policy. A bylaw. A council resolution. A procedure. A report from three years ago. A contract. A meeting minute. An email. […]
content:
The Future of Work Isn’t Searching. It’s Asking.

Think about how much time your organization spends looking for information.

Not creating it.

Not analyzing it.

Not acting on it.

Simply looking for it.

A policy.

A bylaw.

A council resolution.

A procedure.

A report from three years ago.

A contract.

A meeting minute.

An email.

A records retention schedule.

If you’ve worked in local government for any length of time, you’ve probably heard some version of the following:

“Where did we save that?”

“Who has the latest version?”

“I know we discussed this before.”

“Wasn’t there a policy about that?”

“Can somebody find the report?”

These questions consume an astonishing amount of organizational time.

And that may be about to change.

The Shift Microsoft Is Betting On

Microsoft recently redesigned Microsoft 365 Copilot with a faster experience, cleaner interface, and deeper integration into daily work.

Most people see this as a software update.

I think it signals something much larger.

For decades, work has been built around searching.

Searching folders.

Searching drives.

Searching email.

Searching records.

Searching policies.

Searching meeting minutes.

Searching databases.

Searching websites.

Searching institutional memory.

The future Microsoft appears to be building is different.

Instead of searching, people ask.

Instead of hunting for information, they request it.

Instead of navigating systems, they interact with an intelligent layer sitting across those systems.

That is a profound shift.

Why This Matters for Local Government

Local governments generate enormous amounts of information.

Every year municipalities create:

  • Council reports
  • Meeting minutes
  • Bylaws
  • Policies
  • Procedures
  • Financial reports
  • Development applications
  • Asset management plans
  • Public engagement materials
  • Contracts
  • Records

The challenge is rarely a lack of information.

The challenge is finding the right information when it is needed.

Many organizations have spent years building repositories, shared drives, records systems, and databases.

Yet staff still spend significant time trying to locate information.

That creates costs.

It creates delays.

And it creates frustration.

AI has the potential to change that.

Imagine This Scenario

A manager asks:

“What is our policy regarding remote work?”

Instead of searching multiple folders, emails, and policy repositories, the answer appears immediately.

Along with:

  • Related procedures
  • Council decisions
  • Previous reports
  • Relevant legislation
  • Recent updates
  • Suggested next steps

The productivity benefit is obvious.

But this is where many organizations stop the conversation.

And where the most important questions begin.

Better Answers Require Better Information

AI does not magically solve information management problems.

In fact, it often exposes them.

If records are poorly organized, AI will struggle.

If policies are outdated, AI may surface outdated information.

If information governance is inconsistent, results become unreliable.

The quality of the answer depends heavily on the quality of the underlying information.

This is why records management professionals, Corporate Officers, information managers, and governance specialists have become some of the most important people in the AI conversation.

The organizations with strong information governance will have a significant advantage.

The Real Opportunity Is Organizational

Most AI discussions focus on technology.

The bigger opportunity is organizational.

If staff spend less time searching, what happens next?

More time for strategic work.

More time serving residents.

More time analyzing issues.

More time supporting decision-making.

More time focused on community outcomes.

The value of AI may not come from finding information faster.

It may come from allowing people to spend more time on the work that actually matters.

The New Questions Leaders Need to Ask

As AI becomes the interface between people and information, leadership teams should be asking questions such as:

  • Is our information organized well enough for AI?
  • Are our policies current?
  • What information should AI access?
  • What information should remain restricted?
  • How do we verify outputs?
  • How do records retention requirements apply?
  • What governance framework is required?
  • How do we manage risk?

These questions are not technical.

They are organizational.

They are governance questions.

And increasingly, they are leadership questions.

Why Business Risk Identification Matters

One of the most common challenges I see is that organizations focus on AI tools before understanding organizational readiness.

The technology is often the easiest part.

Understanding the implications is much harder.

That is why I offer Business Risk Identification Assessments specifically focused on AI readiness, governance, operational impact, records management, privacy, and organizational risk.

The objective is simple.

Help organizations understand:

  • Where AI creates value
  • Where risks exist
  • Which processes are most likely to change
  • Which governance gaps need attention
  • How to prepare leadership and staff

Because every organization has different opportunities.

And every organization has different risks.

The Future Is Not More Information

The future is not about creating more information.

Most organizations already have more information than they know what to do with.

The future is about accessing the right information at the right time.

The future is about moving from searching to asking.

And the organizations that prepare for that shift today will be in a much stronger position tomorrow.

Ready to Prepare Your Organization?

If your municipality is exploring AI, governance, records management, information strategy, or organizational readiness, now is the ideal time to begin the conversation.

Through AI Governance Workshops, Council Orientations, Business Risk Identification Assessments, Records Management Reviews, and Executive Training, I help local governments prepare for the realities of AI-enabled work.

Because the question is no longer whether AI can find information.

The question is whether your organization is ready for it to.

title: AI Is No Longer an App. It’s Becoming the Workplace.
author: Daphne
excerpt: Something important just happened. And I suspect many organizations will underestimate its significance. Microsoft is moving Copilot directly into the Windows taskbar. At first glance, that sounds like a routine software update. Another button. Another feature. Another AI announcement. But I think it signals something much bigger. For the past two years, we’ve treated artificial […]
content:
Something important just happened. And I suspect many organizations will underestimate its significance. Microsoft is moving Copilot directly into the Windows taskbar.

At first glance, that sounds like a routine software update. Another button. Another feature. Another AI announcement. But I think it signals something much bigger. For the past two years, we’ve treated artificial intelligence as a destination.

We open ChatGPT. We open Copilot. We ask a question. We complete a task. Then we close the application and return to work. AI has existed alongside our work. Not within it. That appears to be changing.

The Shift Most Organizations Are Missing

For decades, workplace technology has operated in a predictable way. Employees open applications to access information, create documents, communicate with colleagues, and complete tasks. Information lives in separate systems. Emails in one place. Documents in another. Policies somewhere else. Records in another repository. Calendars in another application. Employees spend significant amounts of time moving between systems, searching for information, and connecting pieces together. The emerging vision for AI is different. Instead of navigating systems, users interact with an intelligent layer that sits across those systems. Rather than opening multiple applications, employees simply ask. The AI retrieves information. Connects documents. Provides context. Suggests actions. Drafts content. Summarizes findings.Supports decision-making.

In other words, AI becomes less of an application and more of an operating environment.

Why This Matters for Local Government

This shift has enormous implications for municipalities. Think about the information local governments manage every day. Council reports. Policies. Bylaws. Meeting minutes. Contracts. Records. Emails. Asset management information. Financial reports. Operational procedures. Development applications. Public engagement materials. The list goes on.

Now imagine an AI system that can access, search, summarize, connect, and interpret much of that information within seconds. The productivity opportunities are obvious. But so are the governance questions.

The Conversation Is Changing

Many local governments are still discussing whether staff should use AI. The conversation is rapidly evolving. Because if AI becomes embedded directly into the workplace, the question is no longer whether employees will use it. The question becomes how it should be governed.

This is where the discussion becomes interesting.

Questions local government leaders should be asking include:

  • What information can AI access?
  • What information should AI not access?
  • How are records retained?
  • How are decisions documented?
  • How is information verified?
  • What privacy protections exist?
  • What oversight is required?
  • What training should staff receive?
  • What policies need updating?

These are not technology questions. They are governance questions.

The Rise of the AI Co-Worker

Many organizations still view AI as software. Increasingly, it may be more useful to think of AI as a digital co-worker.

A co-worker that can:

  • Read documents
  • Summarize information
  • Draft reports
  • Analyze data
  • Identify trends
  • Research policies
  • Assist with communications
  • Organize knowledge

Unlike traditional software, AI actively participates in work. That participation creates both opportunities and responsibilities. The organizations that recognize this early will be better positioned to manage both.

The Biggest Risks Are Not Technical

One of the most common misconceptions I encounter is that AI adoption is primarily an IT challenge. In reality, many of the largest risks are organizational.

Governance.

Privacy.

Information management.

Records retention.

Workforce readiness.

Change management.

Policy development.

Decision accountability.

These are leadership issues. Which is why AI governance is becoming one of the most important conversations local governments can have.

Why Business Risk Identification Matters

As AI becomes increasingly integrated into workplace systems, many organizations struggle to understand where their greatest opportunities and risks exist. That is exactly why I now offer Business Risk Identification Assessments focused on AI readiness and organizational impact. The goal is not simply to evaluate technology.

The goal is to understand how AI may affect:

  • Governance structures
  • Operational workflows
  • Information management
  • Records management
  • Privacy obligations
  • Workforce planning
  • Service delivery
  • Organizational risk

Because every organization is different. And every organization will experience AI differently. The Question Every Leadership Team Should Consider Microsoft’s taskbar announcement may seem small. But it points toward a much larger trend. AI is steadily moving closer to the center of everyday work. The future workplace may not involve employees opening AI applications. The future workplace may involve employees working inside AI-enabled environments from the moment they log in. The technology is moving quickly.

If AI becomes the front door to organizational knowledge, what guardrails should be in place before everyone starts walking through it?

title: Canada Is Investing in AI Talent. Is Your Organization Investing in AI Capability?
author: Daphne
excerpt: Canada recently announced a $24 million investment to support 42 Canada CIFAR AI Chairs. At first glance, this might look like another research funding announcement. content:
Canada recently announced a $24 million investment to support 42 Canada CIFAR AI Chairs.

At first glance, this might look like another research funding announcement.

Most people will read the headline and move on.

I think they’re missing the bigger story.

Because this is not really about research.

It’s about capability.

Canada Is Playing a Long Game

Around the world, countries are competing for something increasingly valuable.

AI talent.

Researchers.

Scientists.

Engineers.

Policy experts.

Governance specialists.

The people who will shape how artificial intelligence is built, governed, regulated, and deployed over the next decade.

Canada’s investment sends a clear message.

The country wants to retain expertise.

Develop expertise.

And build expertise.

Because AI is rapidly becoming a strategic asset.

Not unlike transportation infrastructure, energy infrastructure, or telecommunications infrastructure.

The countries that develop strong AI capability will likely have significant advantages in productivity, innovation, economic growth, public services, and competitiveness.

What Does This Have to Do With Local Government?

Quite a lot.

Many local governments are still evaluating whether AI is something they should be paying attention to.

Meanwhile, federal governments, provincial governments, universities, and major corporations are investing heavily because they believe AI will fundamentally influence how organizations operate.

The conversation has moved well beyond:

“Should we use AI?”

The conversation is becoming:

“How prepared are we?”

Because AI is no longer simply a technology discussion.

It is increasingly becoming a leadership discussion.

Talent and Capability Are Not the Same Thing

One of the most interesting aspects of Canada’s investment is that it focuses on people.

Not software.

Not hardware.

People.

That distinction matters.

Because organizations often confuse AI tools with AI capability.

Buying software does not create capability.

Neither does opening a ChatGPT account.

Capability is something much broader.

It includes:

  • Leadership understanding
  • Governance frameworks
  • Policy development
  • Risk management
  • Workforce readiness
  • Process redesign
  • Data practices
  • Change management
  • Organizational culture

The organizations that thrive in the next decade will likely excel in these areas long before they become experts in the technology itself.

The Emerging Risk for Local Government

Every municipality is facing increasing pressure.

More service expectations.

More reporting requirements.

More compliance obligations.

More staffing challenges.

More cybersecurity concerns.

More demand for transparency.

AI has the potential to help address many of these challenges.

But it also introduces new risks.

Questions local government leaders should be asking include:

  • Where is AI already being used in our organization?
  • Do we have governance in place?
  • Have we identified operational risks?
  • Which business processes are most likely to change?
  • What workforce impacts should we prepare for?
  • How will AI affect records management and information governance?
  • Are we building organizational capability or simply experimenting with tools?

These are not future questions.

They are becoming present-day leadership questions.

The Organizations That Start Early Will Have More Options

One observation has become increasingly clear while working with local governments across Canada.

The organizations making the greatest progress are not necessarily the most technologically advanced.

They are the most intentional.

They are taking time to understand the opportunities.

Assess the risks.

Build governance.

Train leadership.

Develop policies.

And think strategically about how AI fits into their organization.

They are building capability.

And capability compounds over time.

Why Business Risk Identification Matters

One of the newest services I offer is Business Risk Identification focused specifically on AI readiness and organizational impact.

Why?

Because most organizations are focused on the technology.

Far fewer are focused on understanding where AI may affect operations, governance, staffing, service delivery, compliance, privacy, and decision-making.

The reality is that every organization has different opportunities and different risks.

What works for one municipality may not work for another.

Before implementing AI, leaders need visibility into where their organization is most vulnerable and where the greatest opportunities exist.

That understanding often creates far more value than the technology itself.

The Bigger Question

Canada is investing millions of dollars to build AI talent.

Universities are building AI expertise.

Governments are developing AI strategies.

Organizations around the world are redesigning how work gets done.

The question is no longer whether AI matters.

The question is whether your organization is building the capability needed to thrive in an AI-enabled future.

Because capability creates options.

And organizations with options are the ones best positioned to succeed.

Through AI Readiness Assessments, Business Risk Identification Reviews, Council Orientations, Executive Workshops, and Governance Strategy Sessions, I help local governments understand both the opportunities and the risks that come with AI adoption.

They may be the ones that prepared first.

title: AI-Native Organizations Are Coming. Is Local Government Ready?
author: Daphne
excerpt: Everyone is talking about AI tools. ChatGPT. Copilot. Claude. Gemini. The conversation usually sounds something like this: “Which tool should we use?” It’s a reasonable question. content:
Everyone is talking about AI tools.

ChatGPT.

Copilot.

Claude.

Gemini.

The conversation usually sounds something like this:

“Which tool should we use?”

It’s a reasonable question.

It is also the wrong question.

Recent analysis from McKinsey suggests that organizations are beginning to move beyond simply adding AI into existing workflows. Instead, they are starting to redesign operations around AI from the ground up.

That distinction matters.

A lot.

We Have Seen This Before

Think back to email.

When email arrived, organizations did not hire “email coordinators.”

They changed how work happened.

Meetings changed.

Communications changed.

Approvals changed.

Response times changed.

Entire workflows evolved.

AI appears to be following the same path.

Today, most organizations are using AI as a productivity assistant.

Tomorrow, many organizations will redesign the process itself.

The difference between those two approaches could define the next decade of organizational performance.

What Does This Mean for Local Government?

Let’s use a council report as an example.

Today, AI helps draft a report.

Staff gather information.

Research legislation.

Compile background materials.

Develop recommendations.

Draft content.

Review and edit.

Submit for approval.

AI may assist at a few points throughout the process.

Now imagine the same workflow redesigned around AI.

Information is gathered automatically.

Relevant legislation is identified.

Previous council decisions are located.

Risks are highlighted.

The first draft is generated.

Supporting documents are linked.

Recommended actions are suggested.

The report is routed through approvals.

Staff review, validate, adjust, and exercise judgment where it matters most.

The difference is not the technology.

The difference is the design of the workflow.

The Biggest AI Risk Is Not Technology

Many local governments are currently evaluating AI tools.

That is important.

But the larger question is organizational.

What happens when AI changes the flow of work itself?

Questions leadership teams should be asking include:

  • Which processes are heavily dependent on repetitive knowledge work?
  • Which services could be redesigned around AI-assisted workflows?
  • Which roles will experience the greatest change?
  • Which policies need updating?
  • What governance structures are required?
  • How will accountability be maintained?
  • How do we ensure transparency and trust?

These are not IT questions.

These are leadership questions.

The Municipalities That Win Will Think Differently

The municipalities that thrive over the next five years may not be the ones that purchase the most AI tools.

They may be the ones that redesign work first.

The organizations that gain the greatest advantage will not simply automate existing inefficiencies.

They will rethink how services are delivered.

How decisions are supported.

How information moves through the organization.

How staff spend their time.

The goal is not more AI.

The goal is better work.

Why This Matters Right Now

Most organizations are still experimenting.

That creates a unique opportunity.

The decisions being made today will shape how work is performed for years to come.

The challenge is that many organizations do not know where to begin.

They know AI is important.

They know change is coming.

They know expectations are shifting.

What they often do not know is where their greatest opportunities and risks actually exist.

Introducing Business Risk Identification for the AI Era

Over the past year, I have worked with local governments across Canada helping leadership teams understand the practical realities of AI adoption.

One theme appears again and again.

The biggest challenges are rarely technical.

They are operational.

Governance related.

Process related.

Strategic.

That is why I now offer Business Risk Identification Assessments focused on:

  • AI readiness
  • Governance and policy gaps
  • Operational vulnerabilities
  • Workflow redesign opportunities
  • Organizational risk exposure
  • Workforce impacts
  • Records management considerations
  • Privacy and accountability risks

The goal is simple.

Help organizations identify where AI creates value, where risk is emerging, and where leadership attention should be focused before problems arise.

The Question Every Leadership Team Should Be Asking

If your municipality was being built from scratch today and AI already existed, would you design your organization exactly the same way?

Most leaders pause when they hear that question.

Because the answer is usually no.

And that is where the real conversation begins.

Let’s Start the Conversation

Whether you are exploring AI governance, developing an AI strategy, reviewing organizational risks, or trying to understand how AI may reshape operations, now is the time to start planning.

The future belongs to organizations that redesign work, not simply add technology.

If your leadership team would benefit from an AI Readiness Assessment, Business Risk Identification Review, Council Orientation, Executive Workshop, or AI Governance Strategy Session, let’s talk.

It may be understanding where your organization is heading before everyone else does.

content:
Fora long time we’ve heard the same question:

“Which jobs will AI replace?”

It is the wrong question.

The better question is:

Which jobs is AI already doing?

Recent labour market research is revealing something many local governments have already started noticing.

The fastest adoption of generative AI is not occurring in heavy equipment operations, public works field activities, water treatment plants, or road maintenance crews.

It is happening in offices.

Administrative work.

Reporting.

Compliance.

Documentation.

Research.

Policy development.

Records management.

Communications.

The very functions that keep local government running every single day.

The Surprising Reality

Think about the average day inside a municipality.

Staff are preparing council reports.

Summarizing meetings.

Drafting policies.

Researching regulations.

Responding to resident inquiries.

Preparing grant applications.

Reviewing procurement documents.

Managing records.

Updating procedures.

Writing communications.

Many of these activities are knowledge-based, repetitive, and highly structured.

In other words, they are exactly the type of work where AI is proving remarkably effective.

This does not mean people become unnecessary.

Far from it.

It means the nature of the work is changing.

The Real Risk Isn’t AI

The real risk is assuming nothing will change.

Many organizations are treating AI like a new software purchase.

They are asking:

“Which tool should we buy?”

The more important question is:

“Which processes should we redesign?”

Because simply adding AI on top of existing workflows rarely creates transformational results.

Organizations that gain the greatest advantage will redesign work itself.

They will rethink approvals.

Reporting structures.

Information flows.

Documentation practices.

Knowledge management.

Decision support.

Service delivery.

The technology is often the easiest part.

The operational redesign is where the real work begins.

A Capacity Opportunity

Imagine your organization suddenly recovered 20 to 30 percent of its administrative capacity.

What would happen?

Would staff have more time for strategic projects?

Would service levels improve?

Would long-delayed initiatives finally move forward?

Or would the organization simply absorb the savings and fill the space with more work?

These are leadership questions.

Not technology questions.

The Next Generation of Organizational Risk

Most organizations understand financial risk.

Many understand cybersecurity risk.

Increasingly, forward-thinking organizations are beginning to examine another category:

Operational AI Risk.

Questions such as:

  • Which roles are most vulnerable to disruption?
  • Which processes are highly dependent on repetitive knowledge work?
  • Where are governance gaps emerging?
  • What happens if staff begin using AI without guidance?
  • Which policies need updating?
  • How will AI affect records management, privacy, and accountability?
  • What opportunities are being missed?

These questions are becoming boardroom questions, council questions, and executive questions.

A New Service: Business Risk Identification

Over the past year, one pattern has become incredibly clear.

Many organizations know AI is important.

Very few know where their biggest opportunities and risks actually exist.

That is why I am now offering Business Risk Identification Assessments focused on AI readiness, governance, operational vulnerabilities, process redesign opportunities, and organizational risk exposure.

The goal is simple:

Help organizations identify where AI creates value, where it introduces risk, and where leadership should focus attention before issues emerge.

Because the organizations that thrive over the next five years will not necessarily be the ones with the most AI.

They will be the ones that understand their risks, redesign their work, and make thoughtful decisions before disruption arrives.

The future of local government is not about replacing people.

It is about helping people focus on the work that matters most.

And that future is already here.

title: Canada’s Federal AI Strategy Is Coming
author: Daphne
excerpt: Canada’s upcoming federal AI strategy is starting to take shape, and the conversations happening around it are getting very practical very quickly. During Web Summit Vancouver, Minister Evan Solomon met with Canadian AI and business leaders to discuss commercialization, workforce impacts, AI adoption, regulation, and Canada’s long-term economic competitiveness. That may sound federal and far […]
content:
Canada’s upcoming federal AI strategy is starting to take shape, and the conversations happening around it are getting very practical very quickly.

During Web Summit Vancouver, Minister Evan Solomon met with Canadian AI and business leaders to discuss commercialization, workforce impacts, AI adoption, regulation, and Canada’s long-term economic competitiveness.

That may sound federal and far away at first glance.

It is not.

The strategy is expected to influence:
• Procurement rules
• Public sector AI standards
• Workforce and training policies
• AI governance expectations
• Sovereign Canadian compute infrastructure
• Regulation and accountability frameworks across government

And yes… this absolutely matters to local government.

AI Is Moving Beyond the IT Department

For years, technology conversations in municipalities mostly stayed within IT.

That is changing fast.

AI is now touching:
• Communications
• Legislative services
• Finance
• HR
• Planning
• Emergency management
• Public engagement
• Records management
• Procurement
• Council operations

This is no longer just a software discussion.

It is becoming:
• a governance issue
• a workforce issue
• a policy issue
• a risk management issue
• and increasingly… a Council table conversation

Questions are already starting to appear:
“How are we using AI?”
“What tools are staff using?”
“Do we have policies?”
“What are the risks?”
“How do we verify outputs?”
“What happens if AI gets something wrong?”

These conversations are only going to increase as federal standards and expectations evolve.

The Risk of “Shiny New Tool Syndrome”

One of the biggest mistakes organizations can make right now is rushing to buy AI tools without understanding workflows, governance, or operational risks first.

Buying random AI software without a plan is not an AI strategy. 😂

It is just expensive chaos with a chatbot attached.

The municipalities making the best progress are usually not the ones chasing every new tool.

They are the ones stepping back and asking smarter questions first:
• What problems are we trying to solve?
• Where are our workflow bottlenecks?
• What repetitive tasks exist today?
• What governance gaps already exist?
• What training do staff and leadership need?
• How do we maintain accountability and transparency?

That is where meaningful AI adoption starts.

Local Government Has a Huge Opportunity Right Now

The exciting part is that local government still has time to shape AI adoption thoughtfully.

Municipalities are not locked into decades of rigid AI infrastructure yet. Many organizations are still experimenting, learning, and figuring out what works.

That creates a massive opportunity to build:
• Practical governance
• Smart procurement practices
• Healthy AI usage habits
• Clear operational policies
• Strong staff training foundations
• Better public transparency around AI use

The organizations that will thrive are probably not the ones using AI the fastest.

They will be the ones using it intentionally.

The Future of AI Governance Is Practical

AI governance does not need to be scary or overwhelming.

In many cases, it starts with simple things:
• Understanding what tools staff are already using
• Building clear expectations around verification and privacy
• Mapping workflows before automating them
• Training leadership teams and Councils
• Reviewing procurement through an AI lens
• Creating practical policies that reflect real operational use

This is where the conversation is heading across Canada.

And local government has every reason to be part of it now, not later.

From Council orientations to workflow reviews, AI governance discussions, operational training, and practical implementation strategies, the goal is always the same:

Helping organizations use AI thoughtfully, realistically, and responsibly.

title: Click the Damn Link and Read It.
author: Daphne
excerpt: One of the most interesting AI studies making the rounds lately has nothing to do with robots taking over the world or replacing entire departments. It is about citations. A recent academic study looking at Microsoft Edge Copilot usage found that workers were far more likely to trust AI generated responses when citations were included. […]
content:
One of the most interesting AI studies making the rounds lately has nothing to do with robots taking over the world or replacing entire departments.

It is about citations.

A recent academic study looking at Microsoft Edge Copilot usage found that workers were far more likely to trust AI generated responses when citations were included. The surprising part? Many users did not independently verify the information before using it in their work.

That should make every local government leader pause for a second.

Because AI tools are quickly becoming part of everyday municipal operations. Staff are using them to summarize reports, draft emails, interpret policies, brainstorm communication strategies, assist with research, and even help prepare Council materials.

And to be fair… these tools can be incredibly useful.

The problem is that AI confidence is not the same thing as AI accuracy.

The Growing Risk of Automation Bias

There is a term for this: automation bias.

It happens when people begin trusting automated systems too quickly, especially when the output looks polished, professional, or authoritative.

And AI is very, very good at sounding confident.

Add a citation underneath the response and suddenly the information feels trustworthy. But the citation itself does not guarantee the AI interpreted the source correctly.

This is where things start getting risky in local government environments where accuracy, transparency, and accountability matter.

Because once incorrect information enters a workflow, it can spread fast:
• Council reports
• Public communication
• HR guidance
• Procurement recommendations
• Policy interpretation
• Bylaw summaries
• Emergency messaging

One bad interpretation can snowball surprisingly quickly.

Click the Damn Link

This might be my favourite AI governance advice lately:

Click the damn link and read it.

Seriously. 😂

If an AI tool provides a source or citation:
• Open it
• Read it yourself
• Confirm the context
• Check the date
• Verify the interpretation
• Make sure the source actually supports the conclusion being presented

This tiny extra step is becoming one of the most important AI literacy skills organizations can build.

Because sometimes the citation is correct… but the summary is not.

Sometimes the source is outdated.

Sometimes the AI pulled one sentence completely out of context.

And sometimes the AI simply misunderstood what it was reading.

Why This Matters for Local Government

Local governments are entering a phase where AI governance is no longer theoretical.

This is now an operational issue.

Councils are asking questions.
Insurance providers are paying attention.
Policies are being drafted.
Staff are experimenting with tools faster than many organizations can keep up.

That is not necessarily a bad thing. In fact, it is exciting.

But it does mean municipalities need to focus on practical AI literacy, not just AI adoption.

The organizations that will thrive with AI are probably not the ones using it the fastest.

They will be the ones using it thoughtfully, transparently, and critically.

Building Healthy AI Habits

Good AI governance does not mean banning tools or creating fear around technology.

It means creating healthy habits:
• Verifying outputs
• Encouraging critical thinking
• Understanding limitations
• Creating policies that actually make sense operationally
• Training staff and leadership teams on responsible use

That is where the real opportunity is.

AI can absolutely help increase capacity, reduce repetitive work, improve workflows, and support better service delivery.

But humans still need to stay in the driver’s seat.

And yes… that includes clicking the citation link. 😅

title: Watch this Space – Canada’s AI and Labour Shift in Local Government
author: Daphne
excerpt: Canada is creating an AI and Labour Advisory Council!! For the last few years, artificial intelligence has often been framed as a technology issue. Faster systems. Better tools. More productivity. New infrastructure. National strategies. Procurement rules. All of that matters. But the federal conversation is now shifting toward something much more practical for public sector […]
content:
Canada is creating an AI and Labour Advisory Council!!

For the last few years, artificial intelligence has often been framed as a technology issue. Faster systems. Better tools. More productivity. New infrastructure. National strategies. Procurement rules.

All of that matters.

But the federal conversation is now shifting toward something much more practical for public sector organizations:

What does AI mean for people?

Recent federal discussions are placing more attention on labour market impacts, workforce adaptation, union engagement, and the role of workers in AI policy. That is an important shift because AI adoption will not succeed through technology alone. It will depend on whether organizations can bring people along with clarity, trust, and practical support.

AI Is Already Showing Up in Local Government

AI is not some distant future issue for municipalities. It is already beginning to appear in records management, customer service, communications, planning, emergency management, finance, human resources, legislative services, and administrative workflows.

In many communities, especially small and rural municipalities, staff are already stretched. Teams are managing growing service expectations, complex reporting requirements, public communication demands, emergency planning pressures, and increasing administrative workloads.

That is where AI has real potential.

Used well, AI can help reduce repetitive work, support better access to information, draft plain language communications, assist with research, improve internal processes, and give staff more time for the work that requires judgment, empathy, and local knowledge.

But that only happens if AI is introduced thoughtfully.

The Workforce Conversation Cannot Come Later

When new tools are introduced without a people-focused plan, staff can quickly become uncertain or resistant. That does not mean people are against innovation. It often means they have reasonable questions that have not been answered.

Staff may be wondering:

  • Will AI change my job?
  • Will I receive training?
  • Will this make my workload easier or more complicated?
  • Will AI be used to monitor performance?
  • Will decisions still involve human judgment?
  • Will employees and unions be part of the conversation?

These are not side questions. They are central to successful AI adoption.

Local governments have an opportunity to lead differently by starting with transparency, training, and trust. That means involving staff early, creating clear internal guidelines, identifying where AI can support work rather than simply adding another tool, and making sure employees understand how decisions will be made.

Why Union Engagement Matters

The federal focus on labour and union engagement is especially relevant for municipalities because many local government workplaces are unionized.

AI adoption should not be treated as something that happens behind closed doors. When technology affects workflows, responsibilities, job design, service delivery, or employee expectations, labour needs to be part of the conversation.

That does not have to slow innovation down. In fact, it can make implementation stronger.

Early engagement can help identify practical risks, training needs, workload concerns, privacy considerations, and opportunities to improve service delivery. It can also reduce fear and build confidence that AI is being used responsibly.

For local government leaders, this means AI planning should include more than IT and senior management. It should involve frontline staff, supervisors, corporate administration, human resources, communications, and labour representatives where appropriate.

Small and Rural Communities Have the Most to Gain

The exciting part is that AI could be especially useful for smaller municipalities.

Small local governments are often asked to meet the same legislative, administrative, and public service expectations as larger organizations, but with far fewer staff. One person may hold several roles. A single vacancy can create major service pressure. Administrative backlogs can build quickly.

AI will not solve every capacity challenge, and it should not replace the importance of skilled public servants. But it can help reduce some of the pressure.

For a small municipality, even modest improvements can matter.

Saving a few hours a week on repetitive administrative work can create more time for residents, council priorities, grant reporting, emergency planning, bylaw work, records management, or service improvements.

That is worth getting excited about.

The Real Leadership Test

Canada’s national AI strategy will likely influence procurement, public sector deployment standards, training programs, infrastructure priorities, and governance expectations.

But at the local level, the real test will be leadership.

Local governments will need to ask practical questions before AI becomes embedded into daily operations:

  • What tasks are appropriate for AI support?
  • What tasks should remain fully human-led?
  • How will staff be trained?
  • How will privacy, records management, and accountability be handled?
  • How will employees be included in implementation?
  • How will elected officials and the public understand the organization’s approach?
  • How will AI use align with public sector values?

The answers do not need to be perfect on day one. But the conversation needs to start early.

AI Strategy Is a People Strategy

AI strategy is no longer just a technology conversation.

It is a workforce conversation.

It is a trust conversation.

It is a governance conversation.

And, most importantly for local government, it is a leadership conversation.

The municipalities that do this well will not be the ones that rush to adopt every new tool. They will be the ones that build a thoughtful approach, support their staff, engage the right people, and use AI in ways that improve public service without losing the human judgment that communities rely on.

Chat to ME

Local governments do not need to wait for AI to become overwhelming before starting the conversation.

Now is the time to review internal workflows, identify training needs, engage staff and labour representatives, and begin developing practical AI guidelines that reflect public sector values.

If your municipality is starting to explore AI adoption, start with the people side first. The technology will keep changing, but trust, transparency, and good governance will always matter. Get in Touch with me to assist you through this transition.

content:
A recent situation out of South Africa is making the rounds.

A national AI policy had to be withdrawn because it included completely fabricated references.

We KNOW AI smoke shrooms on weekends!!!!

It is easy to point at AI and say, “this is the problem.”

It is not.

This is a human problem.

Someone drafted that document.
Someone reviewed it.
Someone approved it.

And at no point did anyone verify the sources.

That is where the failure sits.

AI did what it is designed to do. Generate content quickly and confidently. The breakdown happened in governance, ownership, and basic due diligence.

Verification is not optional.
Verification is not implied.
Verification is the job.

And this is where the conversation becomes very real for local government.

AI is already embedded in daily work.

Staff are using it to draft reports, refine communications, summarize information, and support decision making. It is fast, accessible, and increasingly part of normal operations.

Which is exactly why this matters.

Because the risk is not that AI will produce incorrect information. That is already known.

The risk is that incorrect information looks correct, moves quickly, and is not challenged.

In a municipal context, that can have serious consequences.

Council reports.
Public communications.
Policy drafts.
Operational decisions.

If AI is involved at any stage, there must be a clear, accountable human responsible for verifying the output.

Not assuming. Not skimming. Verifying.

This is not about restricting AI use. It is about governing it properly.

Strong AI governance does not start with complex frameworks. It starts with clarity.

Who is responsible for the final output?
What level of review is required?
Where does verification sit in the workflow?

If those answers are unclear, the organization is exposed.

The South African example is not an isolated incident. It is an early signal of what happens when AI use moves faster than governance.

And that gap is where most municipalities are operating right now.

Adoption is happening quickly. Policies, training, and accountability structures are still catching up.

This is the moment to close that gap.

AI can absolutely improve efficiency, capacity, and service delivery in local government. But it cannot replace responsibility.

Every AI assisted output still needs a human owner.

Every document still needs to be defensible.

Every decision still needs to stand up to scrutiny.

That does not change.

If anything, it becomes more important.

If your municipality is already using AI, this is where to focus next.

I work with local governments to put practical governance in place. Clear policies, defined roles, staff and council training, and workflows that include real verification, not assumed oversight.

If you want to move forward with AI and stay confident in what is being produced, let’s connect.

title: Frontier AI Is Already Here. The Question Is Whether Local Government Is Ready to Govern It
author: Daphne
excerpt: There is a quiet shift happening in AI right now. And it is not coming from a tech company. It is coming from Canada’s Cyber Centre. They are talking about “frontier AI.” The most advanced systems available today. But in practical terms, this is not some distant future state. This is your current environment. Copilots. […]
content:
There is a quiet shift happening in AI right now.

And it is not coming from a tech company. It is coming from Canada’s Cyber Centre.

They are talking about “frontier AI.” The most advanced systems available today. But in practical terms, this is not some distant future state.

This is your current environment.

Copilots.
Chat tools.
Automated workflows.
Systems connecting to other systems.

These tools are already being used across municipalities, often informally, often without clear oversight.

The key message from the Cyber Centre is simple.

Safe AI use cannot be defined by vendors alone.

That is a significant shift.

For a long time, organizations have relied on providers like Microsoft, OpenAI, and Google to set the boundaries for how these tools operate. But this guidance makes it clear that responsibility does not sit with vendors. It sits with the organization using the tools.

For local governments, that creates both pressure and opportunity.

Municipalities operate in a unique environment. Teams are often small. IT and security capacity is limited. Public accountability is high. At the same time, there is increasing pressure to adopt AI quickly to improve service delivery and internal efficiency.

That combination is where risk builds quickly.

The Cyber Centre’s guidance addresses this directly by focusing on practical, applicable controls rather than theory.

It highlights several key risk areas that are already present in municipal operations.

Data exposure is one of the most immediate concerns. Staff may input sensitive information into AI tools without fully understanding how that data is stored or used. This could include HR records, bylaw complaints, legal drafts, or infrastructure details.

Model unpredictability is another. AI outputs can sound confident even when they are incorrect. When those outputs are used in public communications, reports, or policy support, the risk increases.

There is also supply chain complexity. Municipalities are not using a single tool. They are working within ecosystems. AI tools connected to document systems, analytics platforms, and workflow software create multiple layers of dependency and risk.

Autonomy creep is more subtle but equally important. Tools that begin as assistants can gradually influence decisions or automate actions. Governance often lags behind this shift.

Finally, AI is not just a tool used by organizations. It is also being used against them. From phishing to social engineering, the threat landscape is evolving alongside adoption.

What makes this guidance valuable is that it does not stop at identifying risk. It provides a clear starting point for mitigation.

Establishing data control policies is foundational. Organizations need to define what information can and cannot be entered into AI tools, and where enterprise or compliant environments are required.

Maintaining human oversight is critical. Outputs should not be accepted without review, particularly for public facing content, legal material, or operational decisions.

Access controls also matter. Not every staff member requires the same level of AI capability. Roles should guide access.

Logging and monitoring provide visibility. Understanding how tools are used, and where risks may be emerging, is essential.

Vendor due diligence becomes more important as reliance grows. Questions around data storage, retention, training use, and system changes need clear answers.

And perhaps most importantly, training and awareness must be prioritized. Much of the risk comes from well intentioned use rather than misuse.

For municipalities, this guidance offers something that has been missing.

A credible, national baseline.

It provides support when setting internal policy, when evaluating tools, and when pushing back on implementations that may introduce unnecessary risk. It also creates a foundation for building structured AI governance within existing operations.

There is also a broader shift taking place.

The question is no longer just how to use AI.

It is how to use AI in a way that is safe, defensible, and aligned with public sector responsibilities.

That shift changes the conversation entirely.

AI is no longer just a tool. It is part of the operational fabric of local government. And like any critical system, it requires governance, structure, and accountability.

If your municipality is already using AI, even in small ways, this is the moment to take a closer look at how it is being managed.

This is exactly where I support local governments.

From practical AI policies and governance frameworks to staff and council training, I work with municipalities to turn AI from an ad hoc tool into a structured, defensible part of operations.

If you are ready to put the right guardrails in place and move forward with confidence, let’s connect.

title: Is the Next Step in AI Shorter Work Weeks for Humans?
author: Daphne
excerpt: The conversation around AI is shifting again. This time, it is not really about the tools. It is about time. There is growing talk, including signals tied to OpenAI, that AI could drive productivity gains big enough to shrink the traditional five day workweek. Not a small tweak. content:
The conversation around AI is shifting again.

This time, it is not really about the tools. It is about time.

There is growing talk, including signals tied to OpenAI, that AI could drive productivity gains big enough to shrink the traditional five day workweek. Not a small tweak. A real shift in how work gets done.

That is pretty exciting.

Tasks that used to take hours are now getting done in minutes. Drafting, analysis, reporting, comms. You can feel the compression happening.

But then you bring this into local government… and it gets a bit more layered.

Municipalities are not exactly built for fast shifts like this. Roles are defined. Collective agreements are tied to hours. Service expectations are steady. And many teams are still working through basic digital transformation.

So the question is not just “can we work less?”

It is “what do we actually do with the time AI gives back?”

There is the obvious path. Efficiency.

Use AI to do more in less time. Reduce hours. tighten up roles. move faster. That can absolutely help with burnout, retention, and capacity, especially in smaller communities.

But there is a really important counterweight here. O Theory.

O Theory is all about building strong organizations. Investing in people, skills, culture, and long term performance. It is less about squeezing time and more about building capability.

So now you have a bit of a push and pull.

AI pushes for speed and output.
O Theory pushes for strength and sustainability.

Lean too far into efficiency and you risk hollowing things out. Roles shrink, but capability does not grow. People rely on tools without really building the skills to govern or challenge them.

Ignore the efficiency gains and you fall behind.

So it is not either or.

It is a leadership choice.

Do you give some time back to your people?
Do you reinvest it into better services?
Or do you do a bit of both and actually redesign how work happens?

That third option is probably my favorite.

Because AI is not just speeding things up. It is opening the door to rethink roles, expectations, and how value is created inside an organization.

For local government, this is bigger than a tech conversation. It is workforce design, governance, and strategy all rolled into one.

And it is coming faster than most policies are.

If AI gives your organization back time… do you cut it, reinvest it, or use it to build something better?

If you are trying to figure that out right now, you are not alone. This is exactly the space I work in with municipalities. Helping teams put some structure around AI, think through governance, and make practical decisions that actually hold up day to day.

If you want to get ahead of it instead of scrambling later, let’s chat.

title: Musk vs Altman: For Profit vs Not for Profit and Why It Matters for Local Government
author: Daphne
excerpt: The current legal dispute between Elon Musk and Sam Altman is often framed as a clash of personalities. In reality, it is a governance issue with implications that extend well beyond one organization. At the centre of the case is a simple question. Can an organization founded as a public benefit entity evolve into a […]
content:
The current legal dispute between Elon Musk and Sam Altman is often framed as a clash of personalities. In reality, it is a governance issue with implications that extend well beyond one organization.

At the centre of the case is a simple question. Can an organization founded as a public benefit entity evolve into a commercially driven structure without breaching its original purpose?

OpenAI was established in 2015 as a nonprofit with a clear mandate to develop artificial intelligence for the benefit of humanity. Musk’s legal argument is that this mandate has been compromised. He points to the organization’s shift toward a capped for profit model and its partnership with Microsoft as evidence that commercial interests are now taking precedence.

OpenAI disputes this. Their position is that the hybrid model is necessary to support the financial demands of advanced AI development. Training and deploying these systems requires billions in capital. The current structure, where a nonprofit board governs a for profit subsidiary, is designed to balance mission and funding. Investors receive capped returns rather than unlimited equity, and the nonprofit board retains ultimate control.

This case is testing whether that balance holds up under legal scrutiny.

If the court finds that OpenAI has moved too far from its original purpose, it could result in significant changes. Board authority could be redefined. Partnerships with large corporations could face new limits. There may be increased expectations around transparency and accountability.

Even if the court does not rule in Musk’s favour, the process itself is already revealing how governance works inside one of the most influential AI organizations in the world. It is exposing how decisions are made, where influence sits, and how trade offs between safety and commercialization are handled.

For local governments, this is not abstract.

Municipalities are rapidly adopting AI tools across operations. Internal copilots are being used for drafting reports and communications. Chat interfaces are being deployed for public service. AI is assisting with data analysis, records management, and decision support.

This growing reliance raises important governance questions.

Who is accountable for the outputs generated by these systems?
What happens if the governance structure of a key provider changes?
How should municipalities assess risk when relying on privately governed AI infrastructure?

AI is increasingly functioning as critical infrastructure. It supports core operations, influences decision making, and shapes public interaction with government services. However, unlike traditional infrastructure such as energy or telecommunications, it is governed primarily by corporate entities rather than public institutions.

This creates a gap between reliance and control.

The Musk and Altman case highlights that gap in a very visible way. It underscores the need for local governments to move beyond simple adoption and toward structured governance. This includes developing internal policies, understanding vendor dependencies, and establishing clear accountability frameworks for AI use.

The implications also extend across the broader AI industry. Organizations that position themselves as mission driven or focused on public benefit may face increased scrutiny. Future claims around “AI for humanity” may need to be more clearly defined and supported by enforceable governance structures.

At its core, this case is not about individuals. It is about the evolving structure of AI organizations and the tension between public good and private funding.

That tension remains unresolved.

And for local governments, it is a signal to take a more active role in how AI is evaluated, governed, and integrated into public service.

If your municipality is already using AI or considering it, now is the time to get your governance right.

I work with local governments to design practical AI policies, assess risk, train staff and council, and build clear frameworks that actually hold up in real operations.
