title: Shiny New Tools… and the Cost No One Is Talking About
author: Daphne
excerpt: Why Local Government Needs to Rethink AI Before Adding Another Tool There is something happening right now in local government that is easy to miss. New AI tools are showing up everywhere. Every week, there is a new platform. A new feature. A new “must-have” capability. And to be fair, a lot of them are […]
content:
Why Local Government Needs to Rethink AI Before Adding Another Tool

There is something happening right now in local government that is easy to miss.

New AI tools are showing up everywhere.

Every week, there is a new platform. A new feature. A new “must-have” capability. And to be fair, a lot of them are genuinely useful.

But here is the part that deserves a closer look.

What happens when we keep adding… without removing anything?

The Hidden Cost of “Just One More Tool”

A recent McKinsey Technology report, Recalibrating technology budgets for the AI era, highlights a challenge many organizations are now facing.

AI is not just a new investment.

It is increasing the cost of everything already in place.

More systems to maintain

More models to manage

More platforms to govern

All layered on top of existing infrastructure.

In the private sector, they describe this as the “run vs change” problem.

How much are you spending to keep things running…

versus how much are you investing in actually improving them?

Let’s Bring This Into Local Government

If you zoom into a typical municipality, this starts to look very familiar.

Legacy systems that still need to run

New platforms being introduced

Departments experimenting with different tools

Licenses stacking up across teams

And now AI enters the mix.

The question is not whether AI adds value.

It absolutely can.

The question is:

Is it replacing anything… or just being added on?

Because if nothing is being retired, simplified, or consolidated, the result is not transformation.

It is accumulation.

Shiny New Tool Syndrome

This is where things get a little more real.

New tools are exciting.

They promise efficiency. Better service delivery. Faster work.

So naturally:

A pilot gets launched

A license gets approved

Another tool gets added

But rarely do we pause and ask:

  • What can this replace?
  • What can we stop doing?
  • What systems are now redundant?

Without those questions, organizations slowly build layers.

And over time, those layers become harder and more expensive to manage.

What High-Performing Organizations Are Doing Differently

The organizations that are actually getting value from AI are not just investing more.

They are making clearer decisions.

They are:

  • Identifying what to retire or reduce
  • Simplifying existing systems
  • Ensuring new investments lower future costs, not increase them
  • Using AI to replace processes, not duplicate them

In other words, they are creating space for AI to work.

The Case for Systems Audits

This is where local government has a huge opportunity.

Before adding more tools, take a step back.

Run a systems audit.

Not a technical deep dive.

A practical, operational view of:

  • What systems are currently in use
  • Where duplication exists
  • What is no longer delivering value
  • What could be replaced or consolidated

Because without that clarity, AI simply becomes another layer on top of an already complex environment.

A Different Way to Think About AI

Instead of asking:

“What AI tool should we adopt next?”

Try asking:

“What are we willing to stop, simplify, or replace so AI can actually deliver value?”

That shift changes everything.

Let’s Build a Smarter Approach

I work with local governments to:

  • Run practical systems audits
  • Identify opportunities to simplify and consolidate
  • Map out an AI approach that actually creates value

Because the goal is not more tools.

It is better outcomes, with less complexity.

title: Choosing an AI Approach That Actually Works
author: Daphne
excerpt: A Practical Perspective for Local Government There is a question I keep hearing in local government right now: “Which AI tool should we be using?” And I get it. There is a lot of noise. Claude. ChatGPT. Copilot. New tools showing up almost weekly. Each promising to transform how we work. But the more I […]
content:
A Practical Perspective for Local Government

There is a question I keep hearing in local government right now:

“Which AI tool should we be using?”

And I get it. There is a lot of noise.

Claude. ChatGPT. Copilot. New tools showing up almost weekly. Each promising to transform how we work.

But the more I sit with this, the more I think we might be asking the wrong question.

Because the challenge is not choosing a tool.

It is designing an approach.

The Reality on the Ground

Let’s look at how these tools are actually showing up in municipal work.

Claude: The Policy Analyst

Claude is excellent at handling long, complex documents.

  • Bylaws
  • Policies
  • Legislation
  • Council reports

It can take dense material and turn it into structured, readable output. It stays focused. It keeps a neutral tone. It does not get distracted.

In a municipal environment, that is incredibly valuable.

But it is not embedded into your day-to-day systems. It does not automate workflows. It does not connect across platforms.

It is powerful, but in a very specific way.

ChatGPT: The Strategist and Builder

ChatGPT operates differently.

It is strong at:

  • Writing and drafting
  • Brainstorming and strategy
  • Translating ideas into implementation
  • Designing workflows and systems

It helps connect dots.

If you are working on digital transformation, AI policy development, or process improvement, this is where it shines.

But it also requires direction.

Without structure, it can lean too creative or miss the level of formality required for certain outputs.

Copilot: The Embedded Executor

Copilot lives inside your daily tools.

  • Outlook
  • Word
  • Excel
  • Teams

It is built for execution.

  • Drafting emails
  • Summarizing meetings
  • Analyzing spreadsheets

In municipal environments where work is document-heavy and email-driven, this is a natural fit.

But it is not a strategist.

It does not think with you at a deep level. It supports what you are already doing.

The Misconception: One Tool Will Solve It

Each of these tools is strong.

But none of them, on their own, solves the core challenge facing local government.

Because the real issue is not capability.

It is clarity.

Right now, I am seeing:

  • Tools being tested
  • Licenses being purchased
  • Pilots being launched

But not always a clear strategy connecting it all together.

And without that, even the best tools create fragmentation instead of value.

The Shift: From Single Tool to AI Stack

What is actually emerging is not a “winning tool.”

It is a multi-AI environment.

Different tools doing different things.

A realistic workflow might look like:

  1. Claude analyzes a long policy or piece of legislation
  2. ChatGPT turns that analysis into a structured report with recommendations
  3. Copilot integrates it into documents, communications, and internal workflows

This is where the real power sits.

But it also introduces new complexity.

The Questions Local Government Needs to Answer

Once you move into a multi-AI environment, the conversation shifts.

It is no longer just about tools.

It becomes about governance.

For example:

  • Who oversees how these tools are used together?
  • Where does accountability sit?
  • How do we ensure consistency across departments?
  • Are we building internal capability… or just layering tools?

These are not technical questions.

They are leadership questions.

The Risk of Getting It Wrong

Without a clear approach, AI adoption can quickly become:

  • Disconnected
  • Inconsistent
  • Difficult to manage

Instead of transformation, you get fragmentation.

And that is where many organizations stall.

The Opportunity for Local Government

Local government is in a unique position.

You do not need to chase every new tool.

You need to:

  • Define what value looks like for your organization
  • Decide where AI fits into your operations
  • Establish clear governance and oversight
  • Build internal capability alongside adoption

Because the goal is not to use AI.

It is to make it work for you.

The Real Question

So maybe the question is not:

“Which AI tool should we choose?”

Maybe it is:

“How do we design an AI approach that actually works for our organization?”

Let’s Build This Together

If your municipality is trying to make sense of multiple tools, competing priorities, and growing expectations around AI, I would love to help.

I work with local governments to:

  • Connect AI tools into practical workflows
  • Build governance structures that actually make sense
  • Move from experimentation to real outcomes

Because AI is not just about technology.

It is about how you use it, manage it, and align it with your goals.

And that is where the real value is.

title: If AI Creates the Value… Who Gets It?

content:
Rethinking “Robot Tax” and Public Wealth in the Age of AI

There is a conversation starting to gain traction that feels a bit futuristic… but also surprisingly practical.

What if AI-generated value was taxed?

Not in the traditional sense of income or property tax. But something closer to a “robot tax” or a public wealth fund. The idea is that as AI systems take on more work and generate more economic output, a portion of that value could be redistributed back to people.

In some discussions, even homeowners are positioned as potential beneficiaries.

It is a big idea.

And one that raises some very real questions.

Why This Conversation Is Emerging

AI is not just improving efficiency. It is changing how value is created.

Tasks that once required human labour are increasingly being handled by automated systems. Content creation, analysis, customer service, decision support… all moving quickly into AI-assisted or AI-led workflows.

So naturally, the question becomes:

If AI is doing more of the work, who benefits from that shift?

Is it the organizations deploying the technology?

The vendors building it?

The public, whose data and systems often underpin it?

This is where the concept of a “robot tax” or public wealth fund enters the conversation.

Not as a finalized policy. But as a way to start thinking differently about distribution.

The Practical Challenges

As interesting as the idea is, it is not simple.

In fact, it is full of complexity.

For example:

  • What actually counts as “AI-generated value”?
  • How do you measure that across different sectors?
  • How do you separate AI contribution from human contribution?
  • Who is responsible for collecting and distributing that value?

And perhaps most importantly:

Does introducing something like this slow innovation… or create a more balanced system?

There is no clear answer yet.

But the fact that this conversation is happening at all is telling.

What This Means for Local Government

At first glance, this might feel like a federal or global policy discussion.

But there are local implications.

Because municipalities are already:

  • Exploring AI to improve service delivery
  • Managing data that fuels AI systems
  • Navigating workforce changes as roles evolve
  • Thinking about economic development in an AI-driven world

So while local governments may not be setting “robot tax” policy, they will absolutely feel the impact of how these ideas evolve.

And they may also be asked questions like:

Should municipalities benefit from AI-generated efficiencies?

How do we reinvest savings created through automation?

What does equitable access to AI-driven value look like at a community level?

These are not abstract questions for long.

Moving From Concept to Conversation

Right now, the idea of taxing automated labour sits somewhere between theory and early policy thinking.

But it signals something important.

We are moving beyond conversations about using AI…

Into conversations about how AI reshapes economic systems.

And that is a very different level of discussion.

For local government, this is not about having all the answers.

It is about being ready to engage with the questions.

A Question Worth Exploring

If AI is generating more value than ever before…

How should that value be shared?

And what role, if any, should local government play in that conversation?

I help local governments:

  • Understand emerging AI trends in a practical context
  • Translate complex ideas into local relevance
  • Build strategies that align with community values

Because AI is not just changing how we work.

It is changing how value itself is created.

And that is worth paying attention to.

title: Building “Brain Capital” in Local Government
author: Daphne
excerpt: Why AI Makes Human Thinking More Important, Not Less There is a conversation coming out of the private sector right now that I cannot stop thinking about. content:
Why AI Makes Human Thinking More Important, Not Less

There is a conversation coming out of the private sector right now that I cannot stop thinking about.

McKinsey’s Bob Sternfels recently introduced the idea of “brain capital.” The core message is simple, but powerful:

AI does not replace human intelligence.

It makes it more important.

At first glance, that might feel counterintuitive.

We are surrounded by messaging about automation, efficiency, and AI taking on more and more tasks. And yes, that is happening.

But underneath all of that, something more interesting is unfolding.

The Shift No One Is Talking About Enough

AI is getting very good at producing answers.

It can draft, summarize, analyze, and recommend faster than ever before.

But it does not understand context the way people do.

It does not carry accountability.

It does not make judgment calls.

That still sits with us.

Which means the real differentiator is no longer just access to technology.

It is how well people think.

How they interpret outputs.

How they question results.

How they decide what to act on and what to ignore.

That is brain capital.

And according to McKinsey, organizations that recognize and invest in this are already pulling ahead.

What This Means for Local Government

This is where things get really interesting.

In local government, we often focus on:

  • Systems and tools
  • Policy and compliance
  • Procurement and implementation

All of which matter.

But if AI is becoming embedded in everyday work, then the real question shifts:

Are we building teams that know how to think with AI?

Not just how to use it.

Because using AI without strong thinking does not reduce risk. It amplifies it.

And in local government, the stakes are high.

Decisions impact communities.

Outputs influence public trust.

Errors can have real consequences.

Moving Beyond “AI Training”

A lot of organizations are starting to roll out AI training.

Which is great.

But most of it focuses on:

  • How to write prompts
  • How to use specific tools
  • How to save time

That is only part of the picture.

Building brain capital means going further:

  • Teaching staff how to critically assess AI outputs
  • Understanding where AI fits and where it does not
  • Strengthening judgment, not replacing it
  • Encouraging curiosity and challenge, not blind adoption

Because the goal is not faster work.

It is better decisions.

The Real Investment

We often talk about AI as a technology investment.

But this reframes it completely.

The real investment is cognitive.

It is about developing people who can:

  • Navigate ambiguity
  • Ask better questions
  • Apply context
  • Exercise judgment

In a world where AI is accelerating everything, these skills become more valuable, not less.

A Question Worth Asking

So here is the question I keep coming back to:

Are we investing in AI tools… or in the people who will use them well?

Because one without the other will not get you very far.

I help local governments:

  • Build practical AI understanding across teams
  • Strengthen decision-making alongside AI use
  • Develop the “brain capital” needed to actually get value from AI

Because the goal is not just adoption.

It is confidence, clarity, and better outcomes.

content:
What Local Government Councils Need to Know

I came across a piece recently in Directors & Boards (drawing on McKinsey research), and it really made me stop and think.

Over 88% of organizations are already using AI in at least one function.

But most are not seeing meaningful value.

Not because the technology is not working.

Because they have not actually decided what value they want from it.

That distinction matters.

This Isn’t an IT Problem. It’s a Governance One.

In the private sector, this gap is being pushed back to boards.

Not IT teams. Not innovation leads.

Boards.

Because the real challenges are not technical. They are strategic:

  • Unclear priorities
  • Fragmented ownership
  • Lack of accountability for outcomes

And if we are being honest… this feels very familiar in local government.

Let’s Translate This to Council

AI is already showing up across municipalities.

Staff are experimenting.

Departments are testing tools.

Vendors are offering solutions.

But without clear direction, it becomes activity without alignment.

And this is where council comes in.

AI is not just another operational tool. It will influence:

  • How resources are allocated
  • How risk is managed
  • How services are delivered
  • How decisions are supported

That is council-level work.

The Questions Councils Should Be Asking

If councils want to move from curiosity to value, the starting point is not more tools. It is better questions.

For example:

  • What does success with AI actually look like for our community?
  • Where should AI be used… and where should it not?
  • Who is responsible for oversight?

The Opportunity for Council Leadership

  • Establish expectations

In the private sector, organizations with AI-aware boards are already outperforming others.

A Note for 2026 Election Communities

If your municipality is heading into elections this year, this conversation is coming sooner than you think.

They became expected baseline skills for doing the job.

AI is heading in the same direction.

Local governments are in an interesting position.

Which means this shift shows up in multiple ways. Internally, teams are being asked to do more with limited resources. Externally, communities are navigating the same changes in the workforce. If AI fluency becomes a key skill, then the question becomes:

Are we helping our teams build it?

Or are we unintentionally widening the gap? Because AI fluency is not about being technical. It is about:

title: What Happens When AI Becomes the First Stop for Decisions?
author: Daphne
excerpt: McKinsey recently released a piece on something called “agentic commerce.” And while it sounds very private sector, very retail, very “not us”… I actually think it has a lot to do with local government. Maybe more than we realize. What’s actually changing? Here’s the simple version. AI is no longer just helping people do things. […]
content:
McKinsey recently released a piece on something called “agentic commerce.” And while it sounds very private sector, very retail, very “not us”… I actually think it has a lot to do with local government.

Maybe more than we realize.

What’s actually changing?

Here’s the simple version.

AI is no longer just helping people do things.

It is starting to shape how people decide things.

And that is a very different shift.

According to McKinsey:

  • 84% of people are already using AI in their everyday lives
  • 63% are using it to compare options before making decisions
  • this could grow into a $3 to $5 trillion shift by 2030

That is not small.

We are already seeing this behaviour.

People are asking AI before they search.
They are summarizing before they read.
They are comparing before they click.

The decision is being shaped earlier… and differently.

Why this matters for local government

This is where my brain goes.

We often think of this shift as something that impacts:

  • retail
  • e-commerce
  • private sector services

But if AI becomes the place where decisions are shaped first… then it absolutely impacts how residents interact with local government.

Because residents are no longer starting with:

  • your website
  • your report
  • your strategic plan
  • your beautifully formatted PDF

They are starting with AI. And that means something pretty big. AI is becoming the front door.

The “in-between” moment we are in

One thing I found really interesting in the report is this: People are comfortable letting AI help them think But not fully comfortable letting AI act on their behalf yet So we are in this in-between stage. AI is shaping decisions.
But not fully executing them. That window is important. Because it gives us time to adjust.

What might need to change

If this is how communities are starting to operate, then we probably need to start thinking a little differently. Not in a panic way. Just in a… “let’s pay attention” way. Some early questions that come to mind:

  • Is our information clear enough for AI to interpret correctly?
  • Are our policies and services structured in a way that can be easily surfaced?
  • What does trust look like when AI is part of the interaction?
  • How do we ensure accuracy when residents are receiving AI summarized information about our services?

This is not just about digital transformation anymore. This is about decision transformation.

A bigger shift than it seems

What McKinsey is really pointing to is a shift in how decisions happen. And if that changes… Then the way services are accessed, understood, and evaluated changes too. Including public services. This is not just a private sector story. It is a community experience story.

Final thought

I do not think local government needs to have all the answers right now. But I do think we need to start asking the questions. Because if AI is becoming the place where decisions begin… Then we need to think about how we show up there.

Not just on our websites.
Not just in our reports.

But in the systems people are increasingly turning to first.

Let’s explore this together

If your organization is starting to think about how AI fits into your services, communications, or decision making processes, you are not alone. Whether it is training your team, improving how your information shows up in AI, or building practical governance approaches, I would love to help. Because this shift is not just about adopting tools. It is about understanding how the way people make decisions is changing… and making sure local government evolves alongside it.

Let’s keep the conversation going.

title: Who Decides How AI Behaves? The AI Constitution
author: Daphne
excerpt: There’s a growing concept in the AI world called “AI constitutions.” It sounds very official… very structured… maybe even a little comforting. But when you dig into it, it raises some really interesting questions. What is an “AI Constitution” anyway? In simple terms, it’s a set of principles that an AI model is trained to […]
content:
There’s a growing concept in the AI world called “AI constitutions.” It sounds very official… very structured… maybe even a little comforting. But when you dig into it, it raises some really interesting questions.

What is an “AI Constitution” anyway?

In simple terms, it’s a set of principles that an AI model is trained to follow. Instead of relying only on humans reviewing outputs, the model is trained to guide itself based on written rules. Things like:

• safety

• fairness

• avoiding harm

For example, Anthropic uses something called constitutional AI, where the model critiques and improves its own responses based on these principles. OpenAI has explored a slightly different approach by asking the public how AI should behave and using that input to shape systems. So both approaches are trying to answer the same big question:

How should AI behave?

Which naturally leads to the next question…

Who actually decides that?

At first glance, this all might be very responsible. Right now, these “constitutions” are largely written, interpreted, and implemented by private companies. Even when public input is gathered, companies still decide:

• how that input is interpreted

• what gets included

• what gets left out

So while it may feel like a shared process, the final decisions still sit with a relatively small number of organizations. And that is a shift.

A shift in power

Traditionally, rules that shape society come through governments, legislation, and public institutions. There are processes. Oversight. Accountability. Representation. With AI, something different is happening. The “rules” are being built directly into the technology itself, often before formal regulation has a chance to catch up. So instead of:

Policy → Technology

We are starting to see:

Technology → de facto policy

Why this matters more than we think

AI is no longer sitting on the sidelines. It is starting to show up in:

• hiring processes

• public communications

• research and analysis

• policy drafting

And yes… even in local government workflows. Which means these hidden “constitutions” are already influencing real-world outcomes.

And yet:

• there is no elected oversight

• no formal democratic process

• no consistent global standard

That does not make it wrong. But it does make it worth paying attention to. The gap that is forming Right now, there is a bit of a gap opening up. On one side:

Private AI governance

Fast. Flexible. Built directly into systems.

On the other:

Public sector governance

Slower. Consultative. Accountable. Often reactive.

Neither is inherently better. But the gap between them is growing. And gaps tend to create friction. What this means for local government, because municipalities are already:

• using AI tools

• exploring AI for service delivery

• considering AI in communications and reporting

But the tools they are using are shaped by rules they did not create. So naturally, a few questions start to come up:

Do these systems reflect our community values?

How do we explain decisions influenced by AI?

What governance layer are we adding on top?

These are not abstract questions. They are operational ones. So… what do we do with this? I do not think the answer is to stop using AI. Not at all. But it does create an opportunity. An opportunity for public sector organizations to:

• understand how these systems are shaped

• ask better questions about governance

• build their own guardrails

• and maybe even help shape what comes next

Because right now, the window to influence how this evolves is still open. But it probably will not stay open forever.

Final thought

“AI constitutions” are an early attempt to guide how AI behaves. But at the moment, they are still corporate governance frameworks with global reach. And that tension between speed and legitimacy is what makes this conversation so important. It is not just about technology. It is about who gets to write the rules. And that feels like a conversation worth being part of.

Let’s figure this out together

If your local government is starting to explore AI, or already using it and wondering how to put the right guardrails in place, you are not alone in this. Whether it is AI training, practical implementation, or building governance frameworks that actually make sense in a municipal environment, I would love to support your team. Because adopting AI is one thing. Using it responsibly and confidently is something else entirely. And that is where the real work begins.

title: When AI Becomes a Utility: What This Could Mean for Local Government
author: Daphne
excerpt: Recently, Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, suggested something that made me pause for a moment. He floated the idea that one day AI might be sold like a utility. Think electricity. You pay for what you use. Instead of kilowatts, you would be billed for tokens or compute usage. At first glance it sounds a bit […]
content:
Recently, Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, suggested something that made me pause for a moment.

He floated the idea that one day AI might be sold like a utility. Think electricity. You pay for what you use. Instead of kilowatts, you would be billed for tokens or compute usage.

At first glance it sounds a bit futuristic. But the more I think about it, is it really that far-fetched?

Local governments already operate and regulate utilities that communities rely on every day. Water treatment plants. Electrical infrastructure. Broadband networks. These systems require planning, oversight, and long-term investment. If AI becomes something that society relies on in a similar way, then infrastructure, governance, and access will become important public sector conversations.

AI Infrastructure Is Still Infrastructure

Behind every AI tool people use today are data centres. These facilities power the models, store the information, and run the compute that makes modern AI possible.

From a local government perspective, data centres start to look less like abstract technology and more like another form of industrial infrastructure.

They require:

• land
• power
• cooling systems
• reliable connectivity
• long term operational planning

In many ways, they are not so different from other large-scale industrial facilities communities have hosted before.

Could Local Governments Operate Data Centres?

One idea that has started surfacing in discussions is whether local governments could one day operate data centres themselves, similar to how municipalities manage water systems or electricity utilities.

There are some interesting possibilities here.

Public ownership could allow communities to ensure fair access to AI infrastructure, support local innovation, and potentially provide services to regional governments or institutions. In theory, this could help position AI as a public service rather than purely a commercial product.

Regional models could also emerge where multiple communities share access to a jointly operated data centre. Think of it as a regional compute hub.

This might sound ambitious, but so did municipal electricity generation a century ago.

The Rural Canada Reality

Of course, there is a practical reality that cannot be ignored, particularly in rural Canada.

Power supply.

Large-scale AI infrastructure requires significant amounts of electricity. Many rural and northern communities already face constraints when it comes to energy capacity and grid infrastructure. Even modest industrial expansion can strain existing systems.

For communities interested in hosting data centres, this becomes one of the first questions that must be asked:

Do we actually have the power capacity to support it?

Without reliable and scalable energy supply, attracting or operating AI infrastructure becomes extremely difficult.

Data Centres as Economic Development

Even if local governments never operate their own data centres, they may still benefit significantly from hosting them.

Data centres can represent major economic development opportunities for communities.

They often bring:

• long-term property tax revenue
• infrastructure investment
• construction and maintenance jobs
• increased connectivity and digital capacity

They may not be the sexiest economic development attraction compared to tourism or retail, but they can quietly provide stable municipal revenue for decades.

For smaller communities looking to diversify their economic base, this could become an increasingly important opportunity.

The Conversation Is Just Beginning

Right now, much of the discussion around AI focuses on tools, productivity, and policy. But as AI adoption grows, we will likely see a new layer of conversation emerge around infrastructure, energy, and governance.

Who builds the systems that power AI?
Who regulates access?
Who benefits economically?

These are questions that governments, communities, and industry will need to explore together.

We went through similar conversations with electricity, telecommunications, and the internet. AI may simply be the next chapter.

Where this ultimately lands is still unclear.

But one thing feels certain – Local governments should be part of the conversation.

Let’s Keep the Conversation Going

AI is moving quickly, and many organizations are still figuring out where to begin. For local governments in particular, the questions often extend beyond tools. They touch governance, infrastructure, policy, and how communities responsibly adopt emerging technology.

Whether your organization is exploring AI implementation, staff training, or building governance frameworks to guide responsible use, these conversations are becoming increasingly important.

  • Workshops designed specifically for public sector organisations

AI does not have to be complicated. With the right approach, it can become a practical tool that strengthens the work local governments already do every day.

And as this technology evolves, the most important thing is making sure communities are part of shaping how it is used.

title: Cybersecurity Just Moved to the Council Table: GOVERNANCE
author: Daphne
excerpt: For years cybersecurity sat in the IT department. Somewhere between server updates and password resets, someone was “handling it.” That model no longer reflects reality. Modern governance frameworks now treat cybersecurity as a governance responsibility, right alongside financial oversight, risk management, and strategic planning. Cyber risk now belongs in the same conversations as budgets, infrastructure, […]
content:
For years cybersecurity sat in the IT department. Somewhere between server updates and password resets, someone was “handling it.”

That model no longer reflects reality.

Modern governance frameworks now treat cybersecurity as a governance responsibility, right alongside financial oversight, risk management, and strategic planning. Cyber risk now belongs in the same conversations as budgets, infrastructure, and long term planning.

Municipalities hold sensitive data, operate critical infrastructure, and deliver essential public services. When a cyber incident occurs it becomes an operational, financial, and reputational issue for the entire organization.

Which means cybersecurity has officially moved from the server room to the council chamber.

Cybersecurity Is Now a Governance Responsibility

Across public and private sectors, cybersecurity is increasingly recognized as a board-level risk.

Just as councils review financial reports, capital plans, and strategic priorities, they are now expected to understand the organization’s cyber risk posture.

This does not require councillors to become technical experts.

It requires leadership awareness, regular reporting, and governance structures that ensure risks are understood and managed appropriately.

Think of cybersecurity like financial oversight. Council members are not expected to run the accounting system, but they are responsible for understanding the financial health of the organization.

Cyber risk now follows the same model.

Insurance Companies Now Expect Governance Oversight

One of the clearest signals of this shift is coming from the insurance industry.

Cyber insurers are increasingly asking governance questions such as:

• Does the board or council receive cyber risk briefings?
• Is cybersecurity governance formally documented?
• Are incident response plans reviewed by leadership?
• Is the organization tracking its security maturity?

In many cases, cyber insurance coverage now depends on demonstrating governance oversight, not only technical controls.

Why Board Awareness Matters During a Claim

During a cyber incident, insurance providers often review governance documentation as part of the claims process.

They may ask questions such as:

• Was leadership informed about cyber risks?
• Were risk assessments presented to council?
• Were mitigation actions documented?

If governance oversight cannot be demonstrated, insurers may question whether appropriate risk management practices were followed.

Cyber governance therefore plays a role in both risk prevention and claim validation.

Regulators Are Paying Attention Too

Regulators across many jurisdictions are increasingly treating cybersecurity as a fiduciary responsibility.

Leadership is expected to understand and oversee cyber risks in the same way they oversee financial risks.

For municipalities this matters because cyber incidents can affect:

• essential public services
• resident data and privacy
• election integrity
• financial systems
• public trust

Cybersecurity is no longer just a technical concern. It is a governance responsibility tied directly to community resilience.

What Councils Should Be Briefed On

Just like the annual budget process, councils should receive regular briefings on cybersecurity posture. These briefings focus on strategic insight rather than technical detail.

Key briefing areas include:

1. Cyber Risk Landscape

• Emerging threats targeting municipalities
• Trends in ransomware, phishing, and supply chain attacks
• Risks relevant to the organization’s systems and services

2. Organizational Vulnerabilities

• Known weaknesses within systems or processes
• Third party vendor and supplier risks
• Areas where controls need strengthening

3. Security Maturity

• Progress against recognized frameworks such as NIST
• Improvements in security controls and governance
• Benchmarking against best practices

4. Incident Response Preparedness

• Existence and testing of response plans
• Roles and responsibilities during incidents
• Recovery and communication procedures

5. Financial Exposure

• Potential costs associated with cyber incidents
• Operational disruptions and recovery timelines
• Investments required to reduce risk

6. Insurance Coverage Conditions

• Cyber insurance requirements
• Controls needed to maintain coverage
• Documentation expectations for claims

The Good News

Cyber governance does not require councillors to become cybersecurity specialists.

It requires clear reporting, structured oversight, and a governance framework that connects technology risk to organizational decision making.

When that framework exists, cybersecurity becomes a manageable governance topic rather than an abstract technical problem.

Ready to Bring Cyber Governance to the Council Table?

Many municipalities want to strengthen their cybersecurity posture but are unsure how to structure governance, reporting, and oversight.

A well-designed Cyber Governance Framework helps councils understand risks, ensures regular briefings occur, and aligns the organization with insurance and regulatory expectations.

Because cybersecurity is no longer just an IT responsibility. It is a leadership responsibility.

title: AI, Jobs, and a Pattern We Have Seen Before
author: Daphne
excerpt: Last week Anthropic released a report on the labour market impacts of AI. Since then LinkedIn has been buzzing with reactions, predictions, and a fair amount of anxiety about what it might mean for jobs. It is understandable. Work matters deeply to people, and whenever technology moves quickly it raises questions about what comes […]
content:
Last week Anthropic released a report on the labour market impacts of AI. Since then LinkedIn has been buzzing with reactions, predictions, and a fair amount of anxiety about what it might mean for jobs.

It is understandable. Work matters deeply to people, and whenever technology moves quickly it raises questions about what comes next.

But when I read the report, I could not help thinking that we have seen this pattern before.

The researchers tried to answer an important question. Instead of asking what AI could theoretically do, they looked at what people are actually using AI for in their daily work. They combined occupational task data with real usage data from AI systems to estimate which jobs are currently most exposed.

The interesting part is that AI adoption is still far behind its theoretical capability. In some occupations, AI could technically assist with a very large portion of tasks, yet real world usage covers only a fraction of that work.

The report also found something else worth noting. There is currently no clear evidence that AI has increased unemployment in highly exposed jobs. What they do see is a slight slowdown in hiring for younger workers entering some of these occupations.

In other words, the changes are subtle so far.

This is where history helps put things in perspective.

When electricity arrived, entire industries changed. Lamplighters disappeared, but electricians, electrical engineers, and new manufacturing sectors emerged.

When computers became part of everyday office life, typists were once in high demand. Word processors changed that. But the computer era also created millions of new jobs that did not exist before.

Even ATMs caused concern when they first appeared. They did reduce the need for some teller tasks, but they also allowed banks to open more branches, which increased overall employment in banking.

Technology rarely just removes work. More often it reshapes it.

AI will likely do the same. Some tasks will become easier, some roles will evolve, and entirely new opportunities will appear that we cannot fully imagine yet.

People are incredibly resilient and creative. Throughout history we have adapted to every technological shift that has come our way.

Personally, I am excited about what this next era could bring. With thoughtful deployment and a bit of curiosity, AI has the potential to help people do better work, not replace them.

title: What Local Governments Should Be Paying Attention To: International AI Safety Report 2026
author: catchthebeat
excerpt: I just finished reading the International AI Safety Report 2026. It is more than 200 pages of global experts explaining something many of us are already sensing. AI capabilities are advancing faster than expected, while governance and policy are still catching up. For local governments, the report reads less like science fiction and more like […]
content:
I just finished reading the International AI Safety Report 2026. It is more than 200 pages of global experts explaining something many of us are already sensing. AI capabilities are advancing faster than expected, while governance and policy are still catching up. For local governments, the report reads less like science fiction and more like a familiar policy challenge: powerful new tools arriving before the rulebook is fully written.

AI Capabilities Are Accelerating

The report highlights that modern AI systems are rapidly improving across areas such as mathematics, coding, reasoning, and autonomous task completion. Adoption is also happening faster than previous technologies like personal computers.

For local governments, this means AI tools will increasingly appear in everyday administrative work. Drafting reports, analyzing data, summarizing legislation, and assisting with planning tasks will become more common uses. The key takeaway is that municipal organizations will need to build internal capacity to understand and manage these tools rather than treating them as simple software upgrades.

The “Evidence Dilemma” for Policymakers

One of the most important concepts in the report is the evidence dilemma. Policymakers often need to make decisions about emerging technologies before complete evidence exists. Acting too early risks regulating the wrong problem. Waiting too long risks allowing harms to develop.

Local governments face similar decisions frequently. Climate adaptation, infrastructure planning, and land use policy often require acting under uncertainty. AI governance will likely follow the same pattern. Municipalities should not wait for perfect clarity before establishing policies for responsible AI use, but they should also avoid overly rigid rules that limit innovation.

Reliability and Hallucinations

The report confirms that AI systems still produce hallucinations, meaning confidently stated but incorrect information. Fabricated citations, inaccurate summaries, and misleading outputs remain common challenges.

For municipal operations, reliability matters. Council reports, bylaws, procurement documents, and public communications require accuracy and accountability. AI can assist with drafting and analysis, but human review remains essential. Treating AI as a decision support tool rather than a decision maker is a practical approach for local government workflows.

Cybersecurity and Emerging Threats

Another key section addresses cybersecurity. AI tools are increasingly being used in cyber operations, both defensively and offensively.

Municipal governments already manage sensitive data and critical infrastructure systems. As AI tools become more widely available, cyber threats may become more sophisticated and automated. This makes cybersecurity readiness, staff awareness, and secure procurement practices even more important.

Deepfakes, Misinformation, and Public Trust

The report also highlights improvements in AI generated media such as synthetic images, video, and persuasive text.

For local governments, this raises concerns related to public trust and election integrity. Deepfakes or AI generated misinformation could potentially affect public discourse, especially during elections or controversial policy decisions. Municipal communications teams may need to develop strategies for monitoring and responding to misleading content.

Labour Market Impacts

The labour market analysis in the report suggests that AI will increasingly automate certain cognitive tasks, particularly in knowledge based roles. However, economists still disagree about the long term employment impact.

For municipalities, the most practical response is augmentation rather than replacement. AI can help staff work more efficiently by assisting with research, document drafting, and analysis. The future likely involves public servants supported by better digital tools rather than fewer public servants overall.

Concentration of AI Power

One governance issue highlighted in the report is the concentration of advanced AI development within a small number of countries and technology companies.

For local governments, this raises questions about procurement, resilience, and digital sovereignty. Municipalities may become increasingly dependent on a small group of vendors for critical AI capabilities. Procurement processes will need to consider transparency, security, and long term sustainability when selecting AI tools.

Layered Safeguards and Governance

The report repeatedly emphasizes the need for layered safeguards, meaning that no single mitigation strategy is sufficient. Transparency, evaluation, testing, and governance structures must work together.

In municipal terms, this means AI adoption should include policies, training, oversight mechanisms, and clear accountability. Purchasing an AI tool is only one step. The governance around how it is used is equally important.

What This Means for Local Government

The International AI Safety Report does not suggest that governments should panic about AI. It also does not recommend adopting every new tool without scrutiny.

Instead, it suggests a balanced approach. Move forward with experimentation and adoption, but do so deliberately. Build internal understanding, establish governance frameworks, and ensure that staff are equipped to use AI responsibly.

AI is not simply another IT upgrade. It represents a broader shift in how organizations process information and make decisions.

title: Canada’s AI Strategy: Less Hype, More Hockey Conditioning
author: Daphne
excerpt: Canada is not shouting about AI. It is quietly stretching, checking its gear, and getting ready for a long season. While headlines elsewhere focus on moonshot promises and AI panic cycles, Canada has been doing something refreshingly unflashy: building infrastructur e, setting rules, and making sure public servants are not left guessing. The federal government […]
content:
Canada is not shouting about AI. It is quietly stretching, checking its gear, and getting ready for a long season.

While headlines elsewhere focus on moonshot promises and AI panic cycles, Canada has been doing something refreshingly unflashy: building infrastructur

e, setting rules, and making sure public servants are not left guessing.

The federal government is continuing to roll out its AI Strategy for the Federal Public Service 2025–2027, alongside new compute support initiatives like the AI Compute Access Fund and the Canadian Sovereign AI Compute Strategy. Translation: this is not about chasing shiny tools. It is about making AI usable, responsible, and sustainable.

What Is Actually Happening

At the federal level, the AI Strategy for the Public Service is focused on embedding responsible AI into day-to-day government operations. That means clearer guidance, better governance, and more consistent use of AI to improve public services rather than experimenting in isolation.

At the same time, Canada is investing in the unglamorous but essential backbone of AI: compute.

The AI Compute Access Fund and the Canadian Sovereign AI Compute Strategy are opening access to AI computing resources for small and medium sized enterprises. This matters because without compute, AI innovation stays theoretical or locked behind very expensive doors.

Together, these initiatives aim to modernize public services, support economic growth, and strengthen national AI infrastructure without losing sight of accountability.

Why Local Government Should Pay Attention

Local governments may not be directly applying to federal compute funds, but the signals matter.

This approach reinforces three important realities for municipalities:

First, AI isno longer optional background noise. It is becoming a core operational capability that governments are expected to manage responsibly.

Second, infrastructure and governance come before scale. Canada is not racing to deploy AI everywhere overnight. It is building guardrails, capacity, and shared understanding first.

Third, responsible AI is not just a policy issue. It is a service delivery issue. AI that improves internal workflows, response times, and consistency can directly improve resident experience when done well.

This Is Not a Tech Story. It Is a Capacity Story.

What is striking about Canada’s approach is what it does not emphasize.

There is no promise that AI will replace people.
There is no suggestion that tools alone will fix broken systems.
There is no rush to scale without understanding risk.

Instead, the focus is on:

  • embedding AI thoughtfully into operations

  • improving access to the infrastructure that makes AI usable

  • ensuring public servants understand what AI is and what it is not

That is a very Canadian way to approach transformation. Practical. Measured. Slightly understated.

The Missed Opportunity If Local Governments Sit This Out

Federal strategies set tone and expectations. If local governments wait too long to engage with AI literacy, governance, and operational readiness, the gap between policy and practice will widen quickly.

The risk is not moving too fast.
The risk is being unprepared when expectations catch up.

Final Thought

Canada is not trying to win the AI sprint. It is training for endurance.

Local governments should take note. AI success will not come from chasing every new tool. It will come from building capability, confidence, and clarity over time.

And just like any good long game, the smartest moves are often the quiet ones happening well before the spotlight turns on.

title: What Local Government Can Learn from Athletes About AI and Digital Transformation
author: Daphne
excerpt: Local governments everywhere are being told the same thing:“AI is coming. Digital transformation is urgent. Move faster.” (McKinsey & Company, 2025) And yet, if we are honest, most transformations do not fail because people do not care. They fail because everything becomes a sprint with no plan to recover, reset, or build real capability. An […]
content:
Local governments everywhere are being told the same thing:
“AI is coming. Digital transformation is urgent. Move faster.” (McKinsey & Company, 2025)

And yet, if we are honest, most transformations do not fail because people do not care. They fail because everything becomes a sprint with no plan to recover, reset, or build real capability.

An interesting idea emerging from the private sector reframes this entirely: treat digital transformation the way elite athletes treat training.

Not as a single heroic effort. But as interval training.

Why This Matters Right Now

AI, generative AI, and now agentic AI have raised expectations dramatically. Nearly every organization is experimenting with AI in some way, but very few have actually scaled it in a way that delivers lasting value.

The research is sobering:

  • Most organizations are “doing AI”

  • Very few are seeing meaningful impact

  • Even fewer can sustain improvement over time

Local governments feel this acutely. Limited staff. Limited budgets. High accountability. Little room for failure.

This is where the athlete mindset becomes useful.

The Athlete Mindset Applied to Local Government

Elite athletes do not train at maximum intensity every day forever. They alternate between focused effort and strategic rest. That balance is what allows improvement without burnout or injury.

Digital transformation, especially with AI, works the same way.

1. Clear Purpose Before New Tools

Athletes do not train randomly. They train for something specific.

Local governments often jump straight to AI use cases:

  • AI for reports

  • AI for customer service

  • AI for policy drafting

  • AI for emergency management

Without a clear “why,” this quickly turns into a long list of pilots with little impact.

A stronger approach is to define:

  • What problem are we trying to reduce

  • Where staff are consistently overloaded

  • What outcomes actually matter to residents

AI should serve those goals, not create new ones.

2. Planning Is Not Bureaucracy, It Is Training

In local government, planning sometimes gets framed as slowing things down. In reality, it is how momentum is sustained.

Athletes plan their training schedules. Organizations need the same discipline.

That includes:

  • Involving the right people early, not just IT

  • Understanding policy, privacy, and records implications

  • Acknowledging technical debt that already exists

  • Setting realistic timelines and success measures

Skipping this phase does not make transformation faster. It just makes the recovery longer.

3. Execution Requires Pace, Not Panic

One of the most useful ideas from the article is balance.

Transformation requires:

  • Periods of focused delivery

  • Pauses to reflect, adjust, and learn

  • Ongoing capability building, not one off training

  • Time to clean up technical debt instead of layering new tools on top

Local governments often feel pressure to move continuously, even when teams are clearly stretched. That is not sustainable.

Athletes know when to push and when to recover. Organizations need to learn that too.

AI Capability Is the Real Competitive Advantage

One of the strongest takeaways is that tools do not create transformation. People do.

Organizations that succeed invest heavily in building AI literacy at every level:

  • Basic understanding for all staff

  • Practical application for functional teams

  • Advanced skills for those leading implementation

In local government terms, this means moving beyond “AI awareness sessions” and toward role appropriate, practical training that staff can actually use in their day to day work.

Paying Down Technical Debt Is Part of the Work

AI cannot fix broken systems.

If legacy processes, outdated systems, and inconsistent data are ignored, AI simply exposes those weaknesses faster.

Successful transformation includes:

  • Auditing existing systems

  • Decommissioning what no longer serves the organization

  • Simplifying processes

  • Creating space for sustainable improvement

This is not glamorous work, but it is essential.

The Big Lesson for Local Government

Digital transformation is not a single project. AI adoption is not a one time decision.

Like athletic training, it requires:

  • Clear goals

  • Thoughtful preparation

  • Disciplined execution

  • Regular pauses to adjust

  • Long term commitment to capability building

The organizations that succeed are not the ones moving the fastest. They are the ones pacing themselves intelligently.

Final Thought

Local governments do not need to “keep up” with AI hype. They need to build the capacity to use AI responsibly, sustainably, and in service of real public value.

Interval training beats burnout every time.

And just like athletes, the goal is not a single breakthrough moment. It is staying strong enough to keep improving over time.

title: The Apology Act, AI, and the Radical Idea of Saying “Sorry” in Local Government
author: Daphne
excerpt: Local government has a complicated relationship with the word “sorry.” We have all seen it. A resident is upset. Something went wrong. Everyone agrees the situation is unfortunate. And yet the response reads like it was written by a committee of risk managers who were actively allergic to empathy. Enter the Apology Act. Quietly assented […]
content:
Local government has a complicated relationship with the word “sorry.”

We have all seen it. A resident is upset. Something went wrong. Everyone agrees the situation is unfortunate. And yet the response reads like it was written by a committee of risk managers who were actively allergic to empathy.

Enter the Apology Act.

Quietly assented to in 2006, this Act exists for one very specific reason: saying “sorry” is not the same thing as saying “we are legally liable.”

And as AI starts drafting more of our emails, letters, and public responses, this distinction suddenly matters a lot.

What the Apology Act Actually Says (No Law Degree Required)

The Apology Act makes it very clear that an apology:

  • Is not an admission of fault

  • Does not create legal liability

  • Does not void insurance coverage

  • Cannot be used against you in court or tribunal proceedings

In other words, expressing sympathy or regret will not summon your insurer’s worst nightmare or trigger a legal apocalypse.

You can acknowledge harm without admitting fault. The Act explicitly protects that.

Now Add AI to the Mix

AI is increasingly being used in local government to help draft responses, summarize incidents, and support public communication. This is great for efficiency.

It is less great when the output sounds like a robot who has read the risk register but never met a human.

Left unguided, AI tends to default to overly cautious, emotionally neutral language. The kind that technically answers the question while somehow making the situation worse.

Ironically, in trying to avoid risk, it often escalates it.

Why Empathy Is Not a Compliance Risk

Residents are rarely asking for a legal analysis. They are asking to be heard.

A simple “I’m sorry this happened” can de-escalate a situation faster than three paragraphs of procedural explanation. The Apology Act exists precisely to make room for that response.

AI should help staff get there faster. Not strip empathy out because it feels “safer.”

The Real Risk Is Sounding Like You Don’t Care

When AI is used without guardrails, it can unintentionally:

  • Remove empathy from responses

  • Delay acknowledgment while staff over review

  • Create language that feels dismissive or defensive

None of those reduce risk. They just move it downstream into complaints, escalation, and mistrust.

AI should support human judgment, not replace it. Especially in moments that involve frustration, fear, or real impact on people’s lives.

A Smarter Way to Use AI With the Apology Act in Mind

Responsible AI use in local government means asking a few practical questions:

  • Does this tool allow empathetic language or sanitize it?

  • Is there a human review step for sensitive communication?

  • Do staff understand that apologies are legally protected?

  • Are legal, policy, and communications teams aligned?

If the answer to any of these is “we are not sure,” that is your starting point.

Final Thought

The Apology Act did not give local governments permission to be reckless. It gave permission to be human.

AI does not change that. If anything, it makes it more important.

Because the fastest way to erode trust is not admitting fault. It is sounding like you never noticed the impact in the first place.

And no algorithm can fix that after the fact.

title: Before You Buy the AI Tool: Questions Local Governments Should Ask (So You Don’t Regret It Later)
author: Daphne
excerpt: Artificial intelligence is having a moment. Every week there is a new tool promising to save time, fix workflows, reduce burnout, and somehow also make great coffee. Local governments are understandably curious. We are stretched thin, expected to do more with less, and constantly told that AI is the solution. Sometimes it is. Sometimes it […]
content:
Artificial intelligence is having a moment. Every week there is a new tool promising to save time, fix workflows, reduce burnout, and somehow also make great coffee.

Local governments are understandably curious. We are stretched thin, expected to do more with less, and constantly told that AI is the solution. Sometimes it is. Sometimes it is just a very expensive PDF generator.

Before signing a contract or booking a demo that looks suspiciously slick, here are the questions local governments should ask when considering a new AI tool. These are not “gotcha” questions. They are common sense questions learned the hard way.

1. What problem are we actually trying to solve?

This sounds obvious. It is not.

Are you trying to reduce repetitive admin work
Improve response times
Support emergency management
Help staff write reports faster
Improve public communication

If the answer is “all of the above,” pause. AI works best when it is solving a very specific problem. Buying a tool before you clearly understand the problem usually leads to frustration, low adoption, and a lot of “we thought it did more than this.”

2. Does this replace thinking, or support staff doing their jobs better?

Good AI tools support decision making. Bad ones quietly replace judgment without telling you.

Ask whether the tool is designed to assist staff or automate decisions that should remain human led. In local government, context matters. Policy interpretation, emergency response, and governance decisions still need people in the loop.

If a vendor cannot clearly explain where human oversight sits, that is a red flag.

3. Where does the data live and who owns it?

This is the least fun question and the most important one.

Ask:

  • Where is data stored
  • Who has access to it
  • Whether data is used to train models
  • What happens to data if you cancel the contract

Local governments handle sensitive information. If the answer is vague, overly technical, or buried in terms and conditions, keep digging.

4. Can this integrate with what we already use?

AI tools do not exist in a vacuum. They sit on top of existing systems like records management, document storage, email, and spreadsheets.

Ask whether the tool works with:

  • Your records management system
  • Existing document workflows
  • Common tools staff already use

If the answer is “you just upload everything manually,” that is not AI. That is extra work.

5. How much training is actually required?

If a tool requires extensive training, custom prompts, or one internal expert to keep it running, adoption will be limited.

Good AI tools feel intuitive and reduce cognitive load. Ask what onboarding looks like, how long it takes, and whether non technical staff can use it confidently.

If the tool only works well when one person understands it deeply, you have created a single point of failure.

6. What is the risk level if something goes wrong?

AI makes mistakes. The question is how visible and recoverable those mistakes are.

Ask:

  • What happens if the tool generates incorrect information
  • How errors are flagged
  • Whether outputs can be reviewed before use

In areas like emergency management, policy drafting, or public communication, error tolerance is low. Tools should support review, not bypass it.

7. Is this a capacity tool or a compliance risk?

Some AI tools quietly introduce policy, privacy, or records management issues.

Ask whether the tool aligns with:

  • Records retention requirements
  • Privacy obligations
  • Information management policies
  • Internal governance frameworks

If adopting the tool means creating new policy gaps, factor that work into the cost. AI does not reduce workload if it creates governance cleanup later.

8. What does success actually look like in six months?

This is where honesty matters.

Ask:

  • What measurable outcome improves
  • How staff time is actually reduced
  • Whether the tool can be piloted before full rollout

If success cannot be clearly described, it will be hard to evaluate whether the investment was worth it.

9. Are we buying a tool or buying confidence?

This one stings a little.

Sometimes local governments buy AI tools because everyone else seems to be doing it. That is understandable. But confidence comes from clarity, not software.

The best AI implementations are quiet. They remove friction, reduce duplication, and make work feel lighter without making a big show of it.

Final Thought

AI in local government is not about being cutting edge. It is about being practical, responsible, and realistic.

If a tool helps staff do their work better, reduces repetitive tasks, and fits within existing governance frameworks, it is worth exploring. If it promises transformation without effort, it probably delivers disappointment with a subscription fee.

Ask good questions. Stay curious. And remember: the smartest systems still need smart people.

title: McKinsey Is Using AI in Hiring
author: Daphne
excerpt: Local government should be paying attention This week, McKinsey quietly did something that made me genuinely excited. As part of their graduate recruitment process, they are now asking candidates to work with an AI chatbot during the final stages of interviews. Not as a novelty. Not as a trick. But as a way to understand […]
content:
Local government should be paying attention

This week, McKinsey quietly did something that made me genuinely excited.

As part of their graduate recruitment process, they are now asking candidates to work with an AI chatbot during the final stages of interviews. Not as a novelty. Not as a trick. But as a way to understand how people think, reason, and make decisions when AI is part of the workflow.

They are not testing whether candidates can code or whether they know AI theory. They are testing how candidates use AI as a thinking partner. How they prompt it. How they evaluate what it produces. How they refine, challenge, and apply the output in real problem solving scenarios.

That is a big signal.

This is not about AI skills. It is about judgement.

What McKinsey is really assessing is not technical ability. It is judgement.

Can a person work with AI thoughtfully? Can they spot gaps or errors? Can they apply context, ethics, and reasoning rather than blindly accepting outputs? Can they use AI to enhance their thinking rather than outsource it?

That distinction matters, especially for the public sector.

Local government work is complex, contextual, and accountable. Decisions affect real people, real services, and real trust. AI will never replace that responsibility, but it will increasingly sit alongside it.

Why this matters for local government

It is easy to look at moves like this and think, “That’s private sector. That’s consulting. That’s not us.”

But the reality is that the shift is already happening.

Staff are encountering AI tools whether we formally implement them or not. Generative AI is becoming embedded in everyday software. Expectations around productivity, analysis, and responsiveness are changing.

McKinsey’s move signals that working effectively with AI is becoming a core professional skill, not a niche one.

For local government, this raises important questions:

  • Are we preparing staff to use AI responsibly, or just telling them to avoid it?
  • Do we focus more on restriction than capability?
  • Are we training people to think critically with AI, not just about AI?

From AI policy to AI capability

There is a lot of conversation right now about AI policy, and that is important. Governance, privacy, and accountability matter deeply in public sector environments.

But policy alone does not build confidence.

What builds confidence is capability. Clear frameworks. Practical training. Real examples of how AI can support everyday work without replacing human judgement or responsibility.

What McKinsey is doing in recruitment is essentially saying, “This is how work will happen. Let’s see how you handle it.”

Local government should be asking similar questions. Not in interviews necessarily, but in training, onboarding, and workforce development.

AI as a collaborator, not a shortcut

The future of work is not AI doing the job for us.

It is AI supporting humans who bring context, values, experience, and accountability to the table.

That is especially true in local government, where trust and transparency are foundational.

Seeing AI show up in hiring at this level is not a threat. It is an opportunity. A chance to rethink how we prepare people to do complex, judgement based work in a world where AI is simply part of the environment.

And honestly, as someone who works at the intersection of AI and local government, this is the kind of development that makes me excited.

Because it confirms what many of us already know.

AI is not coming.

It is here.

And how we choose to work with it matters.

title: To AI Policy or NOT to AI Policy?
author: Daphne
excerpt: THAT is the question… As artificial intelligence becomes part of everyday work in local government, I keep coming back to the same question: do we really need a standalone AI policy? It is a fair question, especially when you look at how other technologies have been adopted over time. We do not have a Microsoft […]
content:
THAT is the question…

As artificial intelligence becomes part of everyday work in local government, I keep coming back to the same question: do we really need a standalone AI policy?

It is a fair question, especially when you look at how other technologies have been adopted over time. We do not have a Microsoft policy. We do not have a Grammarly policy. We do not have a specific policy for Google, Canva or shared drives. These tools simply became part of how we do business, guided by existing frameworks around behaviour, accountability, and privacy.

AI is starting to follow the same path.

As staff explore tools that help with drafting, summarizing, research, and analysis, the instinct is often to respond with a new policy. Something formal. Something comprehensive. Something that feels like control. But policies alone do not necessarily create clarity. Sometimes, they create hesitation, confusion, or unnecessary barriers to responsible use.

What feels far more important than another policy document is a clear framework.

Decision-making must remain human. AI can support analysis, efficiency, and consistency, but accountability does not shift. Privacy must be protected, especially in environments that handle sensitive personal and organizational information. And information should not be casually shared simply because a tool makes it easy or fast to do so.

Those principles are not new. They already exist in many local governments through HR policies, Privacy policies, Records Management Practices, and Codes of Conduct. Rather than creating something entirely separate, there is a strong argument for embedding AI expectations into these existing structures where staff already understand the rules and responsibilities.

In many cases, the challenge is not a lack of policy, but a lack of shared understanding. Staff want to know what is appropriate, what is not, and how to use new tools responsibly without fear of getting it wrong. Clear guidance, training, and leadership support often go much further than another policy added to an already long list.

So maybe the question is not whether we need an AI policy at all.

Maybe the better question is whether we need clearer frameworks, better education, and more open conversations about how AI fits into the work we already do.

Because honestly… who needs more policies?

Just thinking out loud.

title: AI and the Legal System: A Useful Tool, Not a Stand In
author: Daphne
excerpt: AI is now part of everyday work. It explains legislation, summarizes reports, drafts content, and answers questions in seconds. In local government and legal-adjacent roles, that speed can feel like a gift. It can also be a quiet risk. In a recent recorded conversation, Daphne Thomson sat down with Scott Parker, a lawyer licensed in […]
content:
AI is now part of everyday work. It explains legislation, summarizes reports, drafts content, and answers questions in seconds. In local government and legal-adjacent roles, that speed can feel like a gift. It can also be a quiet risk.

In a recent recorded conversation, Daphne Thomson sat down with Scott Parker, a lawyer licensed in the Northwest Territories and Nunavut and currently practicing with Lawson Lundell, to talk through what AI is doing well, where it falls short, and why legal work is one area where human judgment still matters deeply.

The conversation was not about fear or banning tools. It was about balance, context, and responsibility.

When AI feels helpful

Many administrators and professionals are already using AI to get oriented. Summarizing new legislation. Comparing bylaws. Drafting early versions of policies. Scott acknowledged that this can be genuinely useful.

As he put it, AI can help people “get a condensed overview so they can have a more literate conversation with a lawyer.”

That distinction matters. AI can help you prepare. It can help you ask better questions. It should not be treated as the final answer.

Where the risk shows up

The real concern begins when AI is used for legal interpretation without oversight. Scott was clear that the consequences of getting it wrong are not small.

“People are asking AI specific legal questions,” he noted, “and the risk is that the answer might be incomplete, misleading, or just wrong. The consequences of that can be very high.”

He gave practical examples. Missing a court filing deadline. Taking action based on an incorrect interpretation of legislation. Drafting a bylaw that quietly conflicts with an overriding section of law.

In municipal settings, that risk can sit unnoticed for years.

“You can have a bylaw that looks fine on its face,” Scott explained, “but it might include a clause that is actually prohibited by legislation. That may not surface until much later, when it becomes a real problem.”

Hallucinations are not hypothetical

The conversation also touched on AI hallucinations, something that has already caused issues in the legal profession.

Scott referenced real cases where lawyers relied on fake cases generated by public AI tools. Courts treated this as an abuse of process.

“That is not a small mistake,” he said. “In law, making up authority, even unintentionally, is extremely serious.”

This is where the difference between open public AI systems and closed legal AI systems matters. Scott explained that law firms use closed systems that rely only on verified cases and commentary, and that provide direct source references that can be checked.

Public tools do not offer that level of reliability.

Human oversight is not optional

A recurring theme in the conversation was that oversight is only meaningful if it comes from someone with the right expertise.

“Oversight requires expertise,” Scott said plainly. “Lawyers are trained to interpret legislation, to understand how sections interact, and to know where the traps are.”

For busy administrators who wear many hats, the practical path is not avoiding AI altogether. It is knowing when to stop and who to involve next.

Scott encouraged establishing a relationship with legal counsel early. Clearing conflicts. Setting up a retainer. Creating a working rhythm where AI assisted drafts can be reviewed efficiently and properly.

That relationship, he noted, saves time and reduces risk in the long run.

AI does not replace due diligence

Daphne raised a thoughtful question during the discussion. If an administrator uses AI carefully, checks sources, and provides a well organized overview to a lawyer, does that reduce legal costs?

Scott agreed that good preparation helps. A client who understands the landscape and can point to relevant sources creates a better starting point.

But he was also clear that it does not replace legal due diligence.

“Even if a client provides a draft,” he said, “the lawyer still has to do their own comprehensive review of the legislation and case law. That responsibility does not go away.”

A question of governance, not speed

One of the most honest moments in the conversation came near the end. Scott cautioned against the pressure to move quickly.

“There can be a bias toward answers that help you get things done faster,” he said. “That can lead people to rely on AI outputs that fit what they want, even if they are not quite right.”

Daphne summed it up simply. AI is powerful. But good governance still depends on critical thinking, source checking, and strong professional relationships.

AI can support the work. It should not quietly replace judgment.

Watch the full conversation

This article only scratches the surface. The full recorded discussion goes deeper into real examples, municipal contexts, and practical guidance for anyone working with legislation, bylaws, or policy.
