title: What Canada’s AI Review Tells Us About the Future of Governance
author: Daphne
excerpt: A recent announcement from Canada’s national security watchdog caught my attention. The National Security and Intelligence Review Agency has launched a review into how federal security agencies are using and governing artificial intelligence. This isn’t a reactionary move. It’s not about halting AI or sounding the alarm. It’s about understanding how AI is already being […]
content:
A recent announcement from Canada’s national security watchdog caught my attention. The National Security and Intelligence Review Agency has launched a review into how federal security agencies are using and governing artificial intelligence.

This isn’t a reactionary move. It’s not about halting AI or sounding the alarm. It’s about understanding how AI is already being used, how decisions are made, what oversight exists, and where potential gaps or risks may need attention.

That distinction matters.

AI has quietly become part of everyday operations across government. In the federal security space, it is already being used for things like document translation and detecting cyber threats. Because of that reality, the conversation has shifted from “should we use AI” to “how do we govern it responsibly.”

This is an important signal for local government.

The lesson here isn’t that AI is dangerous. It’s that AI is normalizing faster than many governance structures were designed for. Oversight, clarity, and accountability are now the work. Knowing where AI is used. Understanding why it’s used. Being clear about who remains responsible for outcomes. And making sure there are mechanisms to review and adjust as tools evolve.

What’s encouraging is how this review is being approached. With transparency. With access to information. With the acknowledgment that governance must evolve alongside technology, not trail years behind it.

This is what organizational maturity looks like.

Not bans.

Not panic.

Not pretending AI isn’t already part of the operating environment.

Just thoughtful stewardship catching up with reality.

For municipalities, this is a timely reminder that you don’t need to have every answer today. What matters is starting the right conversations. Building AI literacy at the Council table. Supporting staff with clarity instead of silence. And approaching AI as a governance issue, not just a technical one.

AI governance isn’t about fear.

It’s about responsibility, trust, and leadership.

title: AI and the 2026 Elections: Practical Support, Not Shortcuts
author: Daphne
excerpt: Elections are one of the most demanding responsibilities local governments carry. The timelines are fixed, the legislation is precise, and the margin for error is small. At the same time, many election teams are operating with limited staff, high turnover, and competing priorities. Against that backdrop, conversations about AI can feel uncomfortable or even risky. […]
content:
Elections are one of the most demanding responsibilities local governments carry. The timelines are fixed, the legislation is precise, and the margin for error is small. At the same time, many election teams are operating with limited staff, high turnover, and competing priorities.

Against that backdrop, conversations about AI can feel uncomfortable or even risky. This session was created to change that tone.

Rather than asking whether AI should be used in elections, the more useful question is how it can be used responsibly, transparently, and in a way that supports the people doing the work.

This article shares the thinking behind the session and what you will see in the full video.

What AI Actually Is in an Election Context

One of the first things the session addresses is definition. AI is often described as something mysterious or autonomous, when in practice it behaves much more like a support tool.

In the election environment, AI can help analyze information, draft first versions of documents, organize large volumes of material, and surface patterns that might otherwise be missed. What it cannot do is make decisions, interpret nuance without guidance, or replace professional judgment.

Throughout the session, the emphasis stays clear. AI supports the work. Humans remain accountable for every outcome.

Risk, Bias, and Why Oversight Matters

A recurring theme in the video is that AI is not neutral. It reflects the data it is trained on and the instructions it is given. That means it can be biased, incomplete, or simply wrong.

This is especially important in elections, where fairness, accuracy, and public trust are non negotiable.

The session spends time on how to reduce risk through good inputs, careful review, and clear boundaries. AI outputs should always be checked. Sources should always be verified. The responsibility does not shift simply because a tool was used.

Privacy, Security, and Legislative Realities

Privacy and data protection are not side notes in this conversation. They are foundational.

The video walks through how to think about data residency, platform choice, and minimizing exposure, with a specific focus on British Columbia requirements. Rather than promoting a single tool, the session encourages thoughtful selection based on what data is being used, where it lives, and who has access.

The goal is not to avoid AI altogether, but to use it in places where it makes sense and avoid it where the risk outweighs the benefit.

Using AI to Learn and Refresh Election Legislation

One of the most practical demonstrations in the session shows how AI can be used as a learning companion.

Free tools can be used to help staff refresh their understanding of election legislation, explore “what if” scenarios, or break down complex sections into more digestible explanations. This can be especially helpful for newer staff or teams preparing for an election after a long gap.

The key message is simple. AI can help you learn faster, but only if the source material you provide is accurate and authoritative.

Building an Elections Assistant

A central feature of the session is the idea of creating a dedicated elections assistant.

Rather than using a general AI tool for everything, an elections assistant is trained on the specific legislation, guides, templates, and historical documents relevant to your jurisdiction. When done properly, this creates more consistent and reliable outputs.

In the video, this assistant is used to support election work plans, timelines, internal guides, and drafting tasks. The quality of the output is directly tied to the quality of the information it is given.

Planning, Tracking, and Staying Organized

Elections are as much about logistics as they are about law.

The session shows how AI can support the creation of election work plans, task lists, and timelines, and how those outputs can be connected to simple project tracking tools. Automated reminders and status updates can reduce the mental load on election staff, especially during peak periods.

This is not about adding complexity. It is about reducing the risk of something being missed.

Drafting Notices, Forms, and Communications

Drafting statutory notices, election communications, and internal documents is time consuming, but also highly structured.

The video demonstrates how AI can help draft first versions of these materials when provided with approved templates and clear instructions. Smart forms for nomination intake and document organization are also discussed, showing how digital intake can improve consistency and record keeping.

As always, review and approval remain essential.

Staffing, Budgeting, and Site Planning

Beyond documents and timelines, elections involve people, money, and physical space.

The session explores how AI can support staffing plans, training guides, and advance voting day preparation. Budgeting support is also covered, including how historical election budgets can be used as a reference point for future planning.

Site planning is another practical area where AI can help. By reviewing layouts and requirements, it can assist with accessibility considerations and voting place setup, while final decisions remain with staff on the ground.

Post Election Work and Knowledge Transfer

The work does not end when the ballots are counted.

Post election reporting, council orientation, and operational summaries are critical for accountability and continuity. The video shows how AI can help compile reports and prepare orientation materials using data already generated during the election process.

This helps preserve organizational knowledge and reduces the need to start from scratch next time.

Why This Session Matters Now

Many local governments are already thinking about the 2026 election cycle. Some are eager to explore new tools. Others are understandably cautious.

This session is designed for both

It does not ask you to adopt everything. It invites you to understand what is possible, what is appropriate, and what should remain firmly human.

If nothing else, it offers a clearer lens through which to evaluate AI in an election context.

The full video includes live demonstrations, real examples, and thoughtful questions that reflect the realities election teams face every day.

If you are responsible for election planning, supporting election staff, or advising Council, I hope this session brings you clarity and practical value.

title: From Tools to Support: What AI Really Means for Work Today
author: Daphne
excerpt: AI is now part of everyday work. Not loudly. Not dramatically. It shows up quietly inside documents, emails, searches, and workflows. And while many organizations are experimenting with it, the results are mixed. Not because the technology does not work. But because the way we think about work has not fully caught up. What stands […]
content:
AI is now part of everyday work. Not loudly. Not dramatically. It shows up quietly inside documents, emails, searches, and workflows. And while many organizations are experimenting with it, the results are mixed.

Not because the technology does not work.

But because the way we think about work has not fully caught up.

What stands out most in recent research on AI in the workplace is a simple truth: the real opportunity is not smarter machines. It is better support for people.

AI Is Powerful, but Judgment Still Matters

AI is often compared to big moments in history like the steam engine or the internet. That comparison fits. This technology can summarize, reason, plan, and assist at scale.

But AI does not replace judgment, context, or accountability. Especially in local government, where decisions are public-facing and values-driven, human oversight remains essential.

AI works best when it supports people who stay firmly in control.

Staff Are Ready. Leaders Just Need to Catch Up

One of the most interesting insights is how ready staff already are. Employees are experimenting, learning, and using AI in thoughtful ways, often without formal guidance.

What they are looking for is not permission to automate everything. They want clarity, training, and guardrails. They want to know what is appropriate, what is safe, and how to use these tools responsibly.

Hesitation usually does not come from staff. It comes from leadership uncertainty.

Moving Fast Without Losing Trust

Speed and trust do not have to compete.

People want tools that reduce friction and help them move faster, but concerns around privacy, accuracy, and security are valid. Trust grows when organizations set clear expectations, define boundaries, and communicate openly.

Guardrails are not brakes. They are what make progress sustainable.

Small Pilots Will Only Take You So Far

AI pilots are everywhere, and that is a good thing. But when pilots never turn into new ways of working, the impact stays limited.

The real value of AI shows up when organizations stop asking, “How can this save time?” and start asking, “How could this change how work flows from start to finish?”

Transformation happens when workflows change, not just tools.

Technology Isn’t the Hard Part

This part is often uncomfortable, but important.

The technology largely works. What slows organizations down is alignment, skills, governance, and how work is designed. AI is not a traditional software rollout. It is a shift in how work happens.

Organizations that succeed treat it that way and invest in people, clarity, and operating models.

AI Is Like Power Steering, Not Autopilot

AI is like power steering in your car.

It does not decide where you are going.

You still choose the route. You still hold the wheel.

It just makes turning easier, especially when the road gets busy, heavy, or complex.

When people are trained, trusted, and supported, AI reduces friction instead of creating fear. It helps carry the load without taking away responsibility or judgment.

That is where the real value shows up. Not in AI doing more, but in people being able to do their work with a little less strain and a little more clarity.

Moving Forward Thoughtfully

The future of work is not human or AI.

It is people in control, with better support, done thoughtfully.

For local governments, this means moving beyond experimentation and toward understanding how AI fits into real workflows, real responsibilities, and real public trust.

title: Agentic AI and Local Government: Why Understanding Matters More Than Speed
author: Daphne
excerpt: I’ve been spending time with the latest work on agentic AI, and one idea keeps standing out. Nearly 8 in 10 organizations are using AI, yet most are seeing very little real impact. That gap feels familiar. Across local governments, there is curiosity, experimentation, and a growing sense that AI should probably be part of […]
content:
I’ve been spending time with the latest work on agentic AI, and one idea keeps standing out.

Nearly 8 in 10 organizations are using AI, yet most are seeing very little real impact.

That gap feels familiar.

Across local governments, there is curiosity, experimentation, and a growing sense that AI should probably be part of the conversation. But what is often missing is not intent or effort. It is clarity.

From Helpful Tool to New Way of Working

In many organizations, AI shows up as a helpful add-on. Draft an email. Summarize a report. Speed up a task. These are useful wins, and they matter.

But they are not transformational on their own.

What is being pointed to is a deeper shift. Agentic AI is less about individual tasks and more about how work flows, how decisions are supported, and how people interact with systems over time. It is a move from pilots to purpose. From isolated experiments to intentional ways of working.

That distinction is especially important in local government.

This Is Not a Technology Conversation

For Councils and leadership teams, AI is not really a technology issue. It is a governance issue.

AI raises questions about risk, accountability, transparency, oversight, and human judgment. These questions do not live only with IT or staff. They land at the Council table, whether they are named explicitly or not.

At the same time, AI is already embedded in everyday tools. It is built into operating systems, document workflows, search, and communications. Staff are often using AI-supported systems without realizing it.

So the decision is no longer whether AI will be part of local government.

It already is.

The real question is whether leaders feel equipped to guide it thoughtfully.

Why Councils Need AI Literacy

AI literacy does not mean turning elected officials into technologists. It means giving Councils enough understanding to:

  • Ask better questions
  • Evaluate risk realistically
  • Understand staff recommendations
  • Set policy direction with confidence
  • Keep human judgment at the centre

When Councils have this foundation, conversations become calmer, clearer, and more grounded. AI stops feeling abstract or intimidating and starts feeling manageable.

Looking Ahead to 2026

As we look toward 2026, AI will continue to deepen its presence in municipal operations. The communities that feel most confident will not be the ones that adopted the most tools the fastest. They will be the ones that invested early in understanding, governance, and people.

Sometimes the most powerful move is not adopting faster.

It is understanding better.

title: Preparing Local Governments for 2026: Why Transformation Is No Longer a One-Time Event
author: Daphne
excerpt: As we look toward 2026, one idea keeps surfacing in conversations with local government leaders, staff, and consultants alike: transformation is no longer something we “do” and then move on from. It is becoming a new way of working. Recent insights from McKinsey highlight two major forces leaders have been navigating. The first is the […]
content:
As we look toward 2026, one idea keeps surfacing in conversations with local government leaders, staff, and consultants alike: transformation is no longer something we “do” and then move on from. It is becoming a new way of working.

Recent insights from McKinsey highlight two major forces leaders have been navigating. The first is the growing promise of agentic and generative AI as a way to improve productivity and capacity. The second is ongoing disruption in the broader world, from shifting trade relationships to geopolitical uncertainty. Together, these forces are reshaping how organizations think about growth, resilience, and leadership.

What stands out most is this: AI is progressing faster than most organizations’ ability to respond. The technology itself is not the problem. The challenge lies in adoption, understanding, and change management. Many local governments can see the potential value, but have not yet realized it in a meaningful, day-to-day way.

For local governments, this reality feels especially familiar. Municipalities are not chasing innovation for innovation’s sake. They are balancing public trust, governance, policy cycles, and limited capacity — all while expectations continue to rise.

This is why transformation cannot be treated as a one-off project. It needs to become a steady, human-centred practice. Small steps. Ongoing learning. Clear understanding. And most importantly, investment in people alongside technology.

AI will continue to deepen its presence in everyday tools, workflows, and decision-making. The municipalities that feel most confident in 2026 will not be the ones that adopted the flashiest tools, but the ones that built understanding early and kept human judgement at the centre.

My focus moving into 2026 remains simple: helping local governments build confidence with AI in a way that feels practical, calm, and grounded. When teams understand what AI actually does, where the risks sit, and how to govern it responsibly, transformation becomes manageable — not overwhelming.

title: How AI Can Support Local Election Teams in 2026
author: Daphne
excerpt: And why staff training matters more than ever. Preparing for a local election is a full team effort. It’s detailed, carefully legislated work that relies on accuracy, timing, privacy, and calm coordination. With the updates brought in through Bill 13 and the steady shift toward digital workflows, the work hasn’t become simpler, but the tools […]
content:
And why staff training matters more than ever.

Preparing for a local election is a full team effort. It’s detailed, carefully legislated work that relies on accuracy, timing, privacy, and calm coordination. With the updates brought in through Bill 13 and the steady shift toward digital workflows, the work hasn’t become simpler, but the tools available to us finally have.

AI isn’t here to take away anyone’s role.
It’s here to support election teams so they can focus on people, fairness, and good decision-making instead of spending hours wrestling documents, deadlines, and notices.

With the right training, AI becomes a steady assistant that helps elections run more smoothly and gives staff room to breathe.

Where AI makes the biggest difference

AI fits naturally into the parts of election administration that are repetitive, tightly timed, or heavy on compliance. When used thoughtfully, it reduces manual workload without replacing human judgment.

Here are the areas where election teams feel the strongest benefits during training:

1. Building smarter election workplans

Instead of juggling spreadsheets and sticky notes, AI can create a full 2026 election timeline, pull in every legislative deadline, and keep it updated as you work.
Staff learn how to:
• auto-generate key dates
• set up alerts
• create bylaw-based reminders
• keep everything organized in one place

It immediately takes pressure off.

2. Practical help with nomination submissions

Bill 13 expanded how candidates can submit forms.
AI tools walk staff through how to:
• build a digital intake form
• automatically check if anything is missing
• organize candidate folders
• generate confirmation emails
• prepare summaries for the Chief Election Officer

Once trained, staff feel confident that nothing is slipping through the cracks.

3. Drafting statutory notices quickly and accurately

Notices are time-sensitive and legally required.
Training teaches staff how AI can:
• draft notices in seconds
• format for print, web, and social media
• align with the Local Government Act and Notice Bylaw

This cuts hours of repetitive rewriting.

4. Redacting nomination documents safely

New privacy rules require removing personal information before anything is published online.
AI can help staff:
• identify sensitive details
• apply clean redactions
• generate a public and internal version
• avoid accidental exposure

Good training shows teams exactly when and how to use the tool correctly.

5. Forecasting election budgets with more accuracy

AI tools can analyze past budgets and model 2026 costs.
Training shows staff how to:
• compare manual vs machine counts
• forecast staffing levels
• adjust for inflation
• build contingency

It’s a big relief for anyone responsible for budget planning.

6. Mail ballot workflows that are easier to manage

Mail ballots are now widely available, which increases volume.
AI can automate:
• tracking
• reconciliation
• drop-off locations
• secrecy sleeve instructions

Training covers when to trust AI and when to verify manually.

7. Updating bylaws without starting from scratch

With Bill 13 changes, many election bylaws need refreshing.
AI can help staff:
• compare the old bylaw to new requirements
• flag what needs updating
• create a clean draft for review

It saves days of line-by-line work.

Why training your team matters

AI is powerful, but only when people understand how to use it safely.

Training helps staff:
• learn where AI fits and where it doesn’t
• understand privacy boundaries
• apply BC legislation correctly
• build confidence using the tools
• reduce stress during the election cycle
• improve accuracy and consistency

Teams leave feeling prepared, not overwhelmed.

In other words, AI becomes a support system — not another thing to manage.

Helping election teams feel ready

I train election staff across Canada on how to use AI in a way that feels clear, safe, and grounded in legislation. The sessions focus on real workflows: notices, bylaws, budget planning, nomination forms, mail ballots, and timelines — not abstract theory.

The goal is simple:
give election teams practical tools that make their work easier and help them step into 2026 with confidence.

title: Copilot Gets a “Bye Copilot” Voice Command and Heads to Chrome: What It Means for Local Government
author: Daphne
excerpt: AI tools are becoming more natural to use every day, and Microsoft’s newest updates to Copilot are another small step in that direction. This week, Microsoft quietly added two features that will matter more than people realize, especially inside busy public sector environments. The first is a new “Bye Copilot” voice command in Windows 11. […]
content:
AI tools are becoming more natural to use every day, and Microsoft’s newest updates to Copilot are another small step in that direction. This week, Microsoft quietly added two features that will matter more than people realize, especially inside busy public sector environments.

The first is a new “Bye Copilot” voice command in Windows 11. You can now end a voice session simply by saying goodbye. No clicking, no searching for the close button, no awkward pauses. It is one of those tiny changes that nudges Copilot a little closer to feeling like a hands free digital assistant rather than a separate app you have to manage.

The second update is even bigger.

Microsoft is building a Copilot extension for Google Chrome, bringing Copilot chat and page summarization directly into the browser that most staff already use. For many local governments, this matters. People do not always work in Edge, and asking them to switch browsers just to use AI has been a barrier. With Copilot in Chrome, AI support can meet staff right where they already work.

Why This Matters for Local Government

These updates might seem small on the surface, but they address two very real challenges in municipalities.

1. Staff need AI that blends into existing workflows

Local government teams already juggle multiple systems, logins, and platforms. Adding another tool can feel overwhelming. A simple “Bye Copilot” command and seamless support in Chrome reduces friction. It makes AI feel less like a new system and more like a natural part of the computer.

2. Hands free support saves time

Whether staff are writing reports, researching bylaws, or reviewing lengthy documents, a hands free voice assistant can help keep work flowing. The less clicking and navigating required, the easier it becomes to stay focused.

3. Adoption grows when AI feels familiar

Most people are comfortable with their browser habits. By meeting users in Chrome, Copilot removes one of the biggest adoption barriers: unfamiliar software. When tools feel familiar, use increases naturally.

A Quiet Step Toward a More Supportive Workday

These updates signal a shift toward AI that gently integrates itself into daily work instead of demanding a new way of operating. It is AI that listens, supports, and now even says goodbye.

For local governments exploring AI adoption, these small design improvements matter. They help staff feel less intimidated and more supported, which is ultimately how digital transformation becomes real.

title: Why Local Governments Struggle to Adopt AI: The Power of Status Quo Bias
author: Daphne
excerpt: A recent article from McKinsey highlighted something every organization, especially in local government, eventually learns: the biggest obstacle to AI adoption isn’t the technology. It’s mindset. McKinsey shared the story of a large company that launched an ambitious training program to help employees use generative AI tools. The rollout seemed like a success. More than […]
content:
A recent article from McKinsey highlighted something every organization, especially in local government, eventually learns: the biggest obstacle to AI adoption isn’t the technology. It’s mindset.

McKinsey shared the story of a large company that launched an ambitious training program to help employees use generative AI tools. The rollout seemed like a success. More than 90% of participants rated the program highly, calling it helpful and informative.

But six weeks later, fewer than 10% of those employees were actually using AI in their daily work.

The problem wasn’t access. It wasn’t lack of training.
It was status quo bias — the natural human tendency to stick with familiar ways of working, even when better options exist.

The Cognitive Brakes on the AI Accelerator

Status quo bias is a psychological shortcut where people default to “how things have always been.” It feels safe, predictable, and less risky than change.

In McKinsey’s example, employees avoided using AI tools even when those tools could make their jobs easier and more enjoyable. Why? Because they overestimated the risks of change (“What if this replaces me?”) and underestimated the risks of staying the same (“What if my role becomes obsolete because I don’t evolve?”).

It’s a mindset that can quietly stall innovation in any sector — and it’s especially visible in local government.

How This Shows Up in Local Government

Municipal teams are not strangers to this pattern. Staff attend training sessions, download guides, and even agree that AI could reduce their workload — and then go back to the same processes and paperwork.

Not out of resistance or laziness, but because inertia is comfortable. The routines, approvals, and reporting structures that define government work create a sense of control. Trying something new, especially something that feels “too fast” or “too risky,” can trigger hesitation.

Yet the world outside the office walls is changing quickly. Residents expect faster communication, better access to services, and greater transparency. Standing still feels safe — but in reality, it’s the riskiest move of all.

Breaking Through the Bias: What Works

Overcoming the status quo bias takes more than training or policy. It requires reframing change as normal — not optional. Here are a few proven approaches:

1. Make the new way the default.
When people have to opt in to new tools, most won’t. Instead, make AI tools part of daily workflows — the starting point, not the exception.

2. Show, don’t tell.
Reports rarely inspire change. Demonstrations do. Let staff see AI in action — how it can summarize meeting notes, draft reports, or generate insights that save real time.

3. Celebrate the early adopters.
Highlight “super users” who try, fail, learn, and improve. Their success stories can shift culture faster than any memo.

4. Reframe the risk.
Staying the same isn’t safer. The real risk is falling behind while the rest of the world moves forward.

5. Lead by example.
Executives and department heads who use AI in their own work model the behavior and confidence others need to follow.

Turning Inertia Into Momentum

The McKinsey case study showed that once leadership began addressing AI adoption on a personal level — small team workshops, peer coaching, and visits to organizations already using AI — everything changed.

Employees stopped seeing AI as a disruption and started viewing it as the new normal.
Adoption soared.

That’s a powerful lesson for local governments: people embrace change when it feels safe, supported, and shared.

AI adoption isn’t just a tech rollout — it’s cultural reprogramming.

The Real Takeaway

Technology doesn’t transform organizations. People do.

AI tools can make work faster, smarter, and more creative — but only if they’re embraced consistently. For local governments, this means investing not just in software, but in training, leadership modeling, and everyday use.

The goal isn’t to convince everyone that AI matters — it’s to make it part of how work gets done. When new tools become the default and early adopters are celebrated, momentum follows naturally.

Because in the end, progress happens when the status quo starts feeling like the riskier choice.

title: Microsoft’s MAI Superintelligence Team: Building AI That Fits Like Your Own Snowboard
author: Daphne
excerpt: Microsoft recently announced the creation of its MAI Superintelligence Team, led by Mustafa Suleyman — the co-founder of DeepMind and one of the leading voices in responsible AI development. The goal of this new internal unit is to build next-generation AI models that reflect a “humanist” and value-driven approach. It’s a bold move in a […]
content:
Microsoft recently announced the creation of its MAI Superintelligence Team, led by Mustafa Suleyman — the co-founder of DeepMind and one of the leading voices in responsible AI development. The goal of this new internal unit is to build next-generation AI models that reflect a “humanist” and value-driven approach.

It’s a bold move in a race that has largely been defined by power, scale, and competition. Microsoft’s message stands out because it’s not just about building smarter AI — it’s about building AI that feels right.

The Snowboard Analogy: Why Building Your Own Matters

It reminds me of snowboarding.

You can rent a board for the day, and it’ll get you down the mountain just fine. But it’s never quite tuned to you — the feel is off, the balance isn’t perfect, and you can’t fully trust how it’s going to respond on every turn.

Then there’s riding your own board — one you’ve chosen, customized, and adjusted to match your style. You can feel the snow under your feet, anticipate the turns, and move with complete confidence. It’s yours.

Microsoft forming its own Superintelligence Team is a lot like that. After years of close collaboration with OpenAI, this new unit represents the company taking control of its own ride — shaping AI models that align with its principles, pace, and long-term vision.

Human-Centered AI: The Core of Microsoft’s “Humanist” Focus

Suleyman’s team is expected to focus on AI systems that prioritize human experience, not just performance. This includes building models that are safer, more transparent, and more aligned with real-world values — what Microsoft calls a humanist approach.

That matters because as AI grows more powerful, its influence will increasingly touch how people work, make decisions, and interact with information. Keeping humans at the center of that evolution is not a nice-to-have — it’s essential.

What This Means for Local Government

For local governments and public sector organizations, Microsoft’s announcement offers a useful lesson: technology works best when it’s designed around your own environment.

You can borrow systems or copy someone else’s approach, but real success comes when you build technology that fits your community’s values, workflows, and goals.

AI in local government should never be a one-size-fits-all solution. It should be tuned to reflect your people — your processes, your residents, and your priorities.

Just like a snowboard, when it fits right, everything flows better: communication, collaboration, and trust.

Beyond Smarter AI — Building Trusted AI

In the global race for superintelligence, Microsoft’s human-centered direction is refreshing. It acknowledges that the next phase of AI innovation isn’t about bigger models — it’s about better alignment.

The public sector can take the same approach. Build AI strategies that are not only powerful but also purposeful. Pair innovation with ethics. Balance efficiency with empathy.

Because the real test of technology isn’t how fast it moves — it’s how well it fits.

title: AI Transformation Is Like the Gym: Consistency Wins
author: Daphne
excerpt: According to McKinsey’s State of AI in 2025, 88% of organisations are now using AI in at least one area of their operations. Yet only 7% have successfully scaled it across their entire organization. Those numbers tell an important story: most organisations are trying AI — very few are truly transforming with it. And that […]
content:
According to McKinsey’s State of AI in 2025, 88% of organisations are now using AI in at least one area of their operations. Yet only 7% have successfully scaled it across their entire organization.

Those numbers tell an important story: most organisations are trying AI — very few are truly transforming with it.

And that difference often comes down to one simple thing: consistency.

Transformation Doesn’t Happen Once — It Happens Over Time

AI transformation is a lot like going to the gym. Signing up is easy. Showing up once feels great. But real progress only happens when you commit to coming back — again and again — and start building systems that make it part of your routine.

In local government, it’s tempting to treat AI as a single project — a pilot, a policy draft, or a one-off training session. But sustainable transformation requires small, ongoing steps that build confidence and create visible wins along the way.

Why Consistency Matters in AI Adoption

AI success stories in municipalities rarely start with massive budgets or full-scale strategies. They start with people — curious staff who try something small, make it work, and share the results. That consistency builds credibility and trust, which fuels momentum across departments.

Here’s what consistency looks like in action:

  • Appoint an AI Champion: Someone who experiments, learns, and advocates for practical use cases. Transformation needs a voice that makes AI real, not theoretical.

  • Start Small: Choose one process — like summarizing reports, drafting agendas, or automating data entry — and prove the value before scaling.

  • Show, Don’t Report: Don’t bury progress in memos or long summaries. Demonstrate success with visuals, quick before-and-after comparisons, or real staff stories.

  • Celebrate Wins: Momentum matters. Recognition turns skepticism into participation.

It’s not about perfection — it’s about showing up consistently and learning through practice.

The Role of Culture in AI Transformation

Technology will always evolve faster than culture. That’s why local governments need to focus just as much on people as they do on platforms.

Building AI literacy, encouraging curiosity, and removing the fear of failure create an environment where innovation becomes routine. When staff feel supported to explore and experiment, AI naturally becomes part of the organizational fabric.

Like fitness, the results of consistent effort don’t show overnight — but they compound over time.

From Pilot to Progress

The McKinsey study makes one thing clear: almost everyone is using AI, but very few are getting full value from it. Bridging that gap means replacing one-time adoption with repeatable, team-driven effort.

For local governments, that could mean:

  • Using AI to create consistent monthly reports instead of ad-hoc summaries.

  • Applying AI to automate recurring administrative tasks.

  • Building templates and workflows that grow with staff confidence.

Transformation happens not when you buy the tools, but when you build the habits.

title: The Real Challenge of AI in Local Government: Change Management
author: Daphne
excerpt: McKinsey’s recent report, The State of AI in 2025, reveals just how far organisations have come in adopting artificial intelligence — and how far they still need to go. According to the study, nearly nine out of ten organisations now use AI in at least one business function. Yet most still struggle to scale it […]
content:
McKinsey’s recent report, The State of AI in 2025, reveals just how far organisations have come in adopting artificial intelligence — and how far they still need to go.

According to the study, nearly nine out of ten organisations now use AI in at least one business function. Yet most still struggle to scale it into enterprise-level value. The technology is here, the awareness is high, but the deep transformation — the kind that changes how teams work and decisions are made — is still out of reach for many.

And that’s because the biggest challenge with AI isn’t the technology itself.
It’s change.

A Lesson from Moving to Japan

When I moved to Japan, everything changed at once, the language, the culture, the size of my apartment, even what and when I ate. It wasn’t just about learning new things; it was about rethinking how I lived.

That’s exactly what AI transformation feels like for many organisations, especially in local government. It’s not about plugging in a new tool. It’s about reshaping how people communicate, collaborate, and make decisions. The entire system — not just the software — has to adapt.

AI adoption without cultural and structural change is like moving to Japan and insisting on living exactly as you did before. You can, technically, but you’ll miss most of what makes it worth it.

Adoption Is Easy. Transformation Takes Intention.

Most municipalities have started exploring AI in small ways — automating reports, summarising emails, or improving workflows. Those pilot projects are important, but they’re just the first step.

To unlock true value, local governments need to:

  • Rethink processes: Don’t just automate; redesign how information moves across departments.

  • Invest in people: Training, communication, and clear roles turn AI from a tool into a teammate.

  • Build governance early: Set policies for transparency, data management, and ethical use before scaling up.

  • Lead with empathy: Successful digital transformation starts with listening to staff fears, community concerns, and the realities of daily operations.

Technology can amplify capacity, but people determine impact.

The Future of AI in Local Government

McKinsey’s findings reinforce what many municipal leaders already know: AI is everywhere, but transformation is uneven. For local governments, the next phase isn’t about trying new AI tools, it’s about embedding them into daily practice, guided by policy, training, and strong leadership.

The municipalities that succeed won’t be the ones that adopt AI first.
They’ll be the ones that adapt best.

If procurement was as simple as “buy the thing,” we’d all be home before dinner.

But anyone who’s ever worked in local government knows better. Between policy hoops, budget caps, and the timeless mystery of who actually approves this, most of us are one RFP away from needing another coffee.

The truth is, procurement is one of the most powerful levers local governments have for saving money and improving service delivery — yet it’s also one of the most misunderstood and overcomplicated parts of public administration.

Fortunately, the landscape is changing.

Pooling Power: Why Canoe Procurement Group Matters

For Canadian municipalities, partnerships like the Canoe Procurement Group of Canada are quietly reshaping how procurement gets done. By pooling municipal buying power, Canoe helps communities large and small access competitive pricing, trusted suppliers, and the kind of efficiency that would make any finance officer smile.

Instead of reinventing the wheel (and the RFP) every time, Canoe lets local governments focus on outcomes — not paperwork. That’s a big deal when staff capacity is already stretched thin and expectations keep climbing.

Procurement Doesn’t Have to Be Painful

A recent McKinsey report on Procurement Efficiency: A Modern Strategy for State and Local Leaders found that governments across North America are saving millions by combining traditional procurement best practices with AI-powered tools.

The formula is surprisingly simple:

  • Know your spend. Use data analytics to understand where every dollar goes.
  • Benchmark and collaborate. Compare pricing and performance with peers.
  • Build supplier relationships. The goal isn’t just cost savings — it’s reliability.
  • Add AI into the mix. Let technology handle the repetitive work, from RFP drafting to invoice audits, so people can focus on strategy.

AI can flag maverick spending, predict demand, analyze contracts, and even help staff write or review proposals faster. It doesn’t replace people — it gives them time back.

The Right Stuff, at the Right Time, in the Right Way

Procurement is no longer just about compliance — it’s about strategic value. When local governments use AI tools and cooperative models like Canoe together, they can deliver the right products and services at the right price, with less delay and more transparency.

That means fewer bottlenecks, cleaner audit trails, and happier residents. And let’s be honest — fewer procurement headaches for staff, too.

The Future of Local Government Procurement

Maybe the next big innovation in local government isn’t another policy review or software pilot. Maybe it’s a procurement team that’s caffeinated, confident, and has AI on speed dial.

When we stop treating procurement like a bureaucratic chore and start managing it like a strategic opportunity, we don’t just “buy the thing” — we buy time, trust, and efficiency.

And that’s something worth investing in.

title: When AI Becomes a Teammate (Not Just a Tool)
author: Daphne
excerpt: There’s a difference between using AI and actually working with it. Across Canada, local governments are testing out new AI tools, for everything from budgeting to records management, but most of the conversation still circles around the tech itself. What’s really interesting, though, is what happens when staff start shaping how those tools fit their […]
content:
There’s a difference between using AI and actually working with it.

Across Canada, local governments are testing out new AI tools, for everything from budgeting to records management, but most of the conversation still circles around the tech itself. What’s really interesting, though, is what happens when staff start shaping how those tools fit their work, not the other way around.

McKinsey recently released an article called Reconfiguring Work: Change Management in the Age of Gen AI, and it nails a truth we’re all starting to feel: piloting AI is easy, but creating value is the hard part.

Because AI isn’t just another system upgrade. It’s a complete shift in how we think about work.

What This Looks Like in Local Government

Imagine this:

A finance officer asks AI to draft a variance report instead of spending half a day wrestling with spreadsheets.

A clerk finds a bylaw in seconds instead of digging through folders.

A planner summarizes new legislation in a few clicks rather than flipping through binders.

None of that replaces people. It just gives them more time to do the meaningful work, the part that connects to residents, drives policy, and actually makes the community stronger.

That’s the real potential of AI in local government: capacity without burnout.

Change Management Isn’t What It Used to Be

Traditionally, “change management” meant new software, new forms, and a long training schedule that nobody looked forward to.

In the age of AI, it’s different. It’s not a rollout — it’s a conversation.

It’s about trust, curiosity, and co-creation.

We need to help staff experiment, question, and reshape how things get done. And we have to build space for that learning curve. Not everyone will adapt at the same pace, and that’s okay.

The best transformations happen when people are part of the process, not just on the receiving end of it.

Finding Your North Star

 

Every municipality has its own version of a North Star, that clear direction that keeps the team aligned and inspired. When it comes to AI, that North Star shouldn’t be about the technology at all. It should be about outcomes.

Ask:

What’s the biggest pain point we want to fix?

What could staff do more of if AI took the busywork off their plates?

How will this make our residents’ experience better?

That’s where the value is.

The Human Side of AI

At Catch the Beat, we help local governments reimagine how AI fits into their daily operations, not to replace people, but to make their jobs easier, faster, and a little more enjoyable.

If your community is ready to find its AI North Star, reach out to Daphne at Catch the Beat. She’ll help you uncover where AI can truly make a difference, starting with the people who make your municipality run every day.

Because the future of work in local government isn’t about machines.

It’s about people who know how to use them well.

title: Aardvark and the Future of Cybersecurity in Local Government
author: Daphne
excerpt: Every municipality is only as strong as the trust it protects. OpenAI has just introduced Aardvark, an AI security agent built to think like a researcher. The system is designed to scan, detect, and fix code vulnerabilities automatically, spotting threats before they can become serious breaches. It’s one of the most promising developments in AI-powered […]
content:
Every municipality is only as strong as the trust it protects.


OpenAI has just introduced Aardvark, an AI security agent built to think like a researcher. The system is designed to scan, detect, and fix code vulnerabilities automatically, spotting threats before they can become serious breaches. It’s one of the most promising developments in AI-powered cybersecurity and could have major implications for how local governments protect sensitive data.

What Is Aardvark?

Aardvark is part of OpenAI’s new generation of agentic AI systems — models that can analyze, reason, and act independently within defined boundaries. In this case, Aardvark acts as a digital security researcher, running continuous vulnerability checks, identifying weaknesses in software, and even applying patches when approved.

Why this matters: traditional security tools rely on human input and scheduled scans. Aardvark introduces a proactive, always-on layer of defense, one that can evolve alongside the threats it monitors.

Why Cybersecurity Matters for Local Government

Local governments are uniquely vulnerable to cyberattacks. They manage resident records, payment systems, and critical infrastructure, all of which are prime targets for phishing, ransomware, and data breaches. Yet most municipalities face resource limitations that make continuous monitoring a challenge.

A tool like Aardvark could help fill that gap by:

  • Detecting vulnerabilities early before bad actors exploit them.
  • Automating repetitive security tasks, freeing IT staff to focus on higher-level strategy.
  • Providing real-time monitoring to strengthen overall system resilience.
  • Supporting compliance with data protection standards through documented audit trails.

This kind of autonomous security support could change how local governments manage digital risk, not just reacting to incidents, but preventing them altogether.

Governance in the Age of Autonomous AI

Of course, Aardvark’s power also introduces new questions about governance and accountability.

When AI can detect and fix vulnerabilities on its own, who approves those changes? How do municipalities ensure that actions taken by autonomous systems align with their cybersecurity and privacy policies?

This is where strong AI governance frameworks become critical. Local governments will need clear policies outlining:

  • What types of actions AI systems are authorized to perform.
  • How automated fixes are logged and reviewed.
  • Who remains accountable for final decisions and security compliance.

The goal isn’t to hand over control, it’s to strengthen human oversight with faster, smarter tools.

Hardening Policies as Fast as Code

Cybersecurity isn’t just about defending systems; it’s about maintaining public trust. When residents share information online, they expect it to be handled securely and transparently.

AI agents like Aardvark can help achieve that, but they also remind us that technology moves faster than policy. As local governments modernize, policies around AI use, data storage, and risk management must evolve just as quickly.

The question isn’t just how to harden our code. It’s how to harden our governance frameworks so technology works for, not around, the people we serve.

It means your finance team can ask Copilot to summarize budget discussions right inside a shared group chat. Local government work depends on collaboration. Finance, operations, planning, communications — every department needs access to the same information at the right time. Yet so much staff time is spent chasing documents, rewriting reports, or consolidating updates from different platforms.

For municipalities, this can translate into smoother council meeting prep, faster policy development, and more cohesive cross-departmental planning.

The Future of Teamwork in Local Government

This new evolution of Copilot represents a major step toward AI-powered collaboration in public service. As municipalities continue to modernize, tools like Copilot will help staff focus on strategy, communication, and service delivery — while the AI handles routine organization and data gathering.

Microsoft has just rolled out a major Windows 11 update, and it’s one of the most powerful steps yet toward everyday AI integration. The update gives every PC voice, vision, and “agentic” AI powers through Microsoft Copilot, expanding the way users interact with their computers and making work more intuitive than ever.

For local governments, where efficiency and communication are key, this is more than a technical upgrade. It’s a glimpse of how AI could soon assist staff across departments, streamline workflows, and support better service delivery to residents.

What’s New in Windows 11 with Copilot

The latest Windows 11 release introduces several next-generation features:

1. “Hey Copilot” Voice Activation

Users can now activate Microsoft Copilot hands-free with a simple voice command — “Hey Copilot.” This makes it easier for staff to work while multitasking, whether they’re updating a report, checking schedules, or managing records.

2. Copilot Vision (Now Global)

Copilot Vision gives your PC the ability to interpret what it “sees.” By using your device’s camera and screen content, Copilot can understand visual context — such as identifying charts, analyzing documents, or assisting with accessibility features.

3. Copilot Actions (Agentic AI)

Perhaps the biggest leap forward, Copilot Actions allows the AI to act on your behalf. This “agentic” capability means Copilot can take action in supported applications — such as creating emails, organizing files, or launching workflows — based on context and instructions.

In short, Windows 11 has gone from a tool you use to a digital assistant that works alongside you.

Why This Matters for Local Government

Municipal teams rely on coordination, communication, and documentation. Staff handle everything from council reports and budgeting to emergency management and citizen correspondence, often under time pressure and with limited capacity.

The new Windows 11 update could enhance how local government staff work in several ways:

  • Hands-free productivity: Voice-activated AI could support operations staff, planners, or managers who need to work across multiple screens or environments.
  • Smarter document management: Copilot Vision could recognize forms, data tables, or images in reports and assist in summarizing or formatting them.
  • Task automation: Copilot Actions could trigger follow-up emails, schedule reminders, or generate draft documents — saving hours of manual effort.
  • Accessibility improvements: Voice and vision AI features make municipal workplaces more inclusive by supporting different working styles and accessibility needs.

Balancing Innovation with Responsibility

Of course, with every new capability comes a conversation about governance and privacy. Agentic AI — systems that can act on behalf of users — must be deployed thoughtfully, especially in public sector environments where data security, accountability, and transparency are essential.

Municipal IT teams will need to establish clear parameters for what Copilot can and cannot do, ensuring its use aligns with privacy policies, records management standards, and ethical AI guidelines.

AI should make government work easier — not risk the trust that residents place in their local institutions.

The Takeaway

The Windows 11 AI update isn’t just about convenience; it’s about redefining the relationship between people and technology. By combining voice, vision, and action, Microsoft Copilot is evolving into a true partner in productivity — one that can help municipalities deliver faster, smarter, and more responsive public service.

It might sound futuristic, but it’s here today.

And while your PC may not quite have elephant-level memory yet, it’s definitely learning to listen, see, and act, making everyday work in local government a little lighter and a lot smarter.

Excel has always been the backbone of financial analysis. From municipal budget forecasts to capital project tracking, finance professionals in local government rely on spreadsheets to manage millions in public funds. The challenge has always been that the full power of Excel is available only to expert users. Advanced formulas, macros, and data modeling often require years of experience.

This is where Agent Mode in Excel changes everything.

What is Agent Mode in Excel?

Agent Mode is Microsoft’s latest innovation for Excel, built with OpenAI’s most advanced reasoning models. Unlike basic Copilot assistance, Agent Mode can “speak Excel” natively. It does not just generate outputs — it evaluates results, fixes issues, and iterates until the outcome is verified.

Think of it as handing work off to an Excel expert who knows exactly how to build formulas, create models, and deliver polished results, while you remain in control to steer and guide.

For finance teams in local government, this means advanced financial modeling is no longer restricted to Excel power users. The tool democratizes access, allowing anyone in your department to generate expert-level analysis.

 

Why Agent Mode Matters for Local Government Finance

Municipal budgets are complex. Finance professionals juggle operating budgets, capital project funding, debt management, taxation, grants, and utility billing. Errors or inefficiencies in financial models can lead to delays in council reporting, compliance issues, or poor financial planning.

Agent Mode helps solve these challenges by:

  • Automating complex modeling: No need to memorize advanced functions or build macros from scratch.

  • Validating accuracy: Agent Mode checks its own outputs, fixing issues automatically to ensure reliability.

  • Accelerating analysis: From multi-year budget variance reports to loan repayment schedules, tasks that take hours can now be done in minutes.

  • Supporting decision-making: By turning raw numbers into clear visual insights, Agent Mode helps finance officers communicate results effectively to council and residents.

How Agent Mode Performs

Microsoft tested Agent Mode with SpreadsheetBench, which measures how AI performs on common spreadsheet tasks. Agent Mode in Excel achieved an accuracy rate of 57.2 percent — outperforming other benchmarked models like Claude and Shortcut. While not perfect, the ability to validate and iterate means it can continually refine outputs until the results are correct.

Real Prompts for Local Government Finance

Here are a few practical examples of how finance professionals in municipalities could use Agent Mode:

  1. Financial Analysis Prompt

    “Create a monthly financial close report for the City’s Recreation Department, including a breakdown of user fees, facility rentals, and program revenues. Show sequential and year-over-year growth with standard municipal reporting formats.”

  2. Loan Calculator Prompt

    “Build a loan calculator for a capital project borrowing of $5 million at 4 percent over 20 years. Generate a repayment schedule with principal, interest, and remaining balance. Present in a table for council reporting.”

  3. Budget Forecasting Prompt

    “Prepare a five-year budget forecast for utility billing revenues. Include best case, worst case, and most likely scenarios. Apply conditional formatting to highlight variances over 10 percent.”

  4. Grant Tracking Prompt

    “Create a grant funding tracker that monitors approved, pending, and applied-for grants by department. Include summary totals and a dashboard view with charts for council updates.”

The Future of Financial Work in Local Government

By 2035, the way society communicates with technology is expected to change dramatically. For local government finance teams, adopting AI-powered tools like Agent Mode is no longer optional — it is essential for staying efficient, accurate, and transparent.

Agent Mode does not replace the expertise of finance professionals. Instead, it acts as a digital assistant that takes care of the heavy lifting, allowing staff to focus on strategic analysis and decision-making.

For municipal CFOs, finance managers, and budget analysts, this is a powerful shift. Advanced modeling is no longer reserved for Excel specialists — it is accessible to everyone on the team.

Microsoft has just introduced a new feature called Copilot Portraits — giving its AI assistant a human-like face. Announced by Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman on X, the update responds to feedback from users who said they would feel more comfortable talking to a face when using voice.

The Portraits feature allows users to select from a set of stylized avatars that pair with voices, making verbal conversations with the chatbot feel more natural compared to text-based interactions. These avatars are not photorealistic but are designed with human-like expressions, head movements, and lip-sync, powered by Microsoft’s advanced VASA-1 technology.

This is the latest move in Microsoft’s efforts to make Copilot more approachable. Earlier this year, the company rolled out Copilot Appearances, which gave the assistant animated characters. Portraits takes this further by using more human-like visuals while maintaining safety measures such as clear indicators that users are interacting with AI, limited availability, and restrictions to adults 18 and over.

Why This Matters for Local Government

Local government staff are often stretched thin, managing heavy workloads of reports, agendas, minutes, and resident communications. While AI tools like Copilot can significantly reduce administrative burdens, the real challenge is adoption. Many staff members and residents hesitate to engage with AI because it feels cold, unfamiliar, or intimidating.

By giving Copilot a human-like face, Microsoft is lowering that barrier. A friendly avatar makes the technology feel more like a helpful assistant and less like a faceless machine. For municipalities, this can increase staff comfort, improve training outcomes, and encourage wider use of AI tools to handle time-consuming tasks.

The Balance Between AI and Human Connection

Even with features like Portraits, it is important to remember that AI will never replace the human connection at the heart of local government. Council members, administrators, and staff play an irreplaceable role in building trust and serving communities. What AI can do is lighten the administrative load, giving staff more time to focus on people.

Portraits is not just a fun experiment — it is part of a broader shift toward making AI more human-centered, accessible, and safe. For local governments exploring AI implementation, this signals an important lesson: success is not just about the technology itself, but about how approachable and usable it feels for the people who rely on it.

Moving Forward

As Microsoft continues to refine Copilot with features like Portraits, local governments have an opportunity to rethink how AI is introduced to staff and residents. Adoption will always be easier when the technology feels natural and welcoming.

The future of AI in municipalities is not about replacing human interaction. It is about creating more space for it. Features like Portraits can help bridge the gap between advanced AI and the people it is meant to serve — ensuring that technology works with communities, not against them.

title: Microsoft 365 Copilot App to Be Auto-Installed on Windows PCs: What It Means for Users and Teams
author: Daphne
excerpt: Starting in October 2025, Microsoft will take another big step in its AI journey. content:
Starting in October 2025, Microsoft will take another big step in its AI journey. Devices that already have Microsoft 365 desktop apps — such as Word, Excel, and PowerPoint — will automatically receive the Microsoft 365 Copilot app. For personal users, there will be no option to opt out. For enterprise environments, administrators will have some level of control.

This shift signals more than just another software update. It shows how quickly artificial intelligence is moving from an optional add-on to a core part of everyday work tools.

Why Microsoft Is Making This Move

Microsoft has been positioning Copilot as the future of productivity. By embedding AI directly into the tools that people already use daily, the company reduces the friction of adoption. Instead of downloading or enabling AI, it is simply there — ready to summarize a document, generate a draft, organize meeting notes, or analyze a spreadsheet.

This automatic installation ensures that Copilot is available at scale, accelerating how quickly organizations and individuals experience its benefits.

Benefits of Auto-Installation

The decision to make Copilot standard has clear advantages:

  • Mainstream adoption: AI becomes as normal as Word or Outlook.
  • Capacity gains: Teams can shift routine work to Copilot, freeing up people for more strategic tasks.
  • Consistency: With AI available to everyone, collaboration improves because all team members can access the same tools.
  • Integration: Copilot draws on Microsoft Graph to work across Teams, SharePoint, Outlook, and other apps, making workflows smoother.

For organizations focused on reducing burnout and increasing efficiency, this could be a turning point.

Concerns About User Choice

Of course, there are also concerns. Some personal users may feel uneasy about software being installed without the option to decline. Questions around user choice, software clutter, and governance will need to be addressed.

In enterprise environments, IT administrators will play a key role in managing rollout, setting guardrails, and training staff so that Copilot enhances productivity without causing confusion.

A Bigger Trend: AI as Default

The bigger story here is that AI is no longer positioned as an experiment. It is becoming a default part of the digital workplace. Just as email and spreadsheets were once “new tools” that became essential, Copilot is on its way to being standard.

This move shows that Microsoft believes AI is not only here to stay but should be embedded in the daily fabric of work.

The automatic installation of Microsoft 365 Copilot may spark debate, but it also marks a milestone. AI is shifting from something you “try” to something you “use” — part of the basic toolkit for modern work.

For individuals, it is about adapting to a new normal. For organizations, it is about seizing the opportunity to increase capacity, improve collaboration, and reduce burnout.

The future of work is not just about adding AI on top of old tools. It is about building AI into the very foundation of how we work.

title: AI Joins the Team: Collaborative Agents in Microsoft 365 Copilot
author: Daphne

content:
Artificial intelligence has long been viewed as a personal assistant. It drafts your emails, summarizes documents, and organizes your schedule. But work has always been a team sport. The real transformation comes when AI stops working only for individuals and starts supporting entire groups.

Microsoft has taken a bold step in that direction with the release of collaborative AI agents in Microsoft 365 Copilot. These new agents are designed to function like digital teammates, helping groups coordinate, communicate, and execute with greater clarity and less stress.

Collaborative agents are purpose-built AI tools embedded directly into Microsoft Teams, SharePoint, and Viva Engage. Unlike traditional assistants, they do not just respond to one person’s request. Instead, they act as active participants in team projects, meetings, and communities.

Imagine them as colleagues who never forget a detail, keep track of every conversation, and make sure decisions are followed through. They bring context from Microsoft Graph and operate with the same enterprise-grade security and compliance standards as the rest of Microsoft 365.

How They Work in Everyday Scenarios

Here is how collaborative AI agents enhance different parts of teamwork:

  • In Teams: An agent can summarize conversations, draft project plans, and assign follow-ups. For example, a dedicated channel for a product launch might include an agent that keeps all discussions and tasks on track.
  • In Meetings: The Facilitator agent prepares agendas, takes notes, organizes discussions, captures decisions, and turns them into action items with clear accountability. It can even rearrange the agenda or set a meeting timer at the team’s request.
  • In SharePoint: The Knowledge Agent keeps files tagged, organized, and up to date. When someone asks Copilot for the final version of a document, it delivers the authoritative source with citations.
  • In Viva Engage: A Community Agent answers common questions, manages discussions, and ensures communication stays accurate and engaging.

Together, these agents make sure every stage of a project—from planning and execution to communication—runs smoothly.

Why This Matters for Teams

For too long, AI has focused on boosting individual productivity. These new agents shift the focus to team collaboration. By managing repetitive tasks, clarifying information, and keeping projects aligned, AI helps reduce the noise that often slows down teamwork.

The result is more capacity for people to focus on strategy, problem-solving, and creative contributions. It also helps avoid burnout by removing the burden of constant tracking and follow-up.

A Smarter Way to Work Together

Microsoft 365 Copilot’s collaborative agents are now available in public preview. The Facilitator agent for Teams meetings is generally available, meaning organizations can begin experiencing the benefits right away.

This is not just an upgrade to productivity software. It is a shift in how teams can work together. AI is stepping into the role of a teammate, making collaboration smoother, more transparent, and more efficient.

Final Thought

The future of work is not just about doing more with less. It is about creating healthier, more effective teams where people can focus on the work that truly matters. With AI as a teammate, collaboration becomes smarter, projects move faster, and burnout is reduced.

AI is not replacing teamwork. It is reimagining it.

Studies show that when people lean too heavily on AI, their brains can switch off a little. Skills like problem-solving and writing may weaken if AI is always doing the work. This is sometimes called “cognitive debt.”

That doesn’t mean we should avoid AI. It means we should pair AI with learning safeguards. For example, local government staff might draft with AI, then review and refine the work themselves. This keeps skills sharp while still reaping the time savings. Used well, AI can actually increase capacity by reducing burnout, giving staff more energy to focus on creative and strategic thinking.

Experts predict that by 2035, AI will reshape how people think, feel, and interact. That can sound daunting, but it also opens opportunities. AI can improve public engagement, simplify access to services, and reduce barriers for residents who may struggle with traditional systems.

The Bottom Line

Sustainability isn’t just about energy. It’s also about people, skills, and long-term balance. AI has the power to increase capacity, reduce burnout, and help communities do more with less — but only if we adopt it responsibly.

AI is not the enemy of sustainability. Done right, it can be one of the strongest tools we have to protect our planet, elevate our people, and build thriving communities.

title: How AI Is Transforming Emergency Management in Canadian Municipalities
author: Daphne
excerpt: When an emergency strikes, every second counts. Whether it’s a wildfire, flood, or community-wide power outage, the ability to respond quickly and effectively can mean the difference between disruption and disaster. Traditionally, emergency management plans have lived in binders, PDFs, or static documents that outline who does what when things go wrong. Useful? Yes. But […]
content:
When an emergency strikes, every second counts. Whether it’s a wildfire, flood, or community-wide power outage, the ability to respond quickly and effectively can mean the difference between disruption and disaster.

Traditionally, emergency management plans have lived in binders, PDFs, or static documents that outline who does what when things go wrong. Useful? Yes. But fast-moving? Not always.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing that reality. By digitising and supercharging these plans, municipalities across Canada can respond with speed, precision, and confidence.

From Static Plans to Living Systems

AI doesn’t replace the expertise of emergency managers — it amplifies it. Instead of flipping through manuals or relying solely on human recall in the heat of a crisis, AI can step in as a responsive, dynamic partner.

Here’s what an AI-enabled emergency plan can do:

  • Automated alerts and notifications: Ensure the right people get the right information at the right time.

  • Real-time incident summarisation: Condense unfolding events into actionable insights for leaders.

  • Checklist automation and role guidance: Keep every team member focused on their specific tasks during stressful moments.

  • Training and simulation: Run realistic exercises that prepare staff for the unexpected.

  • Post-incident debriefing: Use data-driven insights to learn and adapt after each event.

  • Multilingual and accessible communication: Share updates with all residents, regardless of language or ability.

  • Risk pattern recognition: Spot warning signs early to prevent small issues from escalating.

Why This Matters for Canadian Municipalities

Canada’s municipalities face mounting challenges: climate-driven natural disasters, aging infrastructure, and staffing shortages. Communities need to do more with less, all while keeping residents informed and safe.

By weaving AI into emergency management, local governments can:

  • Cut response times and reduce confusion.

  • Increase transparency and accessibility for diverse populations.

  • Build trust by demonstrating preparedness and professionalism.

  • Improve resilience by learning from data after each incident.

The result is an emergency management system that isn’t just a plan on paper — it’s a living, adaptive tool that grows stronger with every use.

A Force Multiplier, Not a Replacement

It’s important to remember: AI is not here to replace people. The judgment, ethics, and leadership of trained professionals remain at the core of every effective response.

What AI does is free those professionals from repetitive or manual tasks, giving them more time and energy to focus on critical decisions and leadership. In that sense, AI is a force multiplier — it takes the expertise already in place and makes it faster, sharper, and more scalable.

Building Safer, Smarter Communities

Emergency management will always depend on people — their experience, calm under pressure, and ability to adapt. But with AI in the toolbox, Canadian municipalities can move from reactive to proactive, from static to dynamic, and from “good enough” to truly prepared.

In an era where risks are rising, residents deserve nothing less.

title: How to Write an AI Policy for Local Government:
author: Daphne
excerpt: 8 Key Considerations As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes a regular part of daily operations in local government, the need for clear and practical AI policies has never been more urgent. Municipalities, regional districts, and public sector teams across Canada are already experimenting with tools like ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot—but the policies to guide that use […]
content:
8 Key Considerations

As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes a regular part of daily operations in local government, the need for clear and practical AI policies has never been more urgent. Municipalities, regional districts, and public sector teams across Canada are already experimenting with tools like ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot—but the policies to guide that use are still catching up.

So where should you start?

Whether you’re in communications, finance, planning, or IT, these eight key considerations will help you craft an AI policy that is ethical, effective, and future-proof—without overwhelming your team or burying operations in red tape.

1. Clarity of Purpose

Before anything else, ask:

Why is AI being used?

What specific problems is it solving or supporting? This helps ensure your AI policy isn’t just a checkbox but is tied to real operational goals—like reducing administrative workload, improving resident services, or streamlining reporting.

Tip: Keep this section jargon-free. Municipal employees and the public should clearly understand the “why.”

2. Principles Over Platforms

Avoid naming specific platforms like ChatGPT or Copilot in your policy. Focus instead on the intent, function, and outcomes of AI use. Technologies will change, but principles—such as accountability, accuracy, and accessibility—can stand the test of time.

Example: Say “generative AI may be used for draft content creation” instead of naming a specific product.

3. Transparency Without Overload

Yes, residents and staff deserve to know when AI is being used—especially in public-facing services. But avoid creating a disclosure burden that slows down your operations.

Be open, but also practical.

Disclose when it matters, and build trust through consistent communication.

4. Human Accountability

AI can assist—but it should never replace human oversight.

Your policy should clearly define who is responsible for reviewing, approving, or acting on AI-supported outputs.

Make it obvious that people remain in control. AI doesn’t make final decisions—humans do.

5. Privacy, Security, and Data Ethics

Canadian municipalities must follow provincial and federal legislation, including FIPPA, PIPEDA, and emerging AI governance frameworks. Your AI policy should cover:

  • How data is collected, stored, and used

  • Whether the data is anonymized or sensitive

  • Who has access and how it’s protected

Data ethics should be part of every conversation—not just a legal checkmark.

6. Bias and Fairness

AI systems are only as unbiased as the data they’re trained on. Your policy should acknowledge the potential for algorithmic bias and include:

  • A commitment to identifying and mitigating bias

  • Clear review and correction processes

Equity in service delivery matters—especially in small communities and Indigenous partnerships.

7. Training and Literacy

AI is only as effective as the people using it.

Ensure your policy includes ongoing staff training, from front-line workers to senior leaders. Build confidence and competence across departments to ensure ethical, productive use.

Consider hosting AI Literacy Workshops tailored for municipal staff, and revisit training as tools evolve.

8. Review and Evolution

AI is evolving rapidly—your policy should too.

Set a regular review schedule (annually or bi-annually) and make updates part of your policy lifecycle.

Remember: the goal isn’t perfection. It’s adaptability.

Final Thoughts: Why AI Policy Matters for Canadian Municipalities

From Prince Edward Island to British Columbia, local governments are stepping into the world of AI. But without a policy in place, your municipality may be vulnerable to reputational risk, inefficiencies, or even legal exposure.

A well-written AI policy ensures your team uses AI confidently, ethically, and in line with Canadian laws.
